item.title: 视频世界模型记不住，代码生成的世界又没有质感：A Mesh to Remember 用网格当外观记忆 ｜ A Mesh to Remember: Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds
item.description:
一句话：显式 3D 世界的几何与状态「天生持久」，但外观离照片级差得远。

要点：

  • 两条路线的优劣被摆得很清楚：**视频世界模型**能合成照片级的观测，但在长时间交互中**难以保持一致**；而 **coding agent 与 text-to-3D** 生成的是显式 3D 世界，其**几何与状态「由构造本身」持久**，但外观远不如照片真实
  • 已有折中做法是把这类显式世界渲成**粗糙代理**去引导视频模型，但代理只承接结构、不承接外观
  • 这篇因此把**网格当作外观记忆**：让持久的东西从「几何与状态」扩展到「外观」，从而在长交互中把看过的样子留下来

为什么值得看：这是「状态外置」主线最关键的下一步：前面几期解决的都是几何与状态的持久（Evoke、PanoEvo、Lyris、WM^MLLM），但**外观一直要靠模型的上下文记**。把网格接成外观记忆，等于把「长什么样」也纳入可持久的结构。

中文摘要：视频世界模型能针对用户动作合成照片级的观测，但在长时间交互中很难保持一致；相对地，coding agent 与 text-to-3D 模型生成的是显式 3D 世界，其几何与状态「由构造本身」天然持久，可外观离照片级真实还差得远。近期方法把两者结合：把这类显式世界渲染成粗糙代理，再用它引导视频模型——但代理只承接结构与运动，不承接外观。这篇因此提出把网格作为外观记忆，让持久化的对象从「几何与状态」扩展到「外观」，使长时间交互中已经出现过的样子不再依赖生成器的上下文窗口来维持。对正在做「引擎出代理、模型出画面」这条链路的团队，这是把记忆补全的下一步。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

A Mesh to Remember:
Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds

Abstract

Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object’s frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).

1 Introduction

Interactive virtual worlds are essential for applications in gaming, embodied AI, and closed-loop simulation. These use cases require both photorealistic rendering and persistent world state: a door opened by one agent should remain open when another walks by, and the room behind it should look the same each time it is opened (Fig.1). In recent years, two paradigms have emerged that promise to build such worlds automatically: video world models and 3D world generators.

Video world models synthesize observations in response to user actions, from game worlds [4, 80, 27] to photorealistic scenes [27, 63, 1], and increasingly for multiple players [20, 70, 87, 30, 47, 34]. Despite this progress, these models must infer both how the world evolves and how it looks from their own past observations, and errors in either can accumulate over long interactions. Memory mechanisms that retrieve past frames or their cached features, or maintain 3D caches, extend the history a model can draw upon and improve consistency when regions are revisited [93, 76, 102, 89, 106, 71]. However, they tie memory to where content was observed, which no longer holds once the world changes. When an object is carried across a room, its remembered appearance stays where the object used to be, and the model must reinvent it.

3D world generators instead create the world itself, from explorable scenes that text-to-3D models produce given a single prompt [37, 78] to entire dynamic worlds that coding agents write as programs, with articulated furniture [83] and rules for how objects move [13]. As these worlds are explicit, their geometry and state persist by construction, and every agent observes the same world. However, they fall short of photorealism, as even the most sophisticated real-time game renderings remain distinguishable from real imagery [69].

Instead of treating these paradigms as standalone alternatives, recent methods combine their complementary strengths: the explicit world maintains persistent geometry and state, while a video model renders coarse proxies of it (geometry or semantic layouts) into realistic observations [36, 13, 15, 55, 44, 21]. Since these proxies only specify what is where, the renderer must invent the world’s appearance as it is explored, and keep it consistent as agents revisit regions, move objects, and encounter surfaces that others have already seen. A natural place to keep this appearance is the explicit world itself. Existing methods paint generated colors back onto its geometry [68, 28, 57, 21], but colors are a lossy copy of what the renderer generated and must be re-rendered and re-encoded at every step, which is slow and accumulates errors (Tab.4).

We instead treat the mesh as an address. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies the surface behind every pixel in every view, even after that surface has moved. We therefore store the renderer’s own features on the surfaces they depict as they are generated, and attend to them whenever those surfaces reappear. This memory has three benefits. First, as memory is indexed by surface instead of time, storage follows scene coverage and observations remain addressable long after leaving the model’s context. Second, when an object moves or articulates, its remembered appearance travels with it, whereas memory tied to camera poses or world positions stays behind. Third, all agents read from and write to the same surfaces, allowing each to render what only others have seen.

We realize this insight in M2R (Mesh to Remember), a real-time video world model that renders worlds of coarse, untextured meshes into photorealistic video from a single initial frame. As users act and the world updates, M2R conditions at every step on renderings of the current meshes and agent boxes from each agent’s viewpoint, reusing stored appearance on observed surfaces and synthesizing newly revealed regions and view-dependent effects. Agents are remembered the same way: M2R generates each agent’s body and motion from its bounding box, and the box carries that appearance with it. We fine-tune a pretrained video diffusion model only on synthetic multi-agent episodes rendered in Unreal Engine with Isekai3D [39] and adapt it into a few-step causal renderer with rollout-based training [35]. As this renderer remembers nothing outside its short context, we train it to write its own features to the surface memory during rollouts and to read them back on palindromic paths that revisit earlier views, so that it learns to use memory that carries its own errors. In summary, our contributions are:

  • 1.

    We design a causal video renderer that conditions on renderings of scene geometry and agent bounding boxes, and reads and updates surface memory indexed by the mesh in each object’s frame, so that remembered appearance follows objects as they move.

  • 2.

    We bound this memory by the observed surface area, compress it 18-fold with transform coding inspired by language-model KV caches [74], and pair it with a fast video autoencoder, allowing M2R to render at 40 FPS and keep 8,000-frame rollouts within 45 GiB of GPU memory.

  • 3.

    Although trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to articulated worlds authored by coding agents, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on revisit, interaction, and multi-agent benchmarks.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive video world models.

    Interactive video world models [4, 80, 27, 1] are progressing from a single player to several [20, 87], who must all observe the same evolving world. Most multi-agent models keep this shared world inside the network, generating all players’ views jointly [70, 30, 47, 58, 34]. Joint generation grows costly as players are added [47, 34], and the shared world can drift once players leave each other’s view [70]. Other methods render each view from an explicit state, such as an editable level map [65], an authoritative game state [7], an entity table [113], or a shared point cloud [31]. While this keeps geometry and state consistent across agents, it does not retain the appearance that each view generates. To share this appearance, recent methods exchange generated frames between agents [116, 100, 96]. M2R instead stores it directly on the mesh surfaces that every agent observes.

    Generative rendering of explicit geometry.

    Generative models increasingly render explicit geometry into realistic footage, from G-buffers, depth, and segmentation maps [43, 62] to renderings of animated meshes, low-poly games, and semantic block worlds [11, 8, 24, 26], some in real time [107, 61]. Executable worlds apply them to scenes written as programs, often by coding agents, with their geometry, state, and rules [13, 44, 15, 36, 55, 108]. However, as geometry alone does not determine materials, colors, or identities [15], the renderer must remember the appearance it invents. Offline methods store this appearance in the 3D representation itself, in mesh textures [68, 28], in the UV space of animated meshes [6], or by distilling refined views into captured scenes [88, 17]. They require the animation or target views in advance, which an interactive world cannot provide. Closest to our renderer, the concurrent AgentGarten [15] adapts the same backbone into a few-step causal renderer of code-defined worlds. While it keeps appearance only in a reference frame and its recent context, and can lose it after long occlusions, M2R stores it on the mesh itself and thus remains consistent over long rollouts (Sec.5.3).

    Memory for long video generation.

    Most memories retrieve past frames by camera pose or view overlap [93, 105, 76, 85] or return the cached keys and values of past chunks [29, 102, 14, 111]. Unless bounded [14, 18], these memories grow with the rollout, reaching an estimated 300 GiB of CPU memory per thousand frames for the concurrent MosaiChunk’s image-to-video backbone [111]. They also leave the network to infer how the retrieved content corresponds to the current view. Geometric memories make this correspondence explicit by storing observations in world-fixed point clouds, surfels, or per-frame geometry [57, 67, 32, 42, 89, 71], lifting features or latent patches into world space [114, 106, 66, 84], or reprojecting tokens with engine depth [56]. However, this correspondence only holds for static content, as moving objects are filtered out [89, 84, 66] or left to the generator [106], and even TourPhysics [110], which routes the generator’s own attention values with simulator geometry, excludes them from long-term memory. Memories that do handle motion replay it from an input video [67, 115], predict it while objects are out of sight [12, 19, 72], or remember objects by identity [94, 18, 82], but none track which of an object’s surfaces is visible. Closest to our memory, the concurrent CoDeR [21] registers generated colors on whitebox surfaces, where later views and other agents observe them. As it renders 124 frames at a time, however, the effect of an action becomes visible to any agent only after a full clip is rendered. It also learns to read colors registered from its training targets instead of its own outputs, which lets its errors accumulate over long rollouts. M2R instead keeps the renderer’s own keys and values, which it writes after every chunk and learns to read back from its own rollouts. Stored in mesh surface cells in each object’s frame, they follow objects as they move, grow only with the surfaces seen, and can be read by any agent in real time.

    3 Preliminaries

    Video diffusion models.

    We build upon video diffusion models, which typically operate in the latent space of a video autoencoder. Flow matching [46] learns to transport Gaussian noise into these latents. Given clean latents z, noise ε∼ℕ(0,I), and flow time τ∈[0,1], we construct z_τ=(1-τ)ε+τz and train a velocity field v_θ by minimizing 𝔼_z,ε,τ∥v_θ(z_τ,τ;c)-(z-ε)∥₂², where c denotes conditioning signals such as actions or renderings of scene geometry. At inference, integrating the field from τ=0 to τ=1 produces clean latents.

    Autoregressive video generation.

    As bidirectional video models denoise all frames of a clip jointly, their memory cost grows with the number of frames. To solve this, long-horizon interactive world models instead generate video autoregressively, one latent chunk at a time. Each chunk attends to the chunks before it [104], whose keys and values are kept in a KV cache. To keep this cache bounded, only a sliding window of recent chunks is typically retained [35, 73], at the cost of reinventing any content that reappears after leaving the window. As autoregressive models condition on their own outputs at inference, Self Forcing [35] trains them on their own rollouts, supervised by distribution matching distillation (DMD) [103] from a bidirectional teacher.

    4 Method

    Given a coarse, untextured mesh, a caption of the scene, and an initial first- or third-person frame for each agent, our goal is to render consistent, photorealistic views in real time as agents explore and change the world. We do so via a few-step causal video renderer that is conditioned on renderings of the mesh and stores generated features in a surface memory shared by all agents (Fig.2). As the mesh identifies the surface behind every pixel, the renderer can retrieve these features whenever the surface they depict reappears, even after it has moved.

    4.1 Geometry Conditioning

    To specify what is visible in each chunk, we rasterize the current mesh and agent boxes from each agent’s camera into a proxy video, with flat shading and one arbitrary color per asset to separate objects. We encode it into the backbone’s latent space and add it to the embedded noisy latents through a zero-initialized patch embedding, which keeps the sequence length unchanged.

    4.2 Surface Memory

    Most autoregressive video models remember between 24 and 72 frames in a key-value cache [35, 99, 73]. Instead, we pair a much smaller temporal cache (8 frames) with a surface memory shared across agents, which indexes keys and values by the mesh surfaces they depict. Once observed surfaces are evicted from the temporal cache, they remain retrievable by any agent that later sees them, and the memory grows with the surfaces observed instead of with time (Fig.7b).

    Cells.

    To index the memory, we divide the surfaces of the mesh and agent boxes into small cells. We define cells in the coordinates of the object they lie on, which lets a cell follow its surface as the object moves or articulates, with no update to the memory (Fig.4). Rasterizing this geometry into a view gives the object o(p) and the surface point x(p) behind each pixel p, and we assign the pixel to the cell that holds this point (Fig.3, top),

    c(p)=(o(p), ⌊Tₒ₍ₚ₎(t) x(p)/s⌋),

    		(1)

    where Tₒ(t) maps world coordinates into the coordinates of object o at time t and s is the cell size. As cells do not depend on any camera, all agents address a surface through the same cell. In practice, we also split cells by the direction the surface faces and keep them at four sizes, so that surfaces seen from afar still fill the coarser cells (AppendixD).

    Writing.

    As the renderer operates on tokens that each span a patch of pixels across several frames, a single token often covers multiple cells. We therefore store each token’s keys and values once and let cells point to it. After generating chunk n, we associate each visible cell c with the token that covers most of its pixels, j=\arg\max_j^′|{p∈Ω_j^′:c(p)=c}|, where Ω_j^′ denotes the pixels of token j^′, and record the observation (n,j) (Fig.3, bottom left). We keep two observations per cell: the first, which we never replace [95] to prevent errors from accumulating across revisits, and the latest, which reflects the surface’s current state.

    Storage.

    Storing the keys and values of every token is expensive [91, 102], amounting to about 54 GiB per minute of 720p video at 30 FPS. To limit this cost, we discard tokens as they leave the temporal cache unless a cell still points to them. We further compress the remaining tokens following key-value compression for language models [74, 9]. We project each token’s keys and values across all layers onto a principal component basis that we fit once on the renderer’s own rollouts, and store the result at 8-bit precision. This shrinks each token 18-fold without degrading consistency (AppendicesD and A1). The temporal cache, which also keeps the initial chunk as an attention sink [92, 99, 50], stays uncompressed.

    Reading.

    For each token i of a new chunk, we look up the first and latest observations of the cells that it covers. Since a token can cover multiple cells, we select the past token that most of its pixels p∈Ωᵢ point to, choosing first its chunk nᵢ and then the token jᵢ within that chunk,

    nᵢ=*arg maxₙ |{ p∈Ωᵢ:(n,·)∈O(p) }|,(2)
    jᵢ=*arg maxⱼ |{ p∈Ωᵢ:(nᵢ,j)∈O(p) }|,

    where O(p) is the first observation of the cell at pixel p. We repeat this selection with the latest observations and retrieve a set ℝᵢ of at most two past tokens (Fig.3, bottom right).

    Memory conditioning.

    Each token attends to the tokens retrieved for its chunk in addition to the temporal cache. We assign each token in ℝᵢ the spatial position of token i, as in the re-positioned frame and patch memories of recent world models [76, 106, 66, 97] (AppendicesD and A3). As each token retrieves at most two past tokens, the cost of rendering stays independent of the length of the interaction.

    Multiple agents.

    With several agents, each agent keeps its own temporal cache, while all agents read from and write to the same surface memory. Each agent can thus render surfaces that only others have seen (Tab.3), even though we train with a single view at a time (AppendixD).

    4.3 Optimization

    Causal renderer.

    We start from a bidirectional image-to-video model and fine-tune it with flow matching on videos paired with mesh renderings and keyboard controls (AppendicesC and E), so that it learns to follow the geometry. For real-time generation, we make it causal and few-step following Causal Forcing++ [112], and then train it on its own rollouts with Self Forcing (Sec.3) to limit how errors compound over long videos. The resulting renderer generates arbitrarily long videos with a few sampling steps per chunk, but remembers nothing outside its temporal cache.

    Memory distillation.

    Although the causal renderer already benefits from the memory without any training (AppendicesB and A1), it has little incentive to rely on it. We therefore apply Self Forcing a second time, except that the renderer now reads from and writes to its memory on rollouts that revisit earlier views (Fig.2b). We construct these rollouts as palindromes, in which the camera goes back and forth up to four times, such that each return can only be rendered from memory (as the temporal cache holds a single chunk). To supervise each return, we use a frozen copy of the causal renderer that attends to the entire rollout (and thus still sees the first visit) as a teacher [48, 111], and minimize the difference between their clean-latent predictions ẑᵀ and ẑ^S at every chunk:

    L_SD=𝔼_n,τ[∥ẑ^S_n,τ-sg (ẑᵀ_n,τ)∥₂²],

    		(3)

    where sg stops gradients. Our final loss is L=L_DMD+λ L_SD, with λ=0.1 (AppendicesE and A5).

    5 Experiments

    We evaluate M2R in the three situations in which an interactive world model must remember appearance: a camera revisits a region, an object moves, and several agents see the same surfaces.

    5.1 Implementation

    We use Cosmos3-Nano [60] as the base model and train on 64 GPUs with paired mesh and RGB videos from Isekai3D [39]. At inference time, we generate eight-frame chunks (two latent frames) with two-step denoising, and measure all timings with a single GB200. To speed up encoding and decoding, we replace the base model’s VAE with FastVAE, a transformer autoencoder that we train from scratch for the same latent space.

    5.2 Static Environments

    Datasets.

    We evaluate on 46 scenes of ScanNet++ [101], real indoor captures with laser-scanned meshes, and on the 18 scenes of Replica [75], whose dense meshes provide ground truth from any viewpoint. We follow the revisit protocol of Orbia [54], in which each 22-second trajectory starts at an input view, discovers a region absent from it, explores elsewhere, and then revisits both. We use Orbia’s trajectories on ScanNet++ and generate four per scene on Replica (Sec.G.1).

    Baselines.

    We compare M2R to three groups of baselines (Tab.1), namely a video world model that takes no geometry [33], methods that store what they generate in a 3D cache [66, 67, 71], and renderers that condition on proxy videos of the geometry [82, 13, 44, 15]. For fairness, we provide the ground-truth mesh to all methods that take geometry.

    Metrics.

    We report the six scores of Orbia [54] using its released evaluator: control alignment, visual quality, 3D consistency, temporal stability, and two memory scores. Input preservation compares later views of the surfaces visible in the input with ground truth, and content persistence compares each revisit of the discovered region with its first generated view. We also measure latency (from an input to the first frame it affects), frame rate, throughput in megapixels per second (MP/s), and peak GPU memory.

    Results.

    We present quantitative results in Tab.1 and qualitative examples in Fig.5. Lyra 2.0 and SolarWM H3 lose the input view, and AgentGarten alters revisited objects. Although trained only on synthetic data, M2R outperforms all baselines on every metric except visual quality, where it performs competitively with the concurrent AgentGarten [15] and Code Video Model [44]. It is also the only method to render 720p video in real time, with 2.7× the throughput of AgentGarten and over 15× that of every other baseline.

    5.3 Dynamic and Multi-Agent Environments

    Datasets and baselines.

    We evaluate on 45 trajectories in five articulated HSSD homes [40, 10] and on 52 in MutableWorlds, eight worlds that we build with a coding agent. The camera returns to rooms it has seen, reopens drawers and doors with objects inside, and revisits objects that have moved. We compare to the same methods as in Sec.5.2.

    Metrics.

    We report control alignment and visual quality as in Sec.5.2. We measure memory by comparing a method’s frames at each revisit with its own frames from the same camera poses on the first visit. Revisit compares the static parts of a view, and object permanence compares the contents of each reopened drawer or door. Moved objects checks that an object appears only at its current location, and that its appearance has not changed. We compute these scores from DINOv2 features [64] and ratings by Gemini 3.7 Flash [25], as detailed in Sec.G.2.

    Results.

    We present quantitative results in Tab.2 and qualitative examples in Fig.6. M2R outperforms all baselines on every metric except visual quality, where it is second only to the concurrent AgentGarten. However, AgentGarten keeps appearance only in a reference frame and its recent context, and often shows new contents when a drawer or door is reopened (Fig.6). We more than double its object permanence (91.5 vs. 34.7 on HSSD and 94.1 vs. 43.4 in MutableWorlds). Our memory does not fade with the time between visits (Fig.7a). GEN3C and Lyra 2.0 index their 3D caches by world position, which leaves a moved object’s appearance where it was first seen (Fig.4). M2R is the only method to preserve appearance when drawers reopen and when objects move.

    Multiple agents.

    In MutableWorlds, we also render 30 two-agent and 23 four-agent episodes, in which each agent later sees what another agent saw first. Cross-agent consistency averages revisit, object permanence, and moved objects when the first visit comes from another agent’s video, and agent persistence compares another agent’s appearance across two separate meetings. The baselines generate each agent’s video separately, and thus give a new appearance to what another agent has already seen. We nearly double the best cross-agent consistency among them (80.0 vs. 42.6 with two agents and 77.1 vs. 42.2 with four) and raise the best agent persistence from 52.8 to 87.3 with two agents and from 37.0 to 73.7 with four (Tabs.3 and 8). M2R is the only method to share appearance between agents.

    5.4 Diagnostics

    We ablate what the memory stores, its compression, revisiting rollouts, the self-distillation loss, and FastVAE (Tab.4). Storing the renderer’s keys and values instead of colors is crucial, as colors on the same surface cells are less consistent (79.6 vs. 86.8 revisit) and must be re-rendered and re-encoded for every chunk, which halves the frame rate. Retrieving latent frames by view frustum instead renders at 15 FPS, and is less consistent on revisits and moved objects in dynamic scenes (AppendicesB, A3 and A1). Compression shrinks the additional K/V store 18-fold at no loss and allows rollouts of over 8,000 frames within 45 GiB (Fig.7b). Revisiting rollouts and the self-distillation loss each improve revisit, and FastVAE doubles the frame rate.

    6 Conclusion

    We present M2R, a real-time video renderer that stores what it generates on the mesh it renders. As it addresses memory by surface, M2R more than doubles the best baseline’s object permanence and nearly doubles cross-agent consistency, with memory that grows only with the surfaces seen, while rendering 720p video at 40 FPS. Although a coarse mesh suffices, M2R assumes that it is accurate, and handling noisy geometry reconstructed from images [5] would be a valuable next step. We discuss limitations in AppendixH.

    We thank Rafał Karp, Gene Liu, and the Isekai3D team [39] for developing and supporting the Isekai3D synthetic data generation platform.

    Supplementary Material

    Contents

    Appendix A Videos

    We recommend watching our videos on our project page at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/m2r/. The page shows single-agent and multi-agent rollouts of M2R across diverse meshes, compares it to AgentGarten [15] and Code World Model [13] on reopened drawers, moved objects, and multiple agents, and includes an 8,001-frame rollout (4 min 27 s).

    Appendix B Additional Diagnostics

    Memory without training.

    To test whether the causal renderer benefits from the memory without any training, we evaluate it before memory distillation (upper rows of Tab.A1). The memory already raises content persistence from 84.45 to 88.48, whereas widening the attention window from 8 to 64 frames only reaches 86.19 and renders slower (35.2 vs. 42.9 FPS). On HSSD, it also raises revisit from 74.33 to 81.98 (Tabs.4 and A2).

    Compression.

    We measure the impact of compression by varying the number of principal components kept per token and the precision at which we store them (Tab.A1). Content persistence improves with the number of components and saturates at 8,192. Storing these components at 8-bit precision yields a memory that is as consistent as the uncompressed one, both before and after memory distillation, with tokens that are 18 times smaller. Compression and decompression have a negligible impact on the frame rate.

    Observations per cell.

    To validate retaining both the first and the latest observation of each cell, we compare to variants that retain only one of the two (Tab.A2). Retaining both is more consistent than either alone, as the first observation preserves the initial appearance of a surface and the latest its most recent one. Averaging the two instead of attending to each degrades consistency.

    Memory structure.

    We ablate what the memory stores by comparing it to variants that instead store colors on the same surface cells or retrieve past latent frames by view frustum [93, 105]. We summarize our results in Tab.A3. In the color variants, each generated chunk writes RGB colors to the same surface cells. For each subsequent chunk, we re-render the stored colors (first, latest, or both) from the current camera, encode them with FastVAE, and pass them as retrieved tokens at t-8 under the same 16-GPU memory distillation. Storing keys and values is more consistent than storing colors on both content persistence and revisit, and renders faster, as colors are a lossy copy of what the renderer generated and must be re-rendered and re-encoded for every chunk. As a retrieved frame shows the scene as it was, retrieving past frames is less consistent in dynamic scenes (Fig.A1, 82.93 vs. 86.78 on revisit and 80.76 vs. 85.98 on moved objects), although it suffices on static scenes such as ScanNet++. On ScanNet++, every trajectory returns to its exact initial pose, and most intermediate revisits come from the same or nearby viewpoints. Our memory is both the fastest and the most consistent on revisits and moved objects in dynamic scenes.

    Appendix C Geometry Conditioning

    Proxy rendering.

    At every video frame, we rasterize the current mesh from each agent’s camera into a proxy video R (Fig.A2). We use flat shading under a fixed directional light and assign each asset one arbitrary color, which separates objects but carries no information about their appearance. Pixels without geometry, such as the sky, remain black. We encode R with the same autoencoder 𝔼 as the video and add it to the video tokens through a zero-initialized projection Wₘ, such that each token i receives the geometry it should depict:

    hᵢ=Wᵥ ℙ(z_τ)ᵢ+Wₘ ℙ(𝔼(R))ᵢ,

    		(A1)

    where hᵢ is the embedding of token i, ℙ patchifies latents, and Wᵥ is the pretrained projection of the noisy latents z_τ.

    Online rasterization.

    At inference and during memory distillation, we rasterize the mesh on the GPU with nvdiffrast[41], in the same process as the renderer. Besides the proxy video, the rasterizer provides the depth, object, and surface normal behind each pixel, which the surface memory uses to assign pixels to cells (AppendixD). To limit the rasterizer’s GPU memory during training, we cap the scene geometry at 4 GiB (about 70 million triangles) and simplify larger training scenes offline to 1% of the triangles of each asset with quadric error metrics [22].

    Agents.

    We draw each agent into the proxy video as a bounding box (Fig.A2), from which the renderer generates the agent’s body and motion. The hue of a box is random per episode and independent of the agent’s identity, while its sides differ in brightness to show the agent’s heading. All human characters share a box of 68×72×184 cm, and each non-human character has a box that fits its asset. A third-person view shows the box of the agent that it follows and the boxes of all other agents in view, whereas a first-person view shows only the boxes of the other agents.

    Keyboard controls.

    The renderer does not require keyboard controls, which serve as a hint for how to animate an agent. During training, each view receives the keys held at each video frame by the agent that it follows (W, A, S, D, space, shift, and ctrl), or a flag that marks them as unknown if the clip has no agents. We embed the keys of the four video frames that each latent frame spans with a two-layer SiLU MLP whose last layer is zero-initialized, and add the embedding to every token of that latent frame. At evaluation, including episodes with agents, keys are unavailable, so instead of synthesizing them from the bounding boxes, we simply mark them as unknown, and the renderer still animates each agent naturally from its box alone.

    Appendix D Surface Memory

    Cells.

    We extend the cells of Eq.1 so that every pixel of a view maps to a cell, and what the renderer generates thus persists on distant surfaces, on thin structures, on agents, and where the mesh has no geometry (Tab.A4). As a pixel covers a larger patch of a surface the farther away the surface is, we keep cells at four sizes s_ℓ, from 3 cm to 1.92 m, and let each view write to those that match what its pixels cover. As a cubic cell can hold surfaces that face different ways, such as the two sides of a thin wall, we also split each cell by the direction d(p) that its surface faces, and Eq.1 becomes

    c_ℓ(p)=(o(p), ⌊Tₒ₍ₚ₎(t) x(p)/s_ℓ⌋, d(p)),

    		(A2)

    where d(p) is one of six directions, the dominant axis and sign of the surface normal in the object’s coordinates. An agent’s box has cells of its own in the coordinates of the box, such that the agent carries its appearance with it (Tab.3).

    Pixels without a surface behind them have no cell under Eq.A2. Where such a pixel is enclosed by geometry, as in the holes of scanned meshes (Fig.A10), we interpolate its depth from its surroundings and use the cells of the resulting point. Otherwise, as for the sky, we define its cells by viewing direction per 2 m camera-position cell, so they also remain bounded by the explored region of the scene.

    Writing.

    Each view writes only to the cells whose size matches the scale at which it sees a surface (fine cells for a close-up and coarse cells for a distant view). We measure this scale by the footprint f(p) of each pixel p, the width of the patch of surface that it covers. As a token j spans many pixels, it covers a larger patch of width F(j). On mesh surfaces, a pixel p of token j writes to the cells of every size from f(p) to F(j),

    W(p)={ℓ:f(p)≤s_ℓ≤F(j)}, p∈Ωⱼ.

    		(A3)

    If no size lies in this range, the pixel ignores the upper bound and writes to the smallest s_ℓ≥f(p). Agent boxes, holes, and the sky each have only two cell sizes (Tab.A4), and their pixels write to both. In practice, we rasterize the mesh at half the video resolution for efficiency, as cells and tokens are both far coarser than a pixel. A token then spans 16×16 pixels, and we set F(j) to 16 times the median footprint of its pixels.

    Storage.

    We compress each stored token 18-fold without degrading consistency (Tab.A1). The keys and values of a token form a vector v of 2×36×8×128=73,728 numbers, over 36 layers with 8 heads of 128 dimensions. We fit a principal component basis to these vectors once, on rollouts of the causal renderer before memory distillation. We then project each vector onto this basis and store its coefficients at 8-bit precision (FP8),

    q=FP8(Λ⁻¹ U^⊤S⁻¹(v-μ)),

    		(A4)

    where μ is the mean of v, the diagonal matrix S holds its standard deviation per head, the columns of U are the 8,192 leading principal components, and the diagonal matrix Λ scales each coefficient to unit variance. When a token is read, we invert these steps, v̂=μ+S UΛ q. Each stored token takes 8,192 bytes instead of 147,456 at 16-bit precision. On the 46 ScanNet++ trajectories, the stored tokens thus take at most 0.21 GiB instead of 3.70 GiB. Over the 8,001-frame rollout of Fig.7b, they take 5.95 GiB instead of 107 GiB. Even a rollout that kept every token it generates would add 1.7 GiB per 1,000 frames at 704×1280 instead of 30 GiB.

    Reading.

    As in writing, each pixel reads at the scale at which it sees a surface. On mesh surfaces, a pixel p reads the finest cell that holds an observation and is at least as large as its footprint (s_ℓ≥f(p)). Without this bound, a distant view would read the fine cells of an earlier close-up instead of the cells at its own scale. For agent boxes, holes, and the sky, we omit this bound, and a pixel reads the finest of its two cells that holds an observation. Each token only retrieves past tokens from earlier visits to a surface. We thus exclude from the selection of Eq.2 the observations made since the surface last came into view, as well as those whose tokens are still in the temporal cache, as the reading token attends to them directly. The selection with the latest observations also skips the chunk already selected with the first observations, such that the two retrieved tokens come from different chunks.

    Memory conditioning.

    In every layer, each token attends to the tokens retrieved for its chunk, both in the denoising steps and when the generated chunk is re-encoded for the temporal cache. We decompress the retrieved tokens into keys and values before attention, and never add them to this cache. As keys are stored without positional encoding [92, 50, 90], we apply the backbone’s rotary encoding [60] when they are read. We give each retrieved token the spatial position of the reading token and a time that is a fixed 8 latents (32 frames) earlier, regardless of when it was observed. A token retrieved by token i at latent time tᵢ and spatial position (hᵢ,wᵢ) is thus placed at

    (tᵢ-8, hᵢ, wᵢ).

    		(A5)

    With chunks of 2 latents and a cache of one chunk, the current chunk sits at {t-1,t}, the previous chunk at {t-3,t-2}, and the re-anchored initial chunk at t-4, such that the retrieved tokens at {t-9,t-8} lie beyond the temporal cache. We compare this placement to alternatives in Fig.A3. Larger offsets (e.g., 16 or 32 latents) also work, while placing retrieved tokens at the time they were observed is less consistent over long rollouts.

    Multiple agents.

    Several agents can share the surface memory although we train with a single view at a time, as the memory indexes tokens by the surfaces they depict rather than by the view that generated them (Tab.3). At inference, all agents generate a chunk before any of them writes, and their observations then enter the memory together, ordered by agent index where several agents write to the same cell. The result thus does not depend on the order in which the agents run. Each agent runs on its own GPU. Each agent reads the observations of the other agents under the same rules as its own, including those from their first frames, which are not in its temporal cache. It skips the observations that another agent made in the previous chunk or since the surface last came into its own view. Two agents that look at the same surface would otherwise read each other’s latest frames at every chunk, causing temporal inconsistencies.

    Agents also keep their appearance from one meeting to the next (Tab.3). In third-person videos, each agent starts from a first frame that shows it only from behind, so another view that first sees its front has to guess its appearance. As a written guess would stay in the memory for the rest of the video, an agent’s box is only written by its own view and by the given first frames of other views, which are not generated. A token on the box in turn attends only to the tokens retrieved for itself, as those retrieved for the rest of its chunk would mix in the appearance of other agents. It also attends to reference tokens of that agent, taken from the agent’s own view (its first frame and its latest chunk that shows the agent) and from the given first frames of other views that show it. We empirically place these references 48 latents before the reading token (16 or 32 also work), apart from the retrieved tokens at t-8, and add \ln4 to their attention logits, which weights them four-fold so that the renderer draws unseen sides of an agent consistently with its observed views (AppendixH).

    Appendix E Training and Inference

    Data.

    Although we fine-tune Cosmos3-Nano [60] (Fig.A4) only on synthetic episodes rendered in Unreal Engine with Isekai3D [39], M2R transfers zero-shot to every dataset that we evaluate on (AppendixG), including real indoor scans and worlds authored by coding agents. The training set has about 200,000 episodes of 60 s at 30 FPS and 720×1280, which span 223 environments. Each episode has one to eight agents drawn from 367 human and 34 non-human characters, and every agent is followed by its own camera, which gives about 850,000 single-view videos. We render non-human characters only in single-agent episodes. We render each video a second time along the same camera path without agents, and each render comes with its proxy video (Fig.A2). Until memory distillation, half of the training clips show agents and the other half do not. We train on one view at a time, on clips of 129 to 513 frames at 480×832 (480p) or 704×1280 (720p). Despite never training on two views of a world together or on more than 513 frames, M2R nearly doubles the best cross-agent consistency among the baselines (Tab.3) on episodes of two to four times that length (Sec.G.3).

    Stages and hyperparameters.

    We train M2R in five stages on 64 GB200 GPUs (Tab.A5), starting each stage from the exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights of the previous one. We first train a bidirectional model for 23,000 iterations on clips of 129, 257, and then 513 frames at both resolutions, using AdamW [53] with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁵. We then make it causal with 2,000 iterations of teacher forcing at the same learning rate, and distill it into four steps with 500 iterations of Causal CD [112] at 2×10⁻⁶. We next train it on its own rollouts with 2,000 iterations of Self Forcing, using learning rates of 2×10⁻⁶ for the generator and 4×10⁻⁷ for the fake score function. Throughout causal training, we draw each chunk’s sliding window uniformly from one to 15 chunks or the entire past. Finally, we teach the renderer to use its memory with only 300 iterations of memory distillation on 513-frame clips at 704×1280, with λ=0.1.

    Memory distillation.

    In each iteration of memory distillation (AlgorithmA1), the renderer rolls out all chunks of a clip with a temporal cache of one chunk, reading from and writing to the surface memory as at inference (AppendixD). In 70% of the iterations, the clip is a palindrome with one, two, or four round trips, which we build from agent-free clips only. In the rest, it is a clip with agents, played forward. We apply L_DMD to every clip, with a teacher and a fake score function that see the whole clip and have no memory. We apply L_SD to palindromes only and vary its weight λ in Fig.A5. In the ablation without revisiting rollouts (Tab.4), we apply L_SD to forward agent-free clips using the same frozen teacher. A larger λ improves consistency but softens textures. Because the synthetic ground-truth renders in Fig.A5 are less vivid and less detailed than photorealistic video, we empirically choose λ=0.1 for the best balance of visual quality and consistency across diverse scenes.

    Sampling.

    At test time, M2R renders each eight-frame chunk in two steps, at noise levels 1 and 0.625, without classifier-free guidance. Although we distill the renderer into four steps, we find that two-step and four-step results differ negligibly, as the mesh geometry and the memory provide strong signals. The renderer is trained on 30 FPS videos, as used in the 8,001-frame rollout of Fig.7b, whereas our quantitative benchmarks follow Orbia’s 16 FPS convention (AppendixG).

    Appendix F FastVAE

    The Wan 2.2 VAE [81] of the base model provides high-quality reconstructions but is slow, taking 225 ms to decode an eight-frame chunk at 704×1280 on a GB200 (and still 143 ms when compiled), more than half of the 416 ms that M2R spends on the chunk when using it. Open-source tiny decoders for the same latents [3, 16, 73] are far faster but degrade PSNR by 4 to 7 dB (Fig.A6). FlashDecoder [38] instead replaces the decoder with a streaming transformer but keeps the original encoder, which M2R runs on the proxy video of every chunk (AppendixC). We thus build upon FlashDecoder and learn the encoder as well, allowing FastVAE to replace the entire Wan 2.2 VAE without changing its latent space (Fig.A8). FastVAE matches the quality of the original while running an order of magnitude faster (Tab.A7), more than doubling the frame rate of M2R (19.2 to 41.1 FPS) without degrading consistency (Tab.4).

    Architecture.

    As in FlashDecoder, our decoder is a streaming transformer that flattens each latent frame of size H^′×W^′ into H^′W^′ tokens, where each latent frame attends to itself and the previous one through cached keys and values (Fig.A8). However, FlashDecoder attends over the whole frame, at a cost that grows quadratically with resolution. We instead use Swin Transformer blocks [51], which attend within 16×16 windows (shifted by 8 tokens in every other block) at a cost that grows only linearly. With full-frame attention, the same decoder takes 37% longer at 704×1280 and 99% longer at 1088×1920 on a GB200, with no noticeable gain in quality. To map tokens to pixels, FlashDecoder uses a single 16× pixel shuffle, whereas we upsample progressively, by 2× with Swin Transformer blocks, by 2× with ConvNeXt blocks [52], and by 4× with a pixel shuffle. We build the encoder from the same blocks over spatiotemporal patches of 4×16×16 pixels, such that it encodes a chunk in 3.5 ms instead of the 63.5 ms of the Wan 2.2 encoder. The decoder comes in four sizes (Tab.A6), which trade speed for quality (Fig.A6). Throughout the paper, M2R uses FastVAE-XL, for both its scores and its frame rate.

    Training.

    As FastVAE has to stay in the latent space of the Wan 2.2 VAE, we train its decoder and encoder one at a time against the frozen original, and then both end to end. The decoder first learns to reconstruct a clip x from the latents of the frozen Wan 2.2 encoder, at 224×224 and then at 480p to 1080p, with

    L_dec=∥x̂-x∥₁+λ₂ ∥x̂-x∥₂²+λₚ LPIPS(x̂,x),

    		(A6)

    where λ₂=10 and λₚ=0.5. We drop the adversarial loss of FlashDecoder, which had a negligible effect on our decoder. The encoder then learns to regress the same latents with the decoder frozen, and a final end-to-end phase trains both networks to reconstruct the clip through the encoder and the decoder. To match the general-purpose latent space of the Wan 2.2 VAE, all phases train FastVAE on a mixture of publicly released web videos [59, 45] and synthetic episodes rendered with Isekai3D [39], whereas the renderer itself is fine-tuned only on synthetic data (AppendixE). We optimize weight matrices with Muon [49] and the remaining parameters with AdamW [53], on 64 A100 GPUs.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：显式 3D 世界的几何与状态「天生持久」，但外观离照片级差得远。

要点：

  • 两条路线的优劣被摆得很清楚：**视频世界模型**能合成照片级的观测，但在长时间交互中**难以保持一致**；而 **coding agent 与 text-to-3D** 生成的是显式 3D 世界，其**几何与状态「由构造本身」持久**，但外观远不如照片真实
  • 已有折中做法是把这类显式世界渲成**粗糙代理**去引导视频模型，但代理只承接结构、不承接外观
  • 这篇因此把**网格当作外观记忆**：让持久的东西从「几何与状态」扩展到「外观」，从而在长交互中把看过的样子留下来

为什么值得看：这是「状态外置」主线最关键的下一步：前面几期解决的都是几何与状态的持久（Evoke、PanoEvo、Lyris、WM^MLLM），但**外观一直要靠模型的上下文记**。把网格接成外观记忆，等于把「长什么样」也纳入可持久的结构。

中文摘要：视频世界模型能针对用户动作合成照片级的观测，但在长时间交互中很难保持一致；相对地，coding agent 与 text-to-3D 模型生成的是显式 3D 世界，其几何与状态「由构造本身」天然持久，可外观离照片级真实还差得远。近期方法把两者结合：把这类显式世界渲染成粗糙代理，再用它引导视频模型——但代理只承接结构与运动，不承接外观。这篇因此提出把网格作为外观记忆，让持久化的对象从「几何与状态」扩展到「外观」，使长时间交互中已经出现过的样子不再依赖生成器的上下文窗口来维持。对正在做「引擎出代理、模型出画面」这条链路的团队，这是把记忆补全的下一步。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

A Mesh to Remember:
Persistent Appearance for Interactive Video Worlds

Abstract

Video world models synthesize photorealistic observations in response to user actions but struggle to remain consistent over long interactions. Coding agents and text-to-3D models instead generate explicit 3D worlds whose geometry and state persist by construction, but whose appearance falls far short of photorealism. Recent methods combine the strengths of both by rendering such worlds into coarse proxies that guide a video model. However, since these proxies only specify where things are, the renderer must invent what they look like as the world is explored, and anything it forgets is reinvented when a surface reappears. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies which surface each pixel shows, across frames and views, even as objects move, allowing it to serve as an address for what the renderer generates. We propose M2R (Mesh to Remember), a few-step causal video renderer that stores its own features on the surfaces they depict, in each object’s frame, and retrieves them by rasterizing the mesh whenever those surfaces come back into view. Appearance thus travels with objects wherever they move, persists across revisits, and is shared by every agent that observes it, while memory grows with the surfaces seen instead of the number of frames. Trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to worlds authored by coding agents. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods in consistency across static, dynamic, and multi-agent benchmarks, more than doubling object permanence and nearly doubling cross-agent consistency, while rendering 720p video in real time (40 FPS).

1 Introduction

Interactive virtual worlds are essential for applications in gaming, embodied AI, and closed-loop simulation. These use cases require both photorealistic rendering and persistent world state: a door opened by one agent should remain open when another walks by, and the room behind it should look the same each time it is opened (Fig.1). In recent years, two paradigms have emerged that promise to build such worlds automatically: video world models and 3D world generators.

Video world models synthesize observations in response to user actions, from game worlds [4, 80, 27] to photorealistic scenes [27, 63, 1], and increasingly for multiple players [20, 70, 87, 30, 47, 34]. Despite this progress, these models must infer both how the world evolves and how it looks from their own past observations, and errors in either can accumulate over long interactions. Memory mechanisms that retrieve past frames or their cached features, or maintain 3D caches, extend the history a model can draw upon and improve consistency when regions are revisited [93, 76, 102, 89, 106, 71]. However, they tie memory to where content was observed, which no longer holds once the world changes. When an object is carried across a room, its remembered appearance stays where the object used to be, and the model must reinvent it.

3D world generators instead create the world itself, from explorable scenes that text-to-3D models produce given a single prompt [37, 78] to entire dynamic worlds that coding agents write as programs, with articulated furniture [83] and rules for how objects move [13]. As these worlds are explicit, their geometry and state persist by construction, and every agent observes the same world. However, they fall short of photorealism, as even the most sophisticated real-time game renderings remain distinguishable from real imagery [69].

Instead of treating these paradigms as standalone alternatives, recent methods combine their complementary strengths: the explicit world maintains persistent geometry and state, while a video model renders coarse proxies of it (geometry or semantic layouts) into realistic observations [36, 13, 15, 55, 44, 21]. Since these proxies only specify what is where, the renderer must invent the world’s appearance as it is explored, and keep it consistent as agents revisit regions, move objects, and encounter surfaces that others have already seen. A natural place to keep this appearance is the explicit world itself. Existing methods paint generated colors back onto its geometry [68, 28, 57, 21], but colors are a lossy copy of what the renderer generated and must be re-rendered and re-encoded at every step, which is slow and accumulates errors (Tab.4).

We instead treat the mesh as an address. Our key insight is that a mesh identifies the surface behind every pixel in every view, even after that surface has moved. We therefore store the renderer’s own features on the surfaces they depict as they are generated, and attend to them whenever those surfaces reappear. This memory has three benefits. First, as memory is indexed by surface instead of time, storage follows scene coverage and observations remain addressable long after leaving the model’s context. Second, when an object moves or articulates, its remembered appearance travels with it, whereas memory tied to camera poses or world positions stays behind. Third, all agents read from and write to the same surfaces, allowing each to render what only others have seen.

We realize this insight in M2R (Mesh to Remember), a real-time video world model that renders worlds of coarse, untextured meshes into photorealistic video from a single initial frame. As users act and the world updates, M2R conditions at every step on renderings of the current meshes and agent boxes from each agent’s viewpoint, reusing stored appearance on observed surfaces and synthesizing newly revealed regions and view-dependent effects. Agents are remembered the same way: M2R generates each agent’s body and motion from its bounding box, and the box carries that appearance with it. We fine-tune a pretrained video diffusion model only on synthetic multi-agent episodes rendered in Unreal Engine with Isekai3D [39] and adapt it into a few-step causal renderer with rollout-based training [35]. As this renderer remembers nothing outside its short context, we train it to write its own features to the surface memory during rollouts and to read them back on palindromic paths that revisit earlier views, so that it learns to use memory that carries its own errors. In summary, our contributions are:

  • 1.

    We design a causal video renderer that conditions on renderings of scene geometry and agent bounding boxes, and reads and updates surface memory indexed by the mesh in each object’s frame, so that remembered appearance follows objects as they move.

  • 2.

    We bound this memory by the observed surface area, compress it 18-fold with transform coding inspired by language-model KV caches [74], and pair it with a fast video autoencoder, allowing M2R to render at 40 FPS and keep 8,000-frame rollouts within 45 GiB of GPU memory.

  • 3.

    Although trained only on synthetic data, M2R transfers zero-shot to real indoor scans and to articulated worlds authored by coding agents, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods on revisit, interaction, and multi-agent benchmarks.

    • 2 Related Work

    Interactive video world models.

    Interactive video world models [4, 80, 27, 1] are progressing from a single player to several [20, 87], who must all observe the same evolving world. Most multi-agent models keep this shared world inside the network, generating all players’ views jointly [70, 30, 47, 58, 34]. Joint generation grows costly as players are added [47, 34], and the shared world can drift once players leave each other’s view [70]. Other methods render each view from an explicit state, such as an editable level map [65], an authoritative game state [7], an entity table [113], or a shared point cloud [31]. While this keeps geometry and state consistent across agents, it does not retain the appearance that each view generates. To share this appearance, recent methods exchange generated frames between agents [116, 100, 96]. M2R instead stores it directly on the mesh surfaces that every agent observes.

    Generative rendering of explicit geometry.

    Generative models increasingly render explicit geometry into realistic footage, from G-buffers, depth, and segmentation maps [43, 62] to renderings of animated meshes, low-poly games, and semantic block worlds [11, 8, 24, 26], some in real time [107, 61]. Executable worlds apply them to scenes written as programs, often by coding agents, with their geometry, state, and rules [13, 44, 15, 36, 55, 108]. However, as geometry alone does not determine materials, colors, or identities [15], the renderer must remember the appearance it invents. Offline methods store this appearance in the 3D representation itself, in mesh textures [68, 28], in the UV space of animated meshes [6], or by distilling refined views into captured scenes [88, 17]. They require the animation or target views in advance, which an interactive world cannot provide. Closest to our renderer, the concurrent AgentGarten [15] adapts the same backbone into a few-step causal renderer of code-defined worlds. While it keeps appearance only in a reference frame and its recent context, and can lose it after long occlusions, M2R stores it on the mesh itself and thus remains consistent over long rollouts (Sec.5.3).

    Memory for long video generation.

    Most memories retrieve past frames by camera pose or view overlap [93, 105, 76, 85] or return the cached keys and values of past chunks [29, 102, 14, 111]. Unless bounded [14, 18], these memories grow with the rollout, reaching an estimated 300 GiB of CPU memory per thousand frames for the concurrent MosaiChunk’s image-to-video backbone [111]. They also leave the network to infer how the retrieved content corresponds to the current view. Geometric memories make this correspondence explicit by storing observations in world-fixed point clouds, surfels, or per-frame geometry [57, 67, 32, 42, 89, 71], lifting features or latent patches into world space [114, 106, 66, 84], or reprojecting tokens with engine depth [56]. However, this correspondence only holds for static content, as moving objects are filtered out [89, 84, 66] or left to the generator [106], and even TourPhysics [110], which routes the generator’s own attention values with simulator geometry, excludes them from long-term memory. Memories that do handle motion replay it from an input video [67, 115], predict it while objects are out of sight [12, 19, 72], or remember objects by identity [94, 18, 82], but none track which of an object’s surfaces is visible. Closest to our memory, the concurrent CoDeR [21] registers generated colors on whitebox surfaces, where later views and other agents observe them. As it renders 124 frames at a time, however, the effect of an action becomes visible to any agent only after a full clip is rendered. It also learns to read colors registered from its training targets instead of its own outputs, which lets its errors accumulate over long rollouts. M2R instead keeps the renderer’s own keys and values, which it writes after every chunk and learns to read back from its own rollouts. Stored in mesh surface cells in each object’s frame, they follow objects as they move, grow only with the surfaces seen, and can be read by any agent in real time.

    3 Preliminaries

    Video diffusion models.

    We build upon video diffusion models, which typically operate in the latent space of a video autoencoder. Flow matching [46] learns to transport Gaussian noise into these latents. Given clean latents z, noise ε∼ℕ(0,I), and flow time τ∈[0,1], we construct z_τ=(1-τ)ε+τz and train a velocity field v_θ by minimizing 𝔼_z,ε,τ∥v_θ(z_τ,τ;c)-(z-ε)∥₂², where c denotes conditioning signals such as actions or renderings of scene geometry. At inference, integrating the field from τ=0 to τ=1 produces clean latents.

    Autoregressive video generation.

    As bidirectional video models denoise all frames of a clip jointly, their memory cost grows with the number of frames. To solve this, long-horizon interactive world models instead generate video autoregressively, one latent chunk at a time. Each chunk attends to the chunks before it [104], whose keys and values are kept in a KV cache. To keep this cache bounded, only a sliding window of recent chunks is typically retained [35, 73], at the cost of reinventing any content that reappears after leaving the window. As autoregressive models condition on their own outputs at inference, Self Forcing [35] trains them on their own rollouts, supervised by distribution matching distillation (DMD) [103] from a bidirectional teacher.

    4 Method

    Given a coarse, untextured mesh, a caption of the scene, and an initial first- or third-person frame for each agent, our goal is to render consistent, photorealistic views in real time as agents explore and change the world. We do so via a few-step causal video renderer that is conditioned on renderings of the mesh and stores generated features in a surface memory shared by all agents (Fig.2). As the mesh identifies the surface behind every pixel, the renderer can retrieve these features whenever the surface they depict reappears, even after it has moved.

    4.1 Geometry Conditioning

    To specify what is visible in each chunk, we rasterize the current mesh and agent boxes from each agent’s camera into a proxy video, with flat shading and one arbitrary color per asset to separate objects. We encode it into the backbone’s latent space and add it to the embedded noisy latents through a zero-initialized patch embedding, which keeps the sequence length unchanged.

    4.2 Surface Memory

    Most autoregressive video models remember between 24 and 72 frames in a key-value cache [35, 99, 73]. Instead, we pair a much smaller temporal cache (8 frames) with a surface memory shared across agents, which indexes keys and values by the mesh surfaces they depict. Once observed surfaces are evicted from the temporal cache, they remain retrievable by any agent that later sees them, and the memory grows with the surfaces observed instead of with time (Fig.7b).

    Cells.

    To index the memory, we divide the surfaces of the mesh and agent boxes into small cells. We define cells in the coordinates of the object they lie on, which lets a cell follow its surface as the object moves or articulates, with no update to the memory (Fig.4). Rasterizing this geometry into a view gives the object o(p) and the surface point x(p) behind each pixel p, and we assign the pixel to the cell that holds this point (Fig.3, top),

    c(p)=(o(p), ⌊Tₒ₍ₚ₎(t) x(p)/s⌋),

    		(1)

    where Tₒ(t) maps world coordinates into the coordinates of object o at time t and s is the cell size. As cells do not depend on any camera, all agents address a surface through the same cell. In practice, we also split cells by the direction the surface faces and keep them at four sizes, so that surfaces seen from afar still fill the coarser cells (AppendixD).

    Writing.

    As the renderer operates on tokens that each span a patch of pixels across several frames, a single token often covers multiple cells. We therefore store each token’s keys and values once and let cells point to it. After generating chunk n, we associate each visible cell c with the token that covers most of its pixels, j=\arg\max_j^′|{p∈Ω_j^′:c(p)=c}|, where Ω_j^′ denotes the pixels of token j^′, and record the observation (n,j) (Fig.3, bottom left). We keep two observations per cell: the first, which we never replace [95] to prevent errors from accumulating across revisits, and the latest, which reflects the surface’s current state.

    Storage.

    Storing the keys and values of every token is expensive [91, 102], amounting to about 54 GiB per minute of 720p video at 30 FPS. To limit this cost, we discard tokens as they leave the temporal cache unless a cell still points to them. We further compress the remaining tokens following key-value compression for language models [74, 9]. We project each token’s keys and values across all layers onto a principal component basis that we fit once on the renderer’s own rollouts, and store the result at 8-bit precision. This shrinks each token 18-fold without degrading consistency (AppendicesD and A1). The temporal cache, which also keeps the initial chunk as an attention sink [92, 99, 50], stays uncompressed.

    Reading.

    For each token i of a new chunk, we look up the first and latest observations of the cells that it covers. Since a token can cover multiple cells, we select the past token that most of its pixels p∈Ωᵢ point to, choosing first its chunk nᵢ and then the token jᵢ within that chunk,

    nᵢ=*arg maxₙ |{ p∈Ωᵢ:(n,·)∈O(p) }|,(2)
    jᵢ=*arg maxⱼ |{ p∈Ωᵢ:(nᵢ,j)∈O(p) }|,

    where O(p) is the first observation of the cell at pixel p. We repeat this selection with the latest observations and retrieve a set ℝᵢ of at most two past tokens (Fig.3, bottom right).

    Memory conditioning.

    Each token attends to the tokens retrieved for its chunk in addition to the temporal cache. We assign each token in ℝᵢ the spatial position of token i, as in the re-positioned frame and patch memories of recent world models [76, 106, 66, 97] (AppendicesD and A3). As each token retrieves at most two past tokens, the cost of rendering stays independent of the length of the interaction.

    Multiple agents.

    With several agents, each agent keeps its own temporal cache, while all agents read from and write to the same surface memory. Each agent can thus render surfaces that only others have seen (Tab.3), even though we train with a single view at a time (AppendixD).

    4.3 Optimization

    Causal renderer.

    We start from a bidirectional image-to-video model and fine-tune it with flow matching on videos paired with mesh renderings and keyboard controls (AppendicesC and E), so that it learns to follow the geometry. For real-time generation, we make it causal and few-step following Causal Forcing++ [112], and then train it on its own rollouts with Self Forcing (Sec.3) to limit how errors compound over long videos. The resulting renderer generates arbitrarily long videos with a few sampling steps per chunk, but remembers nothing outside its temporal cache.

    Memory distillation.

    Although the causal renderer already benefits from the memory without any training (AppendicesB and A1), it has little incentive to rely on it. We therefore apply Self Forcing a second time, except that the renderer now reads from and writes to its memory on rollouts that revisit earlier views (Fig.2b). We construct these rollouts as palindromes, in which the camera goes back and forth up to four times, such that each return can only be rendered from memory (as the temporal cache holds a single chunk). To supervise each return, we use a frozen copy of the causal renderer that attends to the entire rollout (and thus still sees the first visit) as a teacher [48, 111], and minimize the difference between their clean-latent predictions ẑᵀ and ẑ^S at every chunk:

    L_SD=𝔼_n,τ[∥ẑ^S_n,τ-sg (ẑᵀ_n,τ)∥₂²],

    		(3)

    where sg stops gradients. Our final loss is L=L_DMD+λ L_SD, with λ=0.1 (AppendicesE and A5).

    5 Experiments

    We evaluate M2R in the three situations in which an interactive world model must remember appearance: a camera revisits a region, an object moves, and several agents see the same surfaces.

    5.1 Implementation

    We use Cosmos3-Nano [60] as the base model and train on 64 GPUs with paired mesh and RGB videos from Isekai3D [39]. At inference time, we generate eight-frame chunks (two latent frames) with two-step denoising, and measure all timings with a single GB200. To speed up encoding and decoding, we replace the base model’s VAE with FastVAE, a transformer autoencoder that we train from scratch for the same latent space.

    5.2 Static Environments

    Datasets.

    We evaluate on 46 scenes of ScanNet++ [101], real indoor captures with laser-scanned meshes, and on the 18 scenes of Replica [75], whose dense meshes provide ground truth from any viewpoint. We follow the revisit protocol of Orbia [54], in which each 22-second trajectory starts at an input view, discovers a region absent from it, explores elsewhere, and then revisits both. We use Orbia’s trajectories on ScanNet++ and generate four per scene on Replica (Sec.G.1).

    Baselines.

    We compare M2R to three groups of baselines (Tab.1), namely a video world model that takes no geometry [33], methods that store what they generate in a 3D cache [66, 67, 71], and renderers that condition on proxy videos of the geometry [82, 13, 44, 15]. For fairness, we provide the ground-truth mesh to all methods that take geometry.

    Metrics.

    We report the six scores of Orbia [54] using its released evaluator: control alignment, visual quality, 3D consistency, temporal stability, and two memory scores. Input preservation compares later views of the surfaces visible in the input with ground truth, and content persistence compares each revisit of the discovered region with its first generated view. We also measure latency (from an input to the first frame it affects), frame rate, throughput in megapixels per second (MP/s), and peak GPU memory.

    Results.

    We present quantitative results in Tab.1 and qualitative examples in Fig.5. Lyra 2.0 and SolarWM H3 lose the input view, and AgentGarten alters revisited objects. Although trained only on synthetic data, M2R outperforms all baselines on every metric except visual quality, where it performs competitively with the concurrent AgentGarten [15] and Code Video Model [44]. It is also the only method to render 720p video in real time, with 2.7× the throughput of AgentGarten and over 15× that of every other baseline.

    5.3 Dynamic and Multi-Agent Environments

    Datasets and baselines.

    We evaluate on 45 trajectories in five articulated HSSD homes [40, 10] and on 52 in MutableWorlds, eight worlds that we build with a coding agent. The camera returns to rooms it has seen, reopens drawers and doors with objects inside, and revisits objects that have moved. We compare to the same methods as in Sec.5.2.

    Metrics.

    We report control alignment and visual quality as in Sec.5.2. We measure memory by comparing a method’s frames at each revisit with its own frames from the same camera poses on the first visit. Revisit compares the static parts of a view, and object permanence compares the contents of each reopened drawer or door. Moved objects checks that an object appears only at its current location, and that its appearance has not changed. We compute these scores from DINOv2 features [64] and ratings by Gemini 3.7 Flash [25], as detailed in Sec.G.2.

    Results.

    We present quantitative results in Tab.2 and qualitative examples in Fig.6. M2R outperforms all baselines on every metric except visual quality, where it is second only to the concurrent AgentGarten. However, AgentGarten keeps appearance only in a reference frame and its recent context, and often shows new contents when a drawer or door is reopened (Fig.6). We more than double its object permanence (91.5 vs. 34.7 on HSSD and 94.1 vs. 43.4 in MutableWorlds). Our memory does not fade with the time between visits (Fig.7a). GEN3C and Lyra 2.0 index their 3D caches by world position, which leaves a moved object’s appearance where it was first seen (Fig.4). M2R is the only method to preserve appearance when drawers reopen and when objects move.

    Multiple agents.

    In MutableWorlds, we also render 30 two-agent and 23 four-agent episodes, in which each agent later sees what another agent saw first. Cross-agent consistency averages revisit, object permanence, and moved objects when the first visit comes from another agent’s video, and agent persistence compares another agent’s appearance across two separate meetings. The baselines generate each agent’s video separately, and thus give a new appearance to what another agent has already seen. We nearly double the best cross-agent consistency among them (80.0 vs. 42.6 with two agents and 77.1 vs. 42.2 with four) and raise the best agent persistence from 52.8 to 87.3 with two agents and from 37.0 to 73.7 with four (Tabs.3 and 8). M2R is the only method to share appearance between agents.

    5.4 Diagnostics

    We ablate what the memory stores, its compression, revisiting rollouts, the self-distillation loss, and FastVAE (Tab.4). Storing the renderer’s keys and values instead of colors is crucial, as colors on the same surface cells are less consistent (79.6 vs. 86.8 revisit) and must be re-rendered and re-encoded for every chunk, which halves the frame rate. Retrieving latent frames by view frustum instead renders at 15 FPS, and is less consistent on revisits and moved objects in dynamic scenes (AppendicesB, A3 and A1). Compression shrinks the additional K/V store 18-fold at no loss and allows rollouts of over 8,000 frames within 45 GiB (Fig.7b). Revisiting rollouts and the self-distillation loss each improve revisit, and FastVAE doubles the frame rate.

    6 Conclusion

    We present M2R, a real-time video renderer that stores what it generates on the mesh it renders. As it addresses memory by surface, M2R more than doubles the best baseline’s object permanence and nearly doubles cross-agent consistency, with memory that grows only with the surfaces seen, while rendering 720p video at 40 FPS. Although a coarse mesh suffices, M2R assumes that it is accurate, and handling noisy geometry reconstructed from images [5] would be a valuable next step. We discuss limitations in AppendixH.
