    Contents

    Appendix A Videos

    We recommend watching our videos on our project page at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/m2r/. The page shows single-agent and multi-agent rollouts of M2R across diverse meshes, compares it to AgentGarten [15] and Code World Model [13] on reopened drawers, moved objects, and multiple agents, and includes an 8,001-frame rollout (4 min 27 s).

    Appendix B Additional Diagnostics

    Memory without training.

    To test whether the causal renderer benefits from the memory without any training, we evaluate it before memory distillation (upper rows of Tab.A1). The memory already raises content persistence from 84.45 to 88.48, whereas widening the attention window from 8 to 64 frames only reaches 86.19 and renders slower (35.2 vs. 42.9 FPS). On HSSD, it also raises revisit from 74.33 to 81.98 (Tabs.4 and A2).

    Compression.

    We measure the impact of compression by varying the number of principal components kept per token and the precision at which we store them (Tab.A1). Content persistence improves with the number of components and saturates at 8,192. Storing these components at 8-bit precision yields a memory that is as consistent as the uncompressed one, both before and after memory distillation, with tokens that are 18 times smaller. Compression and decompression have a negligible impact on the frame rate.

    Observations per cell.

    To validate retaining both the first and the latest observation of each cell, we compare to variants that retain only one of the two (Tab.A2). Retaining both is more consistent than either alone, as the first observation preserves the initial appearance of a surface and the latest its most recent one. Averaging the two instead of attending to each degrades consistency.

    Memory structure.

    We ablate what the memory stores by comparing it to variants that instead store colors on the same surface cells or retrieve past latent frames by view frustum [93, 105]. We summarize our results in Tab.A3. In the color variants, each generated chunk writes RGB colors to the same surface cells. For each subsequent chunk, we re-render the stored colors (first, latest, or both) from the current camera, encode them with FastVAE, and pass them as retrieved tokens at t-8 under the same 16-GPU memory distillation. Storing keys and values is more consistent than storing colors on both content persistence and revisit, and renders faster, as colors are a lossy copy of what the renderer generated and must be re-rendered and re-encoded for every chunk. As a retrieved frame shows the scene as it was, retrieving past frames is less consistent in dynamic scenes (Fig.A1, 82.93 vs. 86.78 on revisit and 80.76 vs. 85.98 on moved objects), although it suffices on static scenes such as ScanNet++. On ScanNet++, every trajectory returns to its exact initial pose, and most intermediate revisits come from the same or nearby viewpoints. Our memory is both the fastest and the most consistent on revisits and moved objects in dynamic scenes.

    Appendix C Geometry Conditioning

    Proxy rendering.

    At every video frame, we rasterize the current mesh from each agent’s camera into a proxy video R (Fig.A2). We use flat shading under a fixed directional light and assign each asset one arbitrary color, which separates objects but carries no information about their appearance. Pixels without geometry, such as the sky, remain black. We encode R with the same autoencoder 𝔼 as the video and add it to the video tokens through a zero-initialized projection Wₘ, such that each token i receives the geometry it should depict:

    hᵢ=Wᵥ ℙ(z_τ)ᵢ+Wₘ ℙ(𝔼(R))ᵢ,

    		(A1)

    where hᵢ is the embedding of token i, ℙ patchifies latents, and Wᵥ is the pretrained projection of the noisy latents z_τ.

    Online rasterization.

    At inference and during memory distillation, we rasterize the mesh on the GPU with nvdiffrast[41], in the same process as the renderer. Besides the proxy video, the rasterizer provides the depth, object, and surface normal behind each pixel, which the surface memory uses to assign pixels to cells (AppendixD). To limit the rasterizer’s GPU memory during training, we cap the scene geometry at 4 GiB (about 70 million triangles) and simplify larger training scenes offline to 1% of the triangles of each asset with quadric error metrics [22].

    Agents.

    We draw each agent into the proxy video as a bounding box (Fig.A2), from which the renderer generates the agent’s body and motion. The hue of a box is random per episode and independent of the agent’s identity, while its sides differ in brightness to show the agent’s heading. All human characters share a box of 68×72×184 cm, and each non-human character has a box that fits its asset. A third-person view shows the box of the agent that it follows and the boxes of all other agents in view, whereas a first-person view shows only the boxes of the other agents.

    Keyboard controls.

    The renderer does not require keyboard controls, which serve as a hint for how to animate an agent. During training, each view receives the keys held at each video frame by the agent that it follows (W, A, S, D, space, shift, and ctrl), or a flag that marks them as unknown if the clip has no agents. We embed the keys of the four video frames that each latent frame spans with a two-layer SiLU MLP whose last layer is zero-initialized, and add the embedding to every token of that latent frame. At evaluation, including episodes with agents, keys are unavailable, so instead of synthesizing them from the bounding boxes, we simply mark them as unknown, and the renderer still animates each agent naturally from its box alone.

    Appendix D Surface Memory

    Cells.

    We extend the cells of Eq.1 so that every pixel of a view maps to a cell, and what the renderer generates thus persists on distant surfaces, on thin structures, on agents, and where the mesh has no geometry (Tab.A4). As a pixel covers a larger patch of a surface the farther away the surface is, we keep cells at four sizes s_ℓ, from 3 cm to 1.92 m, and let each view write to those that match what its pixels cover. As a cubic cell can hold surfaces that face different ways, such as the two sides of a thin wall, we also split each cell by the direction d(p) that its surface faces, and Eq.1 becomes

    c_ℓ(p)=(o(p), ⌊Tₒ₍ₚ₎(t) x(p)/s_ℓ⌋, d(p)),

    		(A2)

    where d(p) is one of six directions, the dominant axis and sign of the surface normal in the object’s coordinates. An agent’s box has cells of its own in the coordinates of the box, such that the agent carries its appearance with it (Tab.3).

    Pixels without a surface behind them have no cell under Eq.A2. Where such a pixel is enclosed by geometry, as in the holes of scanned meshes (Fig.A10), we interpolate its depth from its surroundings and use the cells of the resulting point. Otherwise, as for the sky, we define its cells by viewing direction per 2 m camera-position cell, so they also remain bounded by the explored region of the scene.

    Writing.

    Each view writes only to the cells whose size matches the scale at which it sees a surface (fine cells for a close-up and coarse cells for a distant view). We measure this scale by the footprint f(p) of each pixel p, the width of the patch of surface that it covers. As a token j spans many pixels, it covers a larger patch of width F(j). On mesh surfaces, a pixel p of token j writes to the cells of every size from f(p) to F(j),

    W(p)={ℓ:f(p)≤s_ℓ≤F(j)}, p∈Ωⱼ.

    		(A3)

    If no size lies in this range, the pixel ignores the upper bound and writes to the smallest s_ℓ≥f(p). Agent boxes, holes, and the sky each have only two cell sizes (Tab.A4), and their pixels write to both. In practice, we rasterize the mesh at half the video resolution for efficiency, as cells and tokens are both far coarser than a pixel. A token then spans 16×16 pixels, and we set F(j) to 16 times the median footprint of its pixels.

    Storage.

    We compress each stored token 18-fold without degrading consistency (Tab.A1). The keys and values of a token form a vector v of 2×36×8×128=73,728 numbers, over 36 layers with 8 heads of 128 dimensions. We fit a principal component basis to these vectors once, on rollouts of the causal renderer before memory distillation. We then project each vector onto this basis and store its coefficients at 8-bit precision (FP8),

    q=FP8(Λ⁻¹ U^⊤S⁻¹(v-μ)),

    		(A4)

    where μ is the mean of v, the diagonal matrix S holds its standard deviation per head, the columns of U are the 8,192 leading principal components, and the diagonal matrix Λ scales each coefficient to unit variance. When a token is read, we invert these steps, v̂=μ+S UΛ q. Each stored token takes 8,192 bytes instead of 147,456 at 16-bit precision. On the 46 ScanNet++ trajectories, the stored tokens thus take at most 0.21 GiB instead of 3.70 GiB. Over the 8,001-frame rollout of Fig.7b, they take 5.95 GiB instead of 107 GiB. Even a rollout that kept every token it generates would add 1.7 GiB per 1,000 frames at 704×1280 instead of 30 GiB.

    Reading.

    As in writing, each pixel reads at the scale at which it sees a surface. On mesh surfaces, a pixel p reads the finest cell that holds an observation and is at least as large as its footprint (s_ℓ≥f(p)). Without this bound, a distant view would read the fine cells of an earlier close-up instead of the cells at its own scale. For agent boxes, holes, and the sky, we omit this bound, and a pixel reads the finest of its two cells that holds an observation. Each token only retrieves past tokens from earlier visits to a surface. We thus exclude from the selection of Eq.2 the observations made since the surface last came into view, as well as those whose tokens are still in the temporal cache, as the reading token attends to them directly. The selection with the latest observations also skips the chunk already selected with the first observations, such that the two retrieved tokens come from different chunks.

    Memory conditioning.

    In every layer, each token attends to the tokens retrieved for its chunk, both in the denoising steps and when the generated chunk is re-encoded for the temporal cache. We decompress the retrieved tokens into keys and values before attention, and never add them to this cache. As keys are stored without positional encoding [92, 50, 90], we apply the backbone’s rotary encoding [60] when they are read. We give each retrieved token the spatial position of the reading token and a time that is a fixed 8 latents (32 frames) earlier, regardless of when it was observed. A token retrieved by token i at latent time tᵢ and spatial position (hᵢ,wᵢ) is thus placed at

    (tᵢ-8, hᵢ, wᵢ).

    		(A5)

    With chunks of 2 latents and a cache of one chunk, the current chunk sits at {t-1,t}, the previous chunk at {t-3,t-2}, and the re-anchored initial chunk at t-4, such that the retrieved tokens at {t-9,t-8} lie beyond the temporal cache. We compare this placement to alternatives in Fig.A3. Larger offsets (e.g., 16 or 32 latents) also work, while placing retrieved tokens at the time they were observed is less consistent over long rollouts.

    Multiple agents.

    Several agents can share the surface memory although we train with a single view at a time, as the memory indexes tokens by the surfaces they depict rather than by the view that generated them (Tab.3). At inference, all agents generate a chunk before any of them writes, and their observations then enter the memory together, ordered by agent index where several agents write to the same cell. The result thus does not depend on the order in which the agents run. Each agent runs on its own GPU. Each agent reads the observations of the other agents under the same rules as its own, including those from their first frames, which are not in its temporal cache. It skips the observations that another agent made in the previous chunk or since the surface last came into its own view. Two agents that look at the same surface would otherwise read each other’s latest frames at every chunk, causing temporal inconsistencies.

    Agents also keep their appearance from one meeting to the next (Tab.3). In third-person videos, each agent starts from a first frame that shows it only from behind, so another view that first sees its front has to guess its appearance. As a written guess would stay in the memory for the rest of the video, an agent’s box is only written by its own view and by the given first frames of other views, which are not generated. A token on the box in turn attends only to the tokens retrieved for itself, as those retrieved for the rest of its chunk would mix in the appearance of other agents. It also attends to reference tokens of that agent, taken from the agent’s own view (its first frame and its latest chunk that shows the agent) and from the given first frames of other views that show it. We empirically place these references 48 latents before the reading token (16 or 32 also work), apart from the retrieved tokens at t-8, and add \ln4 to their attention logits, which weights them four-fold so that the renderer draws unseen sides of an agent consistently with its observed views (AppendixH).

    Appendix E Training and Inference

    Data.

    Although we fine-tune Cosmos3-Nano [60] (Fig.A4) only on synthetic episodes rendered in Unreal Engine with Isekai3D [39], M2R transfers zero-shot to every dataset that we evaluate on (AppendixG), including real indoor scans and worlds authored by coding agents. The training set has about 200,000 episodes of 60 s at 30 FPS and 720×1280, which span 223 environments. Each episode has one to eight agents drawn from 367 human and 34 non-human characters, and every agent is followed by its own camera, which gives about 850,000 single-view videos. We render non-human characters only in single-agent episodes. We render each video a second time along the same camera path without agents, and each render comes with its proxy video (Fig.A2). Until memory distillation, half of the training clips show agents and the other half do not. We train on one view at a time, on clips of 129 to 513 frames at 480×832 (480p) or 704×1280 (720p). Despite never training on two views of a world together or on more than 513 frames, M2R nearly doubles the best cross-agent consistency among the baselines (Tab.3) on episodes of two to four times that length (Sec.G.3).

    Stages and hyperparameters.

    We train M2R in five stages on 64 GB200 GPUs (Tab.A5), starting each stage from the exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights of the previous one. We first train a bidirectional model for 23,000 iterations on clips of 129, 257, and then 513 frames at both resolutions, using AdamW [53] with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁵. We then make it causal with 2,000 iterations of teacher forcing at the same learning rate, and distill it into four steps with 500 iterations of Causal CD [112] at 2×10⁻⁶. We next train it on its own rollouts with 2,000 iterations of Self Forcing, using learning rates of 2×10⁻⁶ for the generator and 4×10⁻⁷ for the fake score function. Throughout causal training, we draw each chunk’s sliding window uniformly from one to 15 chunks or the entire past. Finally, we teach the renderer to use its memory with only 300 iterations of memory distillation on 513-frame clips at 704×1280, with λ=0.1.

    Memory distillation.

    In each iteration of memory distillation (AlgorithmA1), the renderer rolls out all chunks of a clip with a temporal cache of one chunk, reading from and writing to the surface memory as at inference (AppendixD). In 70% of the iterations, the clip is a palindrome with one, two, or four round trips, which we build from agent-free clips only. In the rest, it is a clip with agents, played forward. We apply L_DMD to every clip, with a teacher and a fake score function that see the whole clip and have no memory. We apply L_SD to palindromes only and vary its weight λ in Fig.A5. In the ablation without revisiting rollouts (Tab.4), we apply L_SD to forward agent-free clips using the same frozen teacher. A larger λ improves consistency but softens textures. Because the synthetic ground-truth renders in Fig.A5 are less vivid and less detailed than photorealistic video, we empirically choose λ=0.1 for the best balance of visual quality and consistency across diverse scenes.

    Sampling.

    At test time, M2R renders each eight-frame chunk in two steps, at noise levels 1 and 0.625, without classifier-free guidance. Although we distill the renderer into four steps, we find that two-step and four-step results differ negligibly, as the mesh geometry and the memory provide strong signals. The renderer is trained on 30 FPS videos, as used in the 8,001-frame rollout of Fig.7b, whereas our quantitative benchmarks follow Orbia’s 16 FPS convention (AppendixG).

    Appendix F FastVAE

    The Wan 2.2 VAE [81] of the base model provides high-quality reconstructions but is slow, taking 225 ms to decode an eight-frame chunk at 704×1280 on a GB200 (and still 143 ms when compiled), more than half of the 416 ms that M2R spends on the chunk when using it. Open-source tiny decoders for the same latents [3, 16, 73] are far faster but degrade PSNR by 4 to 7 dB (Fig.A6). FlashDecoder [38] instead replaces the decoder with a streaming transformer but keeps the original encoder, which M2R runs on the proxy video of every chunk (AppendixC). We thus build upon FlashDecoder and learn the encoder as well, allowing FastVAE to replace the entire Wan 2.2 VAE without changing its latent space (Fig.A8). FastVAE matches the quality of the original while running an order of magnitude faster (Tab.A7), more than doubling the frame rate of M2R (19.2 to 41.1 FPS) without degrading consistency (Tab.4).

    Architecture.

    As in FlashDecoder, our decoder is a streaming transformer that flattens each latent frame of size H^′×W^′ into H^′W^′ tokens, where each latent frame attends to itself and the previous one through cached keys and values (Fig.A8). However, FlashDecoder attends over the whole frame, at a cost that grows quadratically with resolution. We instead use Swin Transformer blocks [51], which attend within 16×16 windows (shifted by 8 tokens in every other block) at a cost that grows only linearly. With full-frame attention, the same decoder takes 37% longer at 704×1280 and 99% longer at 1088×1920 on a GB200, with no noticeable gain in quality. To map tokens to pixels, FlashDecoder uses a single 16× pixel shuffle, whereas we upsample progressively, by 2× with Swin Transformer blocks, by 2× with ConvNeXt blocks [52], and by 4× with a pixel shuffle. We build the encoder from the same blocks over spatiotemporal patches of 4×16×16 pixels, such that it encodes a chunk in 3.5 ms instead of the 63.5 ms of the Wan 2.2 encoder. The decoder comes in four sizes (Tab.A6), which trade speed for quality (Fig.A6). Throughout the paper, M2R uses FastVAE-XL, for both its scores and its frame rate.

    Training.

    As FastVAE has to stay in the latent space of the Wan 2.2 VAE, we train its decoder and encoder one at a time against the frozen original, and then both end to end. The decoder first learns to reconstruct a clip x from the latents of the frozen Wan 2.2 encoder, at 224×224 and then at 480p to 1080p, with

    L_dec=∥x̂-x∥₁+λ₂ ∥x̂-x∥₂²+λₚ LPIPS(x̂,x),

    		(A6)

    where λ₂=10 and λₚ=0.5. We drop the adversarial loss of FlashDecoder, which had a negligible effect on our decoder. The encoder then learns to regress the same latents with the decoder frozen, and a final end-to-end phase trains both networks to reconstruct the clip through the encoder and the decoder. To match the general-purpose latent space of the Wan 2.2 VAE, all phases train FastVAE on a mixture of publicly released web videos [59, 45] and synthetic episodes rendered with Isekai3D [39], whereas the renderer itself is fine-tuned only on synthetic data (AppendixE). We optimize weight matrices with Muon [49] and the remaining parameters with AdamW [53], on 64 A100 GPUs.

item.title: 镜头转开再回来，会动的物体就变异或消失了：OmniPersist 把透视视角与全景演化耦合起来 ｜ OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution
item.description:
一句话：受限于有限视角，画外运动实体在潜空间里无法合理演化。

要点：

  • 问题定位：动作条件世界模型对机器人与自动驾驶至关重要，但现有视频扩散模型**难以维持动态物体的持久性**——当相机转开再转回来时，**画外的运动实体在潜空间里无法合理演化，常常变异或直接消失**
  • 根因是表示：**有限的透视视角**里没有承载画外实体的结构
  • OmniPersist 因此把**透视视角与其全景表示耦合**起来做演化，使动态物体在离开视野后仍有可延续的状态

为什么值得看：11-19 的 PanoEvo 解决的是「静态画外世界冻住」，这条进一步处理**会动的**画外物体——难度更高，因为运动也需要被延续。二者合起来说明：全景/球面表示正在成为世界模型的标准状态容器。

中文摘要：动作条件的世界模型在机器人与自动驾驶中很关键，但现有视频扩散模型难以维持动态物体的持久性：当相机转开再转回来时，视野之外的移动实体会在潜空间中演化得不合理，常常发生变异或彻底消失——根本原因是有限的透视视角里没有承载画外实体的结构。OmniPersist 因此提出一个统一框架，把透视视角与全景表示耦合起来做联合演化，使动态物体在离开视野之后仍然保有可延续的状态。与只处理静态画外世界的方案相比，这条把「动态」也纳入了持久性要求。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling
via Coupled Panoramic Evolution

Abstract

Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

1 Introduction

World models [34, 47, 64, 36, 10] aim to predict future states from current observations conditioned on actions, playing an increasingly important role in robotics [19, 52] and autonomous driving [22, 44]. A prevalent paradigm generates future videos via diffusion models [3, 26, 54, 39], guided by textual prompts alongside camera trajectories or discrete motion signals, as demonstrated by LingBot-World [36, 10] and Matrix-Game 3.0 [47]. Despite demonstrating compelling visual fidelity through large-scale training, these models fundamentally struggle to maintain object persistence in dynamic scenes. When the viewpoint shifts away and subsequently returns, out-of-view objects fail to evolve plausibly in the latent space. As a result, their visual consistency and motion continuity break down, even causing returning entities to mutate or vanish entirely.

We attribute this limitation to both training data biases and fundamental modeling bottlenecks. On the data side, current training data for dynamic scenes heavily favor continuous tracking, rarely featuring scenarios where moving entities exit and subsequently re-enter the camera’s field of view (FoV). On the modeling side, vanilla diffusion models are inherently limited in preserving out-of-view dynamics without dedicated constraints and priors. Recent works have recognized this challenge and sought to mitigate it mainly from two perspectives. Some methods utilize retrieval frames [6] and compressed implicit contexts [56] as memory. Others attempt to predict dynamics of specific entity through auxiliary generative models [8] and LLMs [40]. However, the former often recall static appearance cues that fail to reflect continuous natural motion, while the latter introduce heavy system complexity and scale poorly to multi-entity scenarios. Furthermore, these methods are designed primarily for object consistency across temporal chunks. In fact, even within a single video chunk, combining intra-window bidirectional attention with advanced camera control approaches (e.g., UCPE [60]) remains insufficient to sustain out-of-view dynamic evolution.

To address this problem, we propose modeling scene evolution in panoramic space, leveraging complete 360^∘ spatial context to improve the persistence of dynamic world models. This paradigm offers two distinct advantages. First, conceptually, the omnidirectional nature of panoramic space ensures that when an object leaves the camera view, its continuous motion can still be explicitly predicted on a global canvas. Moreover, this formulation naturally supports multiple moving objects and inherently preserves background memory, as shown in Fig. 1. Second, practically, panoramic scenes can be represented as standard 2D frames via equirectangular projection (ERP), allowing existing video diffusion foundation models to adapt seamlessly to panoramic data while fully capitalizing on their strong pretrained priors.

Specifically, we propose OmniPersist, which jointly models the perspective camera view and its panoramic counterpart within a single video diffusion model. This unified framework achieves persistent dynamic world modeling in an end-to-end manner, without relying on auxiliary models or additional input. Since generating a dense panorama for every perspective frame introduces heavy computational overhead, we propose to design the panoramic stream to operate at a lower frame rate. To effectively bridge these two representations across space and time, we introduce two complementary modules, i.e., Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) and Temporal Compensation (TemComp). In particular, GeoAnch establishes explicit geometric correspondences between the perspective and panoramic views, enabling direct feature exchange at synchronized timestamps. Meanwhile, TemComp aggregates features across neighboring frames, effectively compensating for the temporal discrepancy caused by the differing frame rates. Concurrently, AlayaVista [33] (within the past two months) also explores panoramic representations, but relies on a multi-stage pipeline of panoramic initialization, state evolution, and perspective refinement. In contrast, OmniPersist avoids generating redundant full-rate panoramas, establishing a single-stage, unified framework for persistent dynamic world modeling.

To ensure broad applicability, OmniPersist is designed to be agnostic to underlying camera-control architectures. We integrate our framework with two representative paradigms, i.e., latent-level trajectory injection via CameraCtrl [11] and attention-level pose conditioning via UCPE [60]. Furthermore, to benchmark dynamic persistence under complex camera movements, we construct a paired panoramic–perspective dataset featuring diverse trajectory patterns. We systematically evaluate OmniPersist under two settings, namely image-to-video (I2V) generation and video continuation. Extensive experiments across visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence demonstrate that our coupled panoramic evolution yields consistent gains across both control mechanisms.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose OmniPersist, a single-stage unified framework that jointly generates perspective video and temporally sparse panoramic evolution to improve out-of-view dynamic persistence.

  • •

    We introduce GeoAnch and TemComp to couple dense perspective and sparse panoramic streams through synchronized geometric exchange and neighboring-time feature aggregation.

  • •

    We construct a paired panoramic–perspective dynamic dataset and demonstrate consistent gains in dynamic persistence and revisit consistency across diverse camera-control mechanisms.

    • 2 Related Work

    Camera-Controlled Video Generation. Camera trajectory control has become an essential capability for interactive world models [34, 47, 64, 36, 10]. Existing efforts encompass text-to-video [46, 1], image-to-video [21, 28, 63], and video re-shooting [2, 57, 35], and roughly divide into two paradigms. (1) Camera-parameter conditioning directly encodes viewpoints as extrinsic matrices [46], Plücker rays [11, 1], or relative positional embeddings [17, 60, 55]. These representations are used to modulate feature latents via auxiliary branches [11, 1] or inject geometric biases into attention mechanisms [60, 55, 17]. These methods operate strictly within the visible frustum, offering no spatial substrate to sustain the evolution of out-of-view dynamic entities. (2) Explicit 3D reprojection grounds camera trajectories by warping reconstructed 3D geometry into target image or latent spaces. For instance, ViewCrafter [58] and GEN3C [28] condition diffusion on rendered point clouds with iterative scene expansion or 3D caching. MosaicMem [59] retrieves 3D-lifted patches from spatial memory, whereas LSM-World [43] caches 3D latent tokens directly to bypass RGB rendering and re-encoding. However, these approaches rely heavily on external depth estimators and are predominantly restricted to static scenes. In contrast, OmniPersist bypasses 3D reconstruction and provides an omnidirectional canvas that naturally sustains unseen dynamic evolution. It acts as an orthogonal, plug-and-play spatial substrate, seamlessly integrating with the camera-parameter conditioning paradigm.

    Persistent Dynamic World Modeling. World models simulate future states conditioned on current observations and actions. A prevalent paradigm generates future videos guided by text and camera trajectories [47, 64, 36, 10]. However, maintaining the evolving states of dynamic out-of-view entities remains an unresolved challenge. Existing approaches broadly follow three directions. (1) Memory-based modeling. HyDRA [6] and MemLearner [56] query or compress historical observations to preserve generation consistency. ReMind [51] employs a node-structured curriculum that compels the model to retrieve relevant historical states. While historical memory provides informative anchors, these methods inherently infer unobserved evolution from past evidence, often struggling to sustain continuous visual transitions. (2) Auxiliary entity tracking. LiveWorld [8] uses multiple generative monitors to advance unseen entity states within a persistent scene, while WorldDirector [40] employs an LLM to predict object trajectories prior to visual generation. However, relying on external entity-level monitors or LLM planners introduces heavy system overhead, causes pipeline brittleness, and scales poorly to dense, multi-entity interactive scenarios. (3) Panoramic world-state modeling. In concurrent work, AlayaVista [33] first evolves panoramic latent states and then synthesizes perspective observations through viewport rendering and refinement stages. However, it relies on a separate panorama initialization stage and incurs high computational costs by predicting full-rate panoramas. In contrast, OmniPersist derives its panoramic conditions directly from the observed perspective prefix and predicts panoramic states at a lower temporal rate, establishing a single-stage joint diffusion framework.

    Panoramic Video Generation. Panoramic video generation aims to synthesize temporally coherent 360^∘ content, typically achieved by adapting pretrained perspective video diffusion models. Therein, perspective-to-panorama methods expand input videos while preserving their content and dynamics [24, 20, 48, 50], whereas text- and image-conditioned approaches synthesize omnidirectional scenes and motion [42, 61, 9, 49, 50]. Recent methods further extend panoramic synthesis to camera-controlled exploration [18, 32] and 3D world construction [41, 53, 7]. Technically, these methods address spherical distortion and boundary seams through ERP-aware designs [49, 48, 32], cross-view coherence via multi-view attention [9, 50], and exploration consistency through geometric guidance and spatial memory [41, 53, 18, 7]. Collectively, these advances establish the feasibility of using video diffusion models to evolve panoramic states. Unlike prior works targeting standalone panoramic synthesis, OmniPersist couples an efficient, low-rate panoramic stream with perspective rollouts to anchor out-of-view dynamic persistence.

    3 Method

    3.1 Overview

    We study persistent dynamic world modeling where dynamic subjects may leave and subsequently re-enter the camera field of view. Given a textual prompt, an observed perspective prefix X_0:K-1, and a T-frame camera trajectory Cˣ with known intrinsics, the objective is to synthesize the remaining frames of the T-frame perspective video X. Crucially, returning subjects must maintain identity consistency and plausible physical motion throughout the interval spent outside the viewport.

    OmniPersist addresses this task by jointly generating X alongside a temporally sparse panoramic video P. The panoramic stream captures scene evolution across all viewing directions, while the perspective stream adheres to the prescribed camera trajectory (see Fig. 1). Both streams share a single diffusion transformer backbone and exchange features via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) and Temporal Compensation (TemComp), as illustrated in Fig. 2. Both streams rely solely on the perspective prefix, text prompt, and camera parameters, without requiring any auxiliary depth, panoramic images, or video inputs.

    3.2 Coupled Panoramic Evolution

    We jointly denoise the dense perspective stream and the panoramic stream using a shared pretrained video diffusion transformer [39]. Because predicting a full-rate panoramic stream incurs prohibitive computational overhead, we design the panoramic stream to operate at a lower frame rate. With a panoramic sampling interval s, panoramic frame Pⱼ corresponds to perspective frame Xₛⱼ in a T-frame video, yielding J=(T-1)/s+1 states over the same temporal horizon. These states can represent scene dynamics across all viewing directions around the camera, including regions outside the perspective viewport.

    Joint Denoising of Perspective and Panoramic Streams. For each stream, the noisy latents and corresponding VAE-encoded [16] visual conditions are concatenated channel-wise and mapped into token sequences via view-specific input projections. The resulting token sequences from both perspective and panoramic streams are then concatenated along the sequence dimension. Joint spatiotemporal self-attention subsequently processes both streams under a shared text prompt and diffusion timestep, after which a shared prediction head outputs the flow fields to be split and reshaped back into their respective latent grids. Retaining per-view spatial RoPE [30], we assign temporal RoPE coordinates i and sj to perspective and panoramic latent frames i and j (corresponding to original frame timestamps 4i and 4sj under 4× temporal VAE compression), aligning synchronized states.

    Visual Conditions. We construct two visual conditions from the observed perspective prefix X_0:K-1. The perspective condition comprises the VAE encoding of the prefix concatenated with an indicator mask denoting known frames. To construct the panoramic condition, the observed frames are reprojected onto equirectangular projection (ERP) coordinates using camera poses and intrinsics, encoded via the VAE, and concatenated with a spatial visibility mask. Unobserved future frames and unmapped ERP regions are filled with zeros prior to VAE encoding. Crucially, both condition tensors are derived from the single perspective prefix, requiring no auxiliary visual inputs.

    Camera Conditions. We align the initial panoramic coordinate frame with the first perspective view (centered at the ERP center), so both cameras share the same initial orientation. Representing camera-to-world poses as Cₜˣ,Cⱼᵖ∈ℝ^4×4 and the pure-rotation viewport transformation from the perspective to the panoramic frame as Vₜ∈ℝ^4×4 (with V₀=I), the panoramic pose is obtained as Cⱼᵖ=CₛⱼˣVₛⱼ⁻¹. This operation eliminates viewport rotation while preserving shared camera centers, yielding J=(T-1)/s+1 panoramic poses when subsampling every s frames. During training, Vₜ is known from the viewport rotations used to render perspective clips from source panoramas. At inference, the panoramic camera retains the initial perspective orientation R₀ˣ∈ℝ^3×3, setting the rotation component of Vₜ to (R₀ˣ)^⊤Rₜˣ. Consequently, all required poses are determined solely by the input perspective trajectory without additional camera inputs.

    3.3 Geometric Anchoring

    Because spatial RoPE [30] in diffusion transformers operates independently on separate image grids, it does not explicitly capture geometric correspondences between perspective and panoramic views. Although spherical positional embeddings, such as SpheRoPE [13], offer an alternative formulation, directly replacing pretrained spatial RoPE with spherical coordinates disrupts learned spatial priors and impedes joint optimization. We therefore introduce Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) to establish explicit cross-view correspondences while preserving the pretrained spatial encoding.

    Hereafter, i and j index perspective and panoramic latent frames (corresponding to RGB frames 4i and 4j), respectively. Let q denote the image-space patch center of a perspective token, and let Aᵢ∈ℝ^3×3, Rᵢˣ∈ℝ^3×3, and Rⱼᵖ∈ℝ^3×3 denote the corresponding camera intrinsics and rotations. At synchronized timestamps (i=sj), both views share an optical center, yielding the mapping:

    π_i→j(q)=Πₑᵣₚ ((Rⱼᵖ)^⊤RᵢˣAᵢ⁻¹q̃),

    		(1)

    where q̃ is the homogeneous image coordinate and Πₑᵣₚ projects a 3D ray onto the panoramic grid. Conversely, panoramic directions that fall within the perspective field of view are mapped back to the perspective grid using the inverse geometric transformation.

    Based on these geometric correspondences, GeoAnch bilinearly samples aligned features from the other view, concatenates them with the current view’s features, and estimates a residual update using a learned linear layer. Because the perspective camera observes only a sub-region of the visual sphere, updates to the panoramic stream are masked to the perspective field of view. In addition, feature sampling on the ERP grid employs horizontal circular wrapping to preserve spherical boundary continuity.

    3.4 Temporal Compensation

    Due to the temporal sparsity of the panoramic stream, intermediate perspective frames lack synchronized panoramic anchors. Temporal Compensation (TemComp) bridges this gap through bidirectional cross-temporal feature aggregation. For each intermediate perspective frame, TemComp performs interpolation between its two adjacent panoramic states. Conversely, each panoramic frame aggregates a local temporal window of perspective features centered at its synchronized timestamp to learn a correction relative to its synchronized geometric anchor.

    Let g denote a query patch feature representation of the current frame. Following the ray projection in Eq. (1), we map each patch location of the current frame into candidate frames of the other view, bilinearly sampling features to obtain h̃ₖ at candidate timestamp k. Candidate features are aggregated as:

    h̄(g) = ∑_k∈ℕ(g) αₖh̃ₖ, αₖ∝\exp (cos(g,h̃ₖ)/θ),

    		(2)

    where ℕ(g) spans two bracketing panoramic frames for perspective queries, or up to 2⌊s/2⌋+1 centered perspective frames for panoramic queries. The aggregation weights αₖ are normalized to sum to one, and θ=0.2 serves as the temperature hyperparameter. The geometric mapping provides approximate directional correspondences to guide candidate sampling, while feature similarity suppresses incompatible evidence across time.

    To update representations, TemComp incorporates a learned linear residual layer for each exchange direction, preserving base features while attenuating unreliable contributions. Specifically, synchronized perspective frames retain their direct GeoAnch updates, whereas intermediate perspective frames receive a residual computed from the aggregated representation h̄. TemComp is thus formulated as a conservative local feature correction around synchronized geometric anchors, enabling the model to selectively exploit neighboring temporal observations.

    3.5 Training and Inference

    Perspective frames are directly encoded using the pretrained VAE [16]. For panoramic targets, we adopt circular latent encoding [48], which applies horizontal circular padding to ERP frames prior to VAE encoding and subsequently crops the padded latent margins to restore the original grid dimensions. This provides a seamless latent representation across horizontal boundaries for diffusion training.

    Flow matching and loss optimization operate directly on these latent spaces. For each view v∈{x,p}, we sample independent Gaussian noise εᵛ∼ℕ(0,I) at a shared noise level σ∈[0,1] to define the linear interpolation and velocity target:

    z_σᵛ=(1-σ)zᵛ+σεᵛ, uᵛ=εᵛ-zᵛ.

    		(3)

    The diffusion transformer jointly predicts the velocity fields ûˣ and ûᵖ. We train the model by minimizing the weighted objective:

    L = 𝔼_σ,ε [w(σ)/2(∥ûˣ - uˣ∥² + ∥Wₚ⊙(ûᵖ - uᵖ)∥²)],

    		(4)

    where w(σ) is the scheduler weight and Wₚ denotes a normalized, latitude-dependent loss weight for the panoramic canvas. During training, the LoRA [14] parameters, input projections, camera conditioning modules, and cross-view interaction layers are optimized jointly, while the VAE and text encoder remain frozen.

    During inference, the shared VAE can decode both streams. When panoramic visualization is not explicitly required, only the perspective stream is decoded, incurring zero additional decoding overhead.

    4 Experiments
