Second, practically, panoramic scenes can be represented as standard 2D frames via equirectangular projection (ERP), allowing existing video diffusion foundation models to adapt seamlessly to panoramic data while fully capitalizing on their strong pretrained priors.

Specifically, we propose OmniPersist, which jointly models the perspective camera view and its panoramic counterpart within a single video diffusion model. This unified framework achieves persistent dynamic world modeling in an end-to-end manner, without relying on auxiliary models or additional input. Since generating a dense panorama for every perspective frame introduces heavy computational overhead, we propose to design the panoramic stream to operate at a lower frame rate. To effectively bridge these two representations across space and time, we introduce two complementary modules, i.e., Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) and Temporal Compensation (TemComp). In particular, GeoAnch establishes explicit geometric correspondences between the perspective and panoramic views, enabling direct feature exchange at synchronized timestamps. Meanwhile, TemComp aggregates features across neighboring frames, effectively compensating for the temporal discrepancy caused by the differing frame rates. Concurrently, AlayaVista [33] (within the past two months) also explores panoramic representations, but relies on a multi-stage pipeline of panoramic initialization, state evolution, and perspective refinement. In contrast, OmniPersist avoids generating redundant full-rate panoramas, establishing a single-stage, unified framework for persistent dynamic world modeling.

To ensure broad applicability, OmniPersist is designed to be agnostic to underlying camera-control architectures. We integrate our framework with two representative paradigms, i.e., latent-level trajectory injection via CameraCtrl [11] and attention-level pose conditioning via UCPE [60]. Furthermore, to benchmark dynamic persistence under complex camera movements, we construct a paired panoramic–perspective dataset featuring diverse trajectory patterns. We systematically evaluate OmniPersist under two settings, namely image-to-video (I2V) generation and video continuation. Extensive experiments across visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence demonstrate that our coupled panoramic evolution yields consistent gains across both control mechanisms.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose OmniPersist, a single-stage unified framework that jointly generates perspective video and temporally sparse panoramic evolution to improve out-of-view dynamic persistence.

  • •

    We introduce GeoAnch and TemComp to couple dense perspective and sparse panoramic streams through synchronized geometric exchange and neighboring-time feature aggregation.

  • •

    We construct a paired panoramic–perspective dynamic dataset and demonstrate consistent gains in dynamic persistence and revisit consistency across diverse camera-control mechanisms.

    • 2 Related Work

    Camera-Controlled Video Generation. Camera trajectory control has become an essential capability for interactive world models [34, 47, 64, 36, 10]. Existing efforts encompass text-to-video [46, 1], image-to-video [21, 28, 63], and video re-shooting [2, 57, 35], and roughly divide into two paradigms. (1) Camera-parameter conditioning directly encodes viewpoints as extrinsic matrices [46], Plücker rays [11, 1], or relative positional embeddings [17, 60, 55]. These representations are used to modulate feature latents via auxiliary branches [11, 1] or inject geometric biases into attention mechanisms [60, 55, 17]. These methods operate strictly within the visible frustum, offering no spatial substrate to sustain the evolution of out-of-view dynamic entities. (2) Explicit 3D reprojection grounds camera trajectories by warping reconstructed 3D geometry into target image or latent spaces. For instance, ViewCrafter [58] and GEN3C [28] condition diffusion on rendered point clouds with iterative scene expansion or 3D caching. MosaicMem [59] retrieves 3D-lifted patches from spatial memory, whereas LSM-World [43] caches 3D latent tokens directly to bypass RGB rendering and re-encoding. However, these approaches rely heavily on external depth estimators and are predominantly restricted to static scenes. In contrast, OmniPersist bypasses 3D reconstruction and provides an omnidirectional canvas that naturally sustains unseen dynamic evolution. It acts as an orthogonal, plug-and-play spatial substrate, seamlessly integrating with the camera-parameter conditioning paradigm.

    Persistent Dynamic World Modeling. World models simulate future states conditioned on current observations and actions. A prevalent paradigm generates future videos guided by text and camera trajectories [47, 64, 36, 10]. However, maintaining the evolving states of dynamic out-of-view entities remains an unresolved challenge. Existing approaches broadly follow three directions. (1) Memory-based modeling. HyDRA [6] and MemLearner [56] query or compress historical observations to preserve generation consistency. ReMind [51] employs a node-structured curriculum that compels the model to retrieve relevant historical states. While historical memory provides informative anchors, these methods inherently infer unobserved evolution from past evidence, often struggling to sustain continuous visual transitions. (2) Auxiliary entity tracking. LiveWorld [8] uses multiple generative monitors to advance unseen entity states within a persistent scene, while WorldDirector [40] employs an LLM to predict object trajectories prior to visual generation. However, relying on external entity-level monitors or LLM planners introduces heavy system overhead, causes pipeline brittleness, and scales poorly to dense, multi-entity interactive scenarios. (3) Panoramic world-state modeling. In concurrent work, AlayaVista [33] first evolves panoramic latent states and then synthesizes perspective observations through viewport rendering and refinement stages. However, it relies on a separate panorama initialization stage and incurs high computational costs by predicting full-rate panoramas. In contrast, OmniPersist derives its panoramic conditions directly from the observed perspective prefix and predicts panoramic states at a lower temporal rate, establishing a single-stage joint diffusion framework.

    Panoramic Video Generation. Panoramic video generation aims to synthesize temporally coherent 360^∘ content, typically achieved by adapting pretrained perspective video diffusion models. Therein, perspective-to-panorama methods expand input videos while preserving their content and dynamics [24, 20, 48, 50], whereas text- and image-conditioned approaches synthesize omnidirectional scenes and motion [42, 61, 9, 49, 50]. Recent methods further extend panoramic synthesis to camera-controlled exploration [18, 32] and 3D world construction [41, 53, 7]. Technically, these methods address spherical distortion and boundary seams through ERP-aware designs [49, 48, 32], cross-view coherence via multi-view attention [9, 50], and exploration consistency through geometric guidance and spatial memory [41, 53, 18, 7]. Collectively, these advances establish the feasibility of using video diffusion models to evolve panoramic states. Unlike prior works targeting standalone panoramic synthesis, OmniPersist couples an efficient, low-rate panoramic stream with perspective rollouts to anchor out-of-view dynamic persistence.

    3 Method

    3.1 Overview

    We study persistent dynamic world modeling where dynamic subjects may leave and subsequently re-enter the camera field of view. Given a textual prompt, an observed perspective prefix X_0:K-1, and a T-frame camera trajectory Cˣ with known intrinsics, the objective is to synthesize the remaining frames of the T-frame perspective video X. Crucially, returning subjects must maintain identity consistency and plausible physical motion throughout the interval spent outside the viewport.

    OmniPersist addresses this task by jointly generating X alongside a temporally sparse panoramic video P. The panoramic stream captures scene evolution across all viewing directions, while the perspective stream adheres to the prescribed camera trajectory (see Fig. 1). Both streams share a single diffusion transformer backbone and exchange features via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) and Temporal Compensation (TemComp), as illustrated in Fig. 2. Both streams rely solely on the perspective prefix, text prompt, and camera parameters, without requiring any auxiliary depth, panoramic images, or video inputs.

    3.2 Coupled Panoramic Evolution

    We jointly denoise the dense perspective stream and the panoramic stream using a shared pretrained video diffusion transformer [39]. Because predicting a full-rate panoramic stream incurs prohibitive computational overhead, we design the panoramic stream to operate at a lower frame rate. With a panoramic sampling interval s, panoramic frame Pⱼ corresponds to perspective frame Xₛⱼ in a T-frame video, yielding J=(T-1)/s+1 states over the same temporal horizon. These states can represent scene dynamics across all viewing directions around the camera, including regions outside the perspective viewport.

    Joint Denoising of Perspective and Panoramic Streams. For each stream, the noisy latents and corresponding VAE-encoded [16] visual conditions are concatenated channel-wise and mapped into token sequences via view-specific input projections. The resulting token sequences from both perspective and panoramic streams are then concatenated along the sequence dimension. Joint spatiotemporal self-attention subsequently processes both streams under a shared text prompt and diffusion timestep, after which a shared prediction head outputs the flow fields to be split and reshaped back into their respective latent grids. Retaining per-view spatial RoPE [30], we assign temporal RoPE coordinates i and sj to perspective and panoramic latent frames i and j (corresponding to original frame timestamps 4i and 4sj under 4× temporal VAE compression), aligning synchronized states.

    Visual Conditions. We construct two visual conditions from the observed perspective prefix X_0:K-1. The perspective condition comprises the VAE encoding of the prefix concatenated with an indicator mask denoting known frames. To construct the panoramic condition, the observed frames are reprojected onto equirectangular projection (ERP) coordinates using camera poses and intrinsics, encoded via the VAE, and concatenated with a spatial visibility mask. Unobserved future frames and unmapped ERP regions are filled with zeros prior to VAE encoding. Crucially, both condition tensors are derived from the single perspective prefix, requiring no auxiliary visual inputs.

    Camera Conditions. We align the initial panoramic coordinate frame with the first perspective view (centered at the ERP center), so both cameras share the same initial orientation. Representing camera-to-world poses as Cₜˣ,Cⱼᵖ∈ℝ^4×4 and the pure-rotation viewport transformation from the perspective to the panoramic frame as Vₜ∈ℝ^4×4 (with V₀=I), the panoramic pose is obtained as Cⱼᵖ=CₛⱼˣVₛⱼ⁻¹. This operation eliminates viewport rotation while preserving shared camera centers, yielding J=(T-1)/s+1 panoramic poses when subsampling every s frames. During training, Vₜ is known from the viewport rotations used to render perspective clips from source panoramas. At inference, the panoramic camera retains the initial perspective orientation R₀ˣ∈ℝ^3×3, setting the rotation component of Vₜ to (R₀ˣ)^⊤Rₜˣ. Consequently, all required poses are determined solely by the input perspective trajectory without additional camera inputs.

    3.3 Geometric Anchoring

    Because spatial RoPE [30] in diffusion transformers operates independently on separate image grids, it does not explicitly capture geometric correspondences between perspective and panoramic views. Although spherical positional embeddings, such as SpheRoPE [13], offer an alternative formulation, directly replacing pretrained spatial RoPE with spherical coordinates disrupts learned spatial priors and impedes joint optimization. We therefore introduce Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) to establish explicit cross-view correspondences while preserving the pretrained spatial encoding.

    Hereafter, i and j index perspective and panoramic latent frames (corresponding to RGB frames 4i and 4j), respectively. Let q denote the image-space patch center of a perspective token, and let Aᵢ∈ℝ^3×3, Rᵢˣ∈ℝ^3×3, and Rⱼᵖ∈ℝ^3×3 denote the corresponding camera intrinsics and rotations. At synchronized timestamps (i=sj), both views share an optical center, yielding the mapping:

    π_i→j(q)=Πₑᵣₚ ((Rⱼᵖ)^⊤RᵢˣAᵢ⁻¹q̃),

    		(1)

    where q̃ is the homogeneous image coordinate and Πₑᵣₚ projects a 3D ray onto the panoramic grid. Conversely, panoramic directions that fall within the perspective field of view are mapped back to the perspective grid using the inverse geometric transformation.

    Based on these geometric correspondences, GeoAnch bilinearly samples aligned features from the other view, concatenates them with the current view’s features, and estimates a residual update using a learned linear layer. Because the perspective camera observes only a sub-region of the visual sphere, updates to the panoramic stream are masked to the perspective field of view. In addition, feature sampling on the ERP grid employs horizontal circular wrapping to preserve spherical boundary continuity.

    3.4 Temporal Compensation

    Due to the temporal sparsity of the panoramic stream, intermediate perspective frames lack synchronized panoramic anchors. Temporal Compensation (TemComp) bridges this gap through bidirectional cross-temporal feature aggregation. For each intermediate perspective frame, TemComp performs interpolation between its two adjacent panoramic states. Conversely, each panoramic frame aggregates a local temporal window of perspective features centered at its synchronized timestamp to learn a correction relative to its synchronized geometric anchor.

    Let g denote a query patch feature representation of the current frame. Following the ray projection in Eq. (1), we map each patch location of the current frame into candidate frames of the other view, bilinearly sampling features to obtain h̃ₖ at candidate timestamp k. Candidate features are aggregated as:

    h̄(g) = ∑_k∈ℕ(g) αₖh̃ₖ, αₖ∝\exp (cos(g,h̃ₖ)/θ),

    		(2)

    where ℕ(g) spans two bracketing panoramic frames for perspective queries, or up to 2⌊s/2⌋+1 centered perspective frames for panoramic queries. The aggregation weights αₖ are normalized to sum to one, and θ=0.2 serves as the temperature hyperparameter. The geometric mapping provides approximate directional correspondences to guide candidate sampling, while feature similarity suppresses incompatible evidence across time.

    To update representations, TemComp incorporates a learned linear residual layer for each exchange direction, preserving base features while attenuating unreliable contributions. Specifically, synchronized perspective frames retain their direct GeoAnch updates, whereas intermediate perspective frames receive a residual computed from the aggregated representation h̄. TemComp is thus formulated as a conservative local feature correction around synchronized geometric anchors, enabling the model to selectively exploit neighboring temporal observations.

    3.5 Training and Inference

    Perspective frames are directly encoded using the pretrained VAE [16]. For panoramic targets, we adopt circular latent encoding [48], which applies horizontal circular padding to ERP frames prior to VAE encoding and subsequently crops the padded latent margins to restore the original grid dimensions. This provides a seamless latent representation across horizontal boundaries for diffusion training.

    Flow matching and loss optimization operate directly on these latent spaces. For each view v∈{x,p}, we sample independent Gaussian noise εᵛ∼ℕ(0,I) at a shared noise level σ∈[0,1] to define the linear interpolation and velocity target:

    z_σᵛ=(1-σ)zᵛ+σεᵛ, uᵛ=εᵛ-zᵛ.

    		(3)

    The diffusion transformer jointly predicts the velocity fields ûˣ and ûᵖ. We train the model by minimizing the weighted objective:

    L = 𝔼_σ,ε [w(σ)/2(∥ûˣ - uˣ∥² + ∥Wₚ⊙(ûᵖ - uᵖ)∥²)],

    		(4)

    where w(σ) is the scheduler weight and Wₚ denotes a normalized, latitude-dependent loss weight for the panoramic canvas. During training, the LoRA [14] parameters, input projections, camera conditioning modules, and cross-view interaction layers are optimized jointly, while the VAE and text encoder remain frozen.

    During inference, the shared VAE can decode both streams. When panoramic visualization is not explicitly required, only the perspective stream is decoded, incurring zero additional decoding overhead.

    4 Experiments

item.title: 单项技能都很好，连起来就崩：MESSI 说「带球接射门」失败是因为前一个动作把人和球留在了陌生状态 ｜ MESSI: Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration for Physics-Based Character Control
item.description:
一句话：在孤立情况下表现良好的技能，串起来执行时可能失效。

要点：

  • 现象描述精准：基于物理的足球角色需要完成多种运动技能并**平滑地在它们之间切换**（例如带球转为射门）；但**在孤立情况下表现良好的技能，串起来执行时可能失效**
  • 根因是状态：**前一个行为会把角色与球留在训练时没见过的状态里**
  • MESSI（Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration）因此用共享适配来支持多种技能之间的切换，同时保住原本的技能表现

为什么值得看：「技能串接」是物理角色动画里最真实的失败点，也是游戏与体育模拟的共同需求。这条把问题归因到「状态分布漂移」而不是「控制器不够强」，这决定了修法是把技能之间的状态接起来，而不是继续堆单技能的性能。

中文摘要：基于物理的足球角色需要完成多种运动技能，并在它们之间平滑过渡，例如从带球转入射门。作者指出现有方法的一个通病：在孤立场景下表现良好的技能，串联执行时可能失效，原因是前一个动作会把角色与球带入训练时未见过的不熟悉状态。MESSI（Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration）因此提出一个多专家框架，通过共享适配来实现多种足球技能之间的切换，同时保持各单项技能原有的表现水平。对体育类游戏与物理角色动画来说，这条针对的正是「单招练得好、连招就崩」这个长期难点。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

MESSI: Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration for Physics-Based Character Control

Abstract

Physics-based soccer characters must perform diverse motor skills and transition smoothly between them, such as dribbling into a shot. However, skills that perform well in isolation may fail when executed sequentially, as preceding behaviors can leave the character and ball in unfamiliar states. We present MESSI (Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration), a framework that enables multiple soccer skill transitions through shared adaptation while preserving the original skill policy outside transitions. MESSI first trains eight task-competent experts using motion priors and task rewards, then distills them into a unified, skill-conditioned Transformer. Rather than retraining individual experts for different transitions, we train a shared, context-conditioned low-rank adapter on the frozen student through online reinforcement learning. Activated upon skill switching, the adapter helps the target skill handle unfamiliar entry states, while a learned exit mechanism determines when to return control to the original student. By disabling the adapter during native skill execution, MESSI preserves the original student policy by construction. Experiments across individual skills, skill transitions, and continuous skill chains demonstrate substantial improvements over direct switching, including an increase in dribbling-to-shooting success from 19.8% to 61.8%.

1 Introduction

Soccer presents a challenging setting for physics-based character control, combining whole-body coordination with precise interactions with a dynamically moving ball [Hong et al., 2019, Liu et al., 2022, Haarnoja et al., 2024, Kim et al., 2025, Ye et al., 2026]. A versatile soccer character must perform diverse skills, including locomotion, dribbling, shooting, passing, and trapping, while transitioning between them at speed. For example, a player may shoot immediately after dribbling or receive a pass while running. Such transitions are challenging because the character’s posture, momentum, and ball configuration depend on the preceding behavior and may differ substantially from the states encountered during the target skill’s training. Consequently, even well-trained individual skills can fail when executed sequentially, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Recent advances in physics-based character control have enabled reusable motor skills through motion tracking and large-scale motion pretraining [Peng et al., 2018, Peng et al., 2022, Tessler et al., 2024, Juravsky et al., 2024, Shi et al., 2026]. However, tracking reference motions alone does not guarantee task-specific ball control or reliable transitions absent from the motion data. While independently trained, task-competent experts can optimize individual skill objectives, composing their behaviors remains challenging when the target skill encounters unfamiliar body and ball states. Existing approaches address skill transitions in several ways. Some learn skills and transitions jointly, either through unified multi-skill policies [Ye et al., 2026] or augmented interaction trajectories [Yu et al., 2025]. Such approaches may require revisiting joint policy training or transition data when introducing new transitions, potentially affecting previously learned behaviors. Others employ transition-aware initialization or fine-tuning using predecessor-generated states [Kim et al., 2025, Avinash et al., 2026], coupling transition adaptation to individual skill policies. For more challenging transitions, policy composition methods additionally introduce intermediate behaviors when necessary [Xu et al., 2025a], which can increase transition-specific training and maintenance overhead. While these approaches demonstrate effective skill composition, adapting a growing repertoire of skills without repeatedly modifying individual experts or introducing separate transition modules remains challenging. This motivates a shared adaptation strategy that supports diverse skill transitions while limiting interference with established skill behaviors.

To this end, we present MESSI (Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration), a framework for integrating task-competent soccer skills and enabling their transitions within a unified physics-based controller. MESSI incorporates eight skills: off-ball movement, dribbling, shooting, passing, heading, trapping, stop-and-turn, and getting up. We first train skill-specific experts using motion priors, task rewards, and tailored curricula. Their behaviors are then distilled into a shared skill-conditioned student through a unified observation space. Consolidating the experts into a single skill-conditioned policy provides a common backbone for transition adaptation. This enables different skill pairs to share a single adaptation module, rather than requiring separate adaptations of individual expert policies.

Our key insight is that transition adaptation is needed only after a skill switch, where the target skill encounters unfamiliar states generated by its predecessor. Rather than modifying the target skill everywhere, we introduce a shared, gated, context-conditioned low-rank adapter on the frozen student. The gate opens when the skill switches, and a learned exit decides when to close it, allowing the frozen student to resume control. Outside transitions, the adapter never acts. We train the adapter through online reinforcement learning on predecessor-generated states and target-skill rewards. Conditioning the adapter on the skill pair and target command allows a single adaptation module to serve multiple transitions. New transition pairs can be incorporated into the shared adaptation process without modifying the original experts or the student backbone, avoiding the need to maintain separate transition-specific modules. This design improves transition robustness while leaving the native skills exactly unchanged.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We develop a physics-based soccer control framework that consolidates eight independently trained, task-competent experts into a unified skill-conditioned policy, providing a shared backbone for transition adaptation.

  • •

    We propose an online, shared transition adaptation method using a context-conditioned low-rank adapter, enabling joint adaptation across multiple skill pairs without retraining individual experts.

  • •

    We introduce a learned exit mechanism that dynamically determines the duration of transition adaptation, allowing the controller to return to the frozen student when adaptation is no longer needed, while preserving the original policy during native skill execution.

    • 2 Related Work

    Physics-based interaction skills.

    Physics-based character control has progressed from motion tracking [Peng et al., 2018] and adversarial motion priors [Peng et al., 2021, Peng et al., 2022] to scalable, unified controllers [Tessler et al., 2024, Shi et al., 2026]. Athletic ball interactions introduce additional challenges of coordinating whole-body motion with dynamic objects and precisely timed contacts. Early work learned basketball dribbling through trajectory optimization and reinforcement learning [Liu and Hodgins, 2018], and synthesized soccer dribbling and shooting through coupled character–ball control [Hong et al., 2019]. Recent methods have demonstrated basketball interaction skills [Wang et al., 2025], agile humanoid soccer [Haarnoja et al., 2024], accurate shooting [Zhong et al., 2026], and vision-based soccer control [Jin et al., 2026]. These advances motivate learning task-competent skills that optimize physical interaction objectives beyond reference-motion reproduction.

    Skill composition and transitions.

    Prior work addresses skill composition through several strategies. Some methods learn skills and transitions jointly. [Xie et al., 2022] employ a layer-wise mixture-of-experts for soccer juggling and skill switching, while SkillMimic-V2 [Yu et al., 2025] constructs augmented interaction trajectories and state transition fields. SkillX learns multiple soccer skills in a unified policy [Ye et al., 2026] , and SoccerBot combines latent motion priors with transition-state initialization [Shao et al., 2026]. Other methods adapt target skills to states generated by their predecessors, including PhysicsFC [Kim et al., 2025] and Joga [Avinash et al., 2026]. Learning to Ball further combines policy adaptation with intermediate policies for challenging transitions [Xu et al., 2025a]. While effective, extending these approaches to more skills and transitions can require updating shared policies, augmenting transition data, or maintaining specialized adaptation procedures. We instead study transition adaptation after independently trained skills have been consolidated into a single controller.

    Expert distillation and policy adaptation.

    Policy distillation [Rusu et al., 2016] and DAgger [Ross et al., 2011] provide foundations for consolidating expert behaviors. SuperPADL progressively distills specialized RL experts into a scalable controller [Juravsky et al., 2024], while InterMimic combines teacher–student learning with RL refinement for diverse human-object interactions [Xu et al., 2025b]. MaskedManipulator distills a motion-tracking controller into a goal-conditioned policy [Tessler et al., 2025], and TokenHSI uses task tokenization for unified interaction control [Pan et al., 2025]. Post-training adaptation has also been explored through policy refinement [Xu et al., 2023b], conditional low-rank updates [Shi et al., 2026], object-aware residual learning [Zhao et al., 2025], and RL fine-tuning of distilled interaction priors [Xu et al., 2026]. In contrast, MESSI focuses on adapting multiple skill transitions through a single context-conditioned adapter on a frozen student, with a learned exit that restricts adaptation to skill boundaries and preserves native-policy behavior.

    3 Method

    As shown in Figure 3, MESSI consists of three stages: skill-specific expert learning, multi-skill distillation, and unified transition adaptation. At test time, the controller receives the current character and ball states, skill label, and task command. A user or high-level planner specifies the next skill and its command at a scheduled skill switch, without requiring reference motions.

    3.1 Skill-specific Expert Learning

    As shown in Figure 3 (i), we first train each expert policy π̂ᵏ(âₜ|ŝₜ,gᵏₜ) for each skill k. The state ŝₜ contains the character’s proprioception and the ball state relative to the character, and is the same for all skills. The task command gᵏₜ is specific to the skill k. Actions are target joint angles for PD controllers. Each expert is trained in its own environment, with its own motion data, initial-state distribution, and termination rules. These choices are made per skill and are not constrained by the later integration stages.

    Rewards and optimization.

    Each expert maximizes several objectives j: a task reward rᵗᵃˢᵏ defined by the skill, and a style reward from the corresponding adversarial motion prior Mᵏ[Peng et al., 2021],

    rˢᵗʸˡᵉₜ=-\log(1-D(o_t-H+1:t)),

    		(1)

    where D is a discriminator over windows of H character states. For the kicking and heading skills, D is also conditioned on the technique label, and these skills add a small leg-pose objective that keeps the striking leg close to the reference motion. Summing the objectives into one reward lets their effective weights change with the reward scales during training. Inspired by [Xu et al., 2023a], rather than combining task and style rewards into a single scalar objective, we optimize separately normalized advantages to maintain their relative contributions during training.

    Shooting.

    The shooting command specifies the target launch velocity of the ball, the striking foot, and the technique (instep or inside shot). The launch velocity is recorded when the ball is struck. From then until the end of the episode, the task reward pays \exp(-k\lVertv_launch-v^*\rVert²), with a bonus if the commanded foot made the strike. The policy thus receives a dense signal for the quality of a single, brief contact. Before the strike, an approach term draws the striking foot to the ball. After the strike, a recovery term rewards a balanced stance. Commands are sampled from technique-specific ranges of speed, elevation, and direction, and the ball starts either at rest or rolling.

    Dribbling.

    The dribbling command specifies a target direction and speed. The task reward combines velocity tracking with a lead term that keeps the ball at a fixed distance ahead of the character along the target direction. Lateral deviation of the ball is penalized more strongly than longitudinal deviation. The velocity-tracking reward is multiplied by a gate on the character–ball distance. The gate is constant while the ball is within reach and decays beyond it, so the policy gains nothing by running ahead and leaving the ball behind.

    Other skills.

    The remaining skills follow the same template with the commands and task objectives, and their details about rewards, command distributions, initialization, and termination of all eight skills are included in Appendix.

    3.2 Multi-Skill Distillation

    The experts differ in their commands, network inputs, and environments. We distill them into a single student policy π that executes every skill from one observation space and selects the skill by a label.

    Unified observation space.

    The student observes

    oₜ=[sₜ, b¹ₜ,…,b^Mₜ, e_kₜ],

    		(2)

    where sₜ is the shared state of Sec. 3.1, b¹ₜ,…,b^Mₜ are task blocks, and e_kₜ is the one-hot label of the active skill kₜ. The command of each skill is written into one task block. Skills with the same kind of command share a block: dribbling and off-ball movement, for example, both use the steering block. The blocks of the other skills are set to zero. A fixed selection Pₖ recovers the native observation of expert k, Pₖoₜ=(sₜ,gᵏₜ), so the expert of the active skill can label every state the student visits.

    Student architecture.

    The student is a Transformer [Vaswani et al., 2017] over the observation blocks. A proprioception tokenizer, a ball tokenizer, and one task tokenizer per task block each map their block to a token, and an embedding of the skill label is added to every token. Attention is masked: the proprioception token attends to all tokens, while every other token attends only to itself and the proprioception token. A task block shared by several skills, such as steering, therefore never attends directly to a block that only some of them use, such as the ball. A readout layer concatenates the output tokens, and an action layer maps the result to the mean action μ(oₜ).

    Distillation.

    The student is trained to match the experts’ mean actions on an aggregated dataset D of observations and skill labels,

    L_distill=𝔼_(o,k)∼D[\lVertμ(o)-μ̂ₖ(Pₖ o)\rVert²],

    		(3)

    where μ̂ₖ is the mean action of expert π̂ᵏ. We first fill D with rollouts of each expert in its own environment, with the initial states, commands, and terminations of its training, and initialize the student by behavior cloning. The student’s errors then lead it to states that the experts rarely visit. We therefore apply DAgger [Ross et al., 2011]. In each round, the student executes its mean action in the environment of every skill, the expert of that skill labels each visited state, the new samples are added to D, and the student is retrained on all of D. Every skill contributes the same number of samples, and the experts stay frozen. Appendix provides the architecture and the training schedule.

    Each rollout executes a single skill from that skill’s own initial states. Distillation therefore never trains the student to start a skill from the state that its predecessor leaves behind. Sec. 3.3 addresses these transitions.

    3.3 Unified Transition Adaptation

    Although the distilled student preserves individual skill capabilities, directly switching skills can expose the target policy to unfamiliar body and ball states. Fine-tuning on these states may improve transitions but alter the target skill’s performance under native initialization. Our approach instead adapts the frozen student through a single shared module, with two key design choices: conditioning adaptation on the skill transition and learning when to deactivate it.

    Transition schedule.

    As illustrated in Figure 3(iii), the student executes the predecessor skill with the adapter disabled (zₜ=0). At a skill switch, the target skill becomes active and the adapter is enabled (zₜ=1) to handle the unfamiliar entry state. A learned exit policy subsequently determines when to deactivate the adapter, returning control to the original student. Native skill execution always bypasses the adapter.

    Shared conditional adapter.

    Rather than training separate policies or adapters for each skill pair, we use a shared low-rank adapter conditioned on the transition context cₜ, which encodes the predecessor and target skills, target command, and elapsed time since the switch. Following conditional low-rank adaptation [Shi et al., 2026, Hu et al., 2021], each adapted linear layer computes

    y=W₀x+zₜB[(Ax)⊙(1+γ(cₜ))+β(cₜ)],

    		(4)

    where W₀ is frozen, A and B are trainable low-rank matrices, and γ(cₜ) and β(cₜ) modulate the update according to the transition context. This allows the same adapter parameters to serve multiple skill pairs, while zₜ=0 recovers the original student. We apply it to the proprioception tokenizer, Transformer feed-forward layers, and readout.

    Learned exit policy.

    The required adaptation duration varies across transitions and encountered states. A fixed window may terminate adaptation prematurely or keep the adapter active longer than necessary. We therefore learn a state-dependent exit policy that predicts the probability of deactivating the adapter from the observation oₜ and transition context cₜ. The exit policy is trained jointly with the adapter using PPO, balancing target-task rewards against a per-step adapter usage cost. Rewards obtained after an exit also contribute to the return, so the exit decision accounts for the subsequent execution of the frozen student. Exit decisions are allowed after 0.2 s, and the first sampled exit closes the gate until the next skill switch.

    Training.

    After a skill switch, we optimize the target-skill reward with an adapter usage cost and failure penalty:

    rₜ=rₗᵗᵃˢᵏ(sₜ)-0.02zₜ-pₜ,

    		(5)

    where pₜ is 1 for a fall or ball loss and 0.5 for other failures. The adapter and exit policy are optimized jointly using PPO, with the importance ratio computed from the joint log-probability of actions and exit decisions. Only steps with an active adapter contribute policy gradients. The critic is conditioned on cₜ. All transitions are trained jointly through online simulation with shared adapter parameters.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate MESSI at three levels: single skills from their native initial states (Sec. 4.3), single transitions from states produced by a predecessor skill (Secs. 4.4 and 4.5), and continuous chains of skills (Sec. 4.6). GPU PhysX rollouts differ across machines, so every paired comparison runs in the same machine from identical initial states.

    4.1 Implementation Details

    All skills are simulated in Isaac Lab [Mittal et al., 2023] with GPU PhysX at 240 Hz, and all policies run at 60 Hz, the frame rate of the reference motions. The character is a 28-DoF humanoid driven by PD controllers, with shoe-shaped collision meshes for the feet. The rigid-body solver models neither aerodynamics nor rolling resistance, so we add drag and Magnus forces to the ball in flight and a constant rolling resistance on the ground. Each expert is trained on 4 NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs for 13 to 53 hours. Distilling the eight experts into the 5.3M-parameter student takes about 4.4 hours on one GPU (behavior cloning followed by four DAgger rounds), and training the shared adapter takes 11.2 hours on four GPUs. Appendix gives the physical parameters, motion data, network architectures, and training hyperparameters.

    4.2 Baselines

    Skill learning.

    We compare our skill-specific experts and distilled student against TokenHSI* [Pan et al., 2025] and SkillX* [Ye et al., 2026], two adapted baselines trained jointly from scratch across all eight skills using a unified Transformer policy. Both baselines follow their official network architectures and PPO configurations, using our observations, task rewards, and motion data. However, they exclude our skill-specific training strategies, including curricula, failure-weighted sampling, multi-objective advantages, and discriminator labels. To isolate the contribution of DAgger, we additionally evaluate the student trained with behavioral cloning alone.

    Transitions.

    Direct switching activates the target skill without the adapter. Expert + STI fine-tunes the target expert with PPO from predecessor-generated states, following the skill transition-based initialization of PhysicsFC [Kim et al., 2025]. An episode starts from a skill-switching (handover) state with probability 0.7 and from a native initial state otherwise, and the fine-tuning uses the same sample budget per transition as our adapter. One fine-tuned dribbling expert serves all four transitions into dribbling. This is our reimplementation of the published method, not PhysicsFC’s code. To study the exit, we also run our adapter checkpoint with the exit head disabled (Pers.) and with post-hoc cutoffs that close the gate a fixed time after the handover. To evaluate the role of parameter sharing, we additionally compare against a per-transition adapter baseline (Per-trans.), which trains a separate adapter for each skill pair on the same frozen student. We also include full fine-tuning (Full FT), which directly updates the unified student for transition adaptation.

    4.3 Atomic Skills and Distillation

    Each skill is evaluated on 1,024 cases drawn from the initial states and commands of its expert’s training, and all policies run the same cases. Off-ball movement succeeds without a failure and with episode-average velocity and facing errors below 0.75 m/s and 35^∘. Dribbling has no completion event, so we report its velocity error and failure rate. Shooting and passing succeed when the launch azimuth is within 10^∘ of the command and the launch speed reaches at least half the commanded speed; shooting also requires the commanded foot. Heading requires the head to make the first legal touch and an azimuth error below 25^∘. Trapping uses its success bit, stop-and-turn the moment the ball is stopped at the foot, and get-up the recovery flag. The student runs with the adapter off, since no transition precedes these episodes.

    Experts.

    Table 1 shows that our skill-specific experts substantially outperform the jointly trained baselines on contact-sensitive tasks such as shooting, passing, and trapping. However, heading remains challenging even for its specialized expert, suggesting that task-specific training alone does not resolve all difficult ball interactions. The dribbling results also reveal a trade-off: TokenHSI* has fewer failures but substantially larger velocity-tracking errors, indicating that retaining ball possession does not necessarily imply accurate command following.

    Distillation.

    Behavioral cloning alone substantially degrades several skills, while DAgger recovers most of the lost performance. This highlights the importance of supervising the student on states induced by its own actions, rather than relying solely on expert demonstrations. The remaining gaps, particularly in heading, largely reflect limitations of the original experts rather than distillation.

    Shooting accuracy.

    The shooting bearing metric in Table 1 evaluates the horizontal launch direction, minimum launch speed, and correct kicking foot, but does not assess the ball’s final placement. To further evaluate shooting accuracy, we measure where the ball crosses the goal plane relative to the commanded target. We command our policy to shoot and aim at points on a 7.32×2.44 m goal 11 m away, as shown in Figure 5. A shot succeeds when the ball crosses the goal plane inside the frame, struck with the commanded foot at no less than half the commanded speed. Of 4,096 shots, 3,479 aim inside the frame, and 87.2% of these succeed. The rate varies little across the goal mouth, between 76% and 92% per target cell. The remaining error is systematic rather than random. The median launch reaches 89% of the commanded speed, so high targets land about 1.0 m low on average, and shots aimed at the posts drift about 0.9 m inward.

    4.4 Skill Transitions

    We evaluate five transitions from handover states produced by the frozen student executing the predecessor until its handover condition holds, about 400 to 510 per transition. Every method takes over from the identical states. Dribble→Shoot succeeds under the native shooting rule above. A transition into dribbling succeeds when the character has not fallen and has settled into dribbling by a 4 s deadline: a velocity error below 0.75 m/s over the last second, with the ball within 2.5 m. We additionally evaluate each deployed policy under native skill initialization to examine whether transition adaptation affects the original skills. For MESSI, the adapter gate remains closed in these episodes, so its actions are identical to those of the distilled student by construction. This evaluation verifies native-mode policy preservation, while the ability of the frozen student to continue execution after an adapter exit is assessed through transition rollouts.

    Quantitative results.

    Table 2 highlights the gap between individual skill competence and transition robustness. Although the distilled student succeeds in 77.9% of native shooting episodes, direct switching from dribbling reduces success to 19.8%, exposing a substantial mismatch in entry-state distributions. Full fine-tuning improves transition performance but degrades native shooting success from 77.93% to 54.82%, illustrating the trade-off between adaptation and preserving previously learned behavior. Our gated adapter avoids this trade-off in native execution by keeping the original student unchanged. Compared with per-transition adaptation, our shared adapter achieves the highest success rate on four of five transitions, although specialization benefits dribble→shoot. These results suggest that sharing adaptation parameters can provide competitive performance without separately modifying each skill policy.

    Qualitative comparison.

    Since TokenHSI* and SkillX* exhibit poor performance even under native skill initialization, we focus our qualitative comparison on three major transition strategies applied to our trained skills. Figure 4 illustrates a dribbling-to-shooting transition under three approaches. Direct switching produces a weak kick that fails to reach the goal. The STI-fine-tuned expert successfully scores but misses the commanded target by 0.9 m. In contrast, our shared adapter achieves a more accurate shot, with the ball reaching within 0.03 m of the target.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：在孤立情况下表现良好的技能，串起来执行时可能失效。

要点：

  • 现象描述精准：基于物理的足球角色需要完成多种运动技能并**平滑地在它们之间切换**（例如带球转为射门）；但**在孤立情况下表现良好的技能，串起来执行时可能失效**
  • 根因是状态：**前一个行为会把角色与球留在训练时没见过的状态里**
  • MESSI（Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration）因此用共享适配来支持多种技能之间的切换，同时保住原本的技能表现

为什么值得看：「技能串接」是物理角色动画里最真实的失败点，也是游戏与体育模拟的共同需求。这条把问题归因到「状态分布漂移」而不是「控制器不够强」，这决定了修法是把技能之间的状态接起来，而不是继续堆单技能的性能。

中文摘要：基于物理的足球角色需要完成多种运动技能，并在它们之间平滑过渡，例如从带球转入射门。作者指出现有方法的一个通病：在孤立场景下表现良好的技能，串联执行时可能失效，原因是前一个动作会把角色与球带入训练时未见过的不熟悉状态。MESSI（Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration）因此提出一个多专家框架，通过共享适配来实现多种足球技能之间的切换，同时保持各单项技能原有的表现水平。对体育类游戏与物理角色动画来说，这条针对的正是「单招练得好、连招就崩」这个长期难点。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

MESSI: Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration for Physics-Based Character Control

Abstract

Physics-based soccer characters must perform diverse motor skills and transition smoothly between them, such as dribbling into a shot. However, skills that perform well in isolation may fail when executed sequentially, as preceding behaviors can leave the character and ball in unfamiliar states. We present MESSI (Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration), a framework that enables multiple soccer skill transitions through shared adaptation while preserving the original skill policy outside transitions. MESSI first trains eight task-competent experts using motion priors and task rewards, then distills them into a unified, skill-conditioned Transformer. Rather than retraining individual experts for different transitions, we train a shared, context-conditioned low-rank adapter on the frozen student through online reinforcement learning. Activated upon skill switching, the adapter helps the target skill handle unfamiliar entry states, while a learned exit mechanism determines when to return control to the original student. By disabling the adapter during native skill execution, MESSI preserves the original student policy by construction. Experiments across individual skills, skill transitions, and continuous skill chains demonstrate substantial improvements over direct switching, including an increase in dribbling-to-shooting success from 19.8% to 61.8%.

1 Introduction

Soccer presents a challenging setting for physics-based character control, combining whole-body coordination with precise interactions with a dynamically moving ball [Hong et al., 2019, Liu et al., 2022, Haarnoja et al., 2024, Kim et al., 2025, Ye et al., 2026]. A versatile soccer character must perform diverse skills, including locomotion, dribbling, shooting, passing, and trapping, while transitioning between them at speed. For example, a player may shoot immediately after dribbling or receive a pass while running. Such transitions are challenging because the character’s posture, momentum, and ball configuration depend on the preceding behavior and may differ substantially from the states encountered during the target skill’s training. Consequently, even well-trained individual skills can fail when executed sequentially, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Recent advances in physics-based character control have enabled reusable motor skills through motion tracking and large-scale motion pretraining [Peng et al., 2018, Peng et al., 2022, Tessler et al., 2024, Juravsky et al., 2024, Shi et al., 2026]. However, tracking reference motions alone does not guarantee task-specific ball control or reliable transitions absent from the motion data. While independently trained, task-competent experts can optimize individual skill objectives, composing their behaviors remains challenging when the target skill encounters unfamiliar body and ball states. Existing approaches address skill transitions in several ways. Some learn skills and transitions jointly, either through unified multi-skill policies [Ye et al., 2026] or augmented interaction trajectories [Yu et al., 2025]. Such approaches may require revisiting joint policy training or transition data when introducing new transitions, potentially affecting previously learned behaviors. Others employ transition-aware initialization or fine-tuning using predecessor-generated states [Kim et al., 2025, Avinash et al., 2026], coupling transition adaptation to individual skill policies. For more challenging transitions, policy composition methods additionally introduce intermediate behaviors when necessary [Xu et al., 2025a], which can increase transition-specific training and maintenance overhead. While these approaches demonstrate effective skill composition, adapting a growing repertoire of skills without repeatedly modifying individual experts or introducing separate transition modules remains challenging. This motivates a shared adaptation strategy that supports diverse skill transitions while limiting interference with established skill behaviors.

To this end, we present MESSI (Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration), a framework for integrating task-competent soccer skills and enabling their transitions within a unified physics-based controller. MESSI incorporates eight skills: off-ball movement, dribbling, shooting, passing, heading, trapping, stop-and-turn, and getting up. We first train skill-specific experts using motion priors, task rewards, and tailored curricula. Their behaviors are then distilled into a shared skill-conditioned student through a unified observation space. Consolidating the experts into a single skill-conditioned policy provides a common backbone for transition adaptation. This enables different skill pairs to share a single adaptation module, rather than requiring separate adaptations of individual expert policies.

Our key insight is that transition adaptation is needed only after a skill switch, where the target skill encounters unfamiliar states generated by its predecessor. Rather than modifying the target skill everywhere, we introduce a shared, gated, context-conditioned low-rank adapter on the frozen student. The gate opens when the skill switches, and a learned exit decides when to close it, allowing the frozen student to resume control. Outside transitions, the adapter never acts. We train the adapter through online reinforcement learning on predecessor-generated states and target-skill rewards. Conditioning the adapter on the skill pair and target command allows a single adaptation module to serve multiple transitions. New transition pairs can be incorporated into the shared adaptation process without modifying the original experts or the student backbone, avoiding the need to maintain separate transition-specific modules. This design improves transition robustness while leaving the native skills exactly unchanged.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We develop a physics-based soccer control framework that consolidates eight independently trained, task-competent experts into a unified skill-conditioned policy, providing a shared backbone for transition adaptation.

  • •

    We propose an online, shared transition adaptation method using a context-conditioned low-rank adapter, enabling joint adaptation across multiple skill pairs without retraining individual experts.

  • •

    We introduce a learned exit mechanism that dynamically determines the duration of transition adaptation, allowing the controller to return to the frozen student when adaptation is no longer needed, while preserving the original policy during native skill execution.

    • 2 Related Work

    Physics-based interaction skills.

    Physics-based character control has progressed from motion tracking [Peng et al., 2018] and adversarial motion priors [Peng et al., 2021, Peng et al., 2022] to scalable, unified controllers [Tessler et al., 2024, Shi et al., 2026]. Athletic ball interactions introduce additional challenges of coordinating whole-body motion with dynamic objects and precisely timed contacts. Early work learned basketball dribbling through trajectory optimization and reinforcement learning [Liu and Hodgins, 2018], and synthesized soccer dribbling and shooting through coupled character–ball control [Hong et al., 2019]. Recent methods have demonstrated basketball interaction skills [Wang et al., 2025], agile humanoid soccer [Haarnoja et al., 2024], accurate shooting [Zhong et al., 2026], and vision-based soccer control [Jin et al., 2026]. These advances motivate learning task-competent skills that optimize physical interaction objectives beyond reference-motion reproduction.

    Skill composition and transitions.

    Prior work addresses skill composition through several strategies. Some methods learn skills and transitions jointly. [Xie et al., 2022] employ a layer-wise mixture-of-experts for soccer juggling and skill switching, while SkillMimic-V2 [Yu et al., 2025] constructs augmented interaction trajectories and state transition fields. SkillX learns multiple soccer skills in a unified policy [Ye et al., 2026] , and SoccerBot combines latent motion priors with transition-state initialization [Shao et al., 2026]. Other methods adapt target skills to states generated by their predecessors, including PhysicsFC [Kim et al., 2025] and Joga [Avinash et al., 2026]. Learning to Ball further combines policy adaptation with intermediate policies for challenging transitions [Xu et al., 2025a]. While effective, extending these approaches to more skills and transitions can require updating shared policies, augmenting transition data, or maintaining specialized adaptation procedures. We instead study transition adaptation after independently trained skills have been consolidated into a single controller.

    Expert distillation and policy adaptation.

    Policy distillation [Rusu et al., 2016] and DAgger [Ross et al., 2011] provide foundations for consolidating expert behaviors. SuperPADL progressively distills specialized RL experts into a scalable controller [Juravsky et al., 2024], while InterMimic combines teacher–student learning with RL refinement for diverse human-object interactions [Xu et al., 2025b]. MaskedManipulator distills a motion-tracking controller into a goal-conditioned policy [Tessler et al., 2025], and TokenHSI uses task tokenization for unified interaction control [Pan et al., 2025]. Post-training adaptation has also been explored through policy refinement [Xu et al., 2023b], conditional low-rank updates [Shi et al., 2026], object-aware residual learning [Zhao et al., 2025], and RL fine-tuning of distilled interaction priors [Xu et al., 2026]. In contrast, MESSI focuses on adapting multiple skill transitions through a single context-conditioned adapter on a frozen student, with a learned exit that restricts adaptation to skill boundaries and preserves native-policy behavior.

    3 Method

    As shown in Figure 3, MESSI consists of three stages: skill-specific expert learning, multi-skill distillation, and unified transition adaptation. At test time, the controller receives the current character and ball states, skill label, and task command. A user or high-level planner specifies the next skill and its command at a scheduled skill switch, without requiring reference motions.

    3.1 Skill-specific Expert Learning

    As shown in Figure 3 (i), we first train each expert policy π̂ᵏ(âₜ|ŝₜ,gᵏₜ) for each skill k. The state ŝₜ contains the character’s proprioception and the ball state relative to the character, and is the same for all skills. The task command gᵏₜ is specific to the skill k. Actions are target joint angles for PD controllers. Each expert is trained in its own environment, with its own motion data, initial-state distribution, and termination rules. These choices are made per skill and are not constrained by the later integration stages.

    Rewards and optimization.

    Each expert maximizes several objectives j: a task reward rᵗᵃˢᵏ defined by the skill, and a style reward from the corresponding adversarial motion prior Mᵏ[Peng et al., 2021],

    rˢᵗʸˡᵉₜ=-\log(1-D(o_t-H+1:t)),

    		(1)

    where D is a discriminator over windows of H character states. For the kicking and heading skills, D is also conditioned on the technique label, and these skills add a small leg-pose objective that keeps the striking leg close to the reference motion. Summing the objectives into one reward lets their effective weights change with the reward scales during training. Inspired by [Xu et al., 2023a], rather than combining task and style rewards into a single scalar objective, we optimize separately normalized advantages to maintain their relative contributions during training.

    Shooting.

    The shooting command specifies the target launch velocity of the ball, the striking foot, and the technique (instep or inside shot). The launch velocity is recorded when the ball is struck. From then until the end of the episode, the task reward pays \exp(-k\lVertv_launch-v^*\rVert²), with a bonus if the commanded foot made the strike. The policy thus receives a dense signal for the quality of a single, brief contact. Before the strike, an approach term draws the striking foot to the ball. After the strike, a recovery term rewards a balanced stance. Commands are sampled from technique-specific ranges of speed, elevation, and direction, and the ball starts either at rest or rolling.

    Dribbling.

    The dribbling command specifies a target direction and speed. The task reward combines velocity tracking with a lead term that keeps the ball at a fixed distance ahead of the character along the target direction. Lateral deviation of the ball is penalized more strongly than longitudinal deviation. The velocity-tracking reward is multiplied by a gate on the character–ball distance. The gate is constant while the ball is within reach and decays beyond it, so the policy gains nothing by running ahead and leaving the ball behind.

    Other skills.

    The remaining skills follow the same template with the commands and task objectives, and their details about rewards, command distributions, initialization, and termination of all eight skills are included in Appendix.

    3.2 Multi-Skill Distillation

    The experts differ in their commands, network inputs, and environments. We distill them into a single student policy π that executes every skill from one observation space and selects the skill by a label.

    Unified observation space.

    The student observes

    oₜ=[sₜ, b¹ₜ,…,b^Mₜ, e_kₜ],

    		(2)

    where sₜ is the shared state of Sec. 3.1, b¹ₜ,…,b^Mₜ are task blocks, and e_kₜ is the one-hot label of the active skill kₜ. The command of each skill is written into one task block. Skills with the same kind of command share a block: dribbling and off-ball movement, for example, both use the steering block. The blocks of the other skills are set to zero. A fixed selection Pₖ recovers the native observation of expert k, Pₖoₜ=(sₜ,gᵏₜ), so the expert of the active skill can label every state the student visits.

    Student architecture.

    The student is a Transformer [Vaswani et al., 2017] over the observation blocks. A proprioception tokenizer, a ball tokenizer, and one task tokenizer per task block each map their block to a token, and an embedding of the skill label is added to every token. Attention is masked: the proprioception token attends to all tokens, while every other token attends only to itself and the proprioception token. A task block shared by several skills, such as steering, therefore never attends directly to a block that only some of them use, such as the ball. A readout layer concatenates the output tokens, and an action layer maps the result to the mean action μ(oₜ).

    L_distill=𝔼_(o,k)∼D[\lVertμ(o)-μ̂ₖ(Pₖ o)\rVert²],

    		(3)

    where μ̂ₖ is the mean action of expert π̂ᵏ. We first fill D with rollouts of each expert in its own environment, with the initial states, commands, and terminations of its training, and initialize the student by behavior cloning. The student’s errors then lead it to states that the experts rarely visit. We therefore apply DAgger [Ross et al., 2011]. In each round, the student executes its mean action in the environment of every skill, the expert of that skill labels each visited state, the new samples are added to D, and the student is retrained on all of D. Every skill contributes the same number of samples, and the experts stay frozen. Appendix provides the architecture and the training schedule.

    Each rollout executes a single skill from that skill’s own initial states. Distillation therefore never trains the student to start a skill from the state that its predecessor leaves behind. Sec. 3.3 addresses these transitions.

    Although the distilled student preserves individual skill capabilities, directly switching skills can expose the target policy to unfamiliar body and ball states. Following conditional low-rank adaptation [Shi et al., 2026, Hu et al., 2021], each adapted linear layer computes

    y=W₀x+zₜB[(Ax)⊙(1+γ(cₜ))+β(cₜ)],

    		(4)

    where W₀ is frozen, A and B are trainable low-rank matrices, and γ(cₜ) and β(cₜ) modulate the update according to the transition context. This allows the same adapter parameters to serve multiple skill pairs, while zₜ=0 recovers the original student. We apply it to the proprioception tokenizer, Transformer feed-forward layers, and readout.

    After a skill switch, we optimize the target-skill reward with an adapter usage cost and failure penalty:

    rₜ=rₗᵗᵃˢᵏ(sₜ)-0.02zₜ-pₜ,

    		(5)

    where pₜ is 1 for a fall or ball loss and 0.5 for other failures. The adapter and exit policy are optimized jointly using PPO, with the importance ratio computed from the joint log-probability of actions and exit decisions. Only steps with an active adapter contribute policy gradients. The critic is conditioned on cₜ. All transitions are trained jointly through online simulation with shared adapter parameters.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate MESSI at three levels: single skills from their native initial states (Sec. 4.3), single transitions from states produced by a predecessor skill (Secs. 4.4 and 4.5), and continuous chains of skills (Sec. 4.6). GPU PhysX rollouts differ across machines, so every paired comparison runs in the same machine from identical initial states.

    4.1 Implementation Details

    All skills are simulated in Isaac Lab [Mittal et al., 2023] with GPU PhysX at 240 Hz, and all policies run at 60 Hz, the frame rate of the reference motions. The character is a 28-DoF humanoid driven by PD controllers, with shoe-shaped collision meshes for the feet.     4.2 Baselines

    Skill learning.

    We compare our skill-specific experts and distilled student against TokenHSI* [Pan et al., 2025] and SkillX* [Ye et al., 2026], two adapted baselines trained jointly from scratch across all eight skills using a unified Transformer policy. Both baselines follow their official network architectures and PPO configurations, using our observations, task rewards, and motion data. However, they exclude our skill-specific training strategies, including curricula, failure-weighted sampling, multi-objective advantages, and discriminator labels. To isolate the contribution of DAgger, we additionally evaluate the student trained with behavioral cloning alone.

    Transitions.

    Direct switching activates the target skill without the adapter. Expert + STI fine-tunes the target expert with PPO from predecessor-generated states, following the skill transition-based initialization of PhysicsFC [Kim et al., 2025]. An episode starts from a skill-switching (handover) state with probability 0.7 and from a native initial state otherwise, and the fine-tuning uses the same sample budget per transition as our adapter. One fine-tuned dribbling expert serves all four transitions into dribbling. This is our reimplementation of the published method, not PhysicsFC’s code. To study the exit, we also run our adapter checkpoint with the exit head disabled (Pers.) and with post-hoc cutoffs that close the gate a fixed time after the handover. To evaluate the role of parameter sharing, we additionally compare against a per-transition adapter baseline (Per-trans.), which trains a separate adapter for each skill pair on the same frozen student. We also include full fine-tuning (Full FT), which directly updates the unified student for transition adaptation.

    4.3 Atomic Skills and Distillation

    Each skill is evaluated on 1,024 cases drawn from the initial states and commands of its expert’s training, and all policies run the same cases. Off-ball movement succeeds without a failure and with episode-average velocity and facing errors below 0.75 m/s and 35^∘. Dribbling has no completion event, so we report its velocity error and failure rate. Shooting and passing succeed when the launch azimuth is within 10^∘ of the command and the launch speed reaches at least half the commanded speed; shooting also requires the commanded foot. Heading requires the head to make the first legal touch and an azimuth error below 25^∘. Trapping uses its success bit, stop-and-turn the moment the ball is stopped at the foot, and get-up the recovery flag. The student runs with the adapter off, since no transition precedes these episodes.

    Experts.

    Table 1 shows that our skill-specific experts substantially outperform the jointly trained baselines on contact-sensitive tasks such as shooting, passing, and trapping. However, heading remains challenging even for its specialized expert, suggesting that task-specific training alone does not resolve all difficult ball interactions. The dribbling results also reveal a trade-off: TokenHSI* has fewer failures but substantially larger velocity-tracking errors, indicating that retaining ball possession does not necessarily imply accurate command following.

    Distillation.

    Behavioral cloning alone substantially degrades several skills, while DAgger recovers most of the lost performance. This highlights the importance of supervising the student on states induced by its own actions, rather than relying solely on expert demonstrations. The remaining gaps, particularly in heading, largely reflect limitations of the original experts rather than distillation.

    Shooting accuracy.

    The shooting bearing metric in Table 1 evaluates the horizontal launch direction, minimum launch speed, and correct kicking foot, but does not assess the ball’s final placement. To further evaluate shooting accuracy, we measure where the ball crosses the goal plane relative to the commanded target. We command our policy to shoot and aim at points on a 7.32×2.44 m goal 11 m away, as shown in Figure 5. A shot succeeds when the ball crosses the goal plane inside the frame, struck with the commanded foot at no less than half the commanded speed. Of 4,096 shots, 3,479 aim inside the frame, and 87.2% of these succeed. The rate varies little across the goal mouth, between 76% and 92% per target cell. The remaining error is systematic rather than random. The median launch reaches 89% of the commanded speed, so high targets land about 1.0 m low on average, and shots aimed at the posts drift about 0.9 m inward.

    4.4 Skill Transitions

    We evaluate five transitions from handover states produced by the frozen student executing the predecessor until its handover condition holds, about 400 to 510 per transition. Every method takes over from the identical states. Dribble→Shoot succeeds under the native shooting rule above. A transition into dribbling succeeds when the character has not fallen and has settled into dribbling by a 4 s deadline: a velocity error below 0.75 m/s over the last second, with the ball within 2.5 m. We additionally evaluate each deployed policy under native skill initialization to examine whether transition adaptation affects the original skills. For MESSI, the adapter gate remains closed in these episodes, so its actions are identical to those of the distilled student by construction. This evaluation verifies native-mode policy preservation, while the ability of the frozen student to continue execution after an adapter exit is assessed through transition rollouts.

    Quantitative results.

    Table 2 highlights the gap between individual skill competence and transition robustness. Although the distilled student succeeds in 77.9% of native shooting episodes, direct switching from dribbling reduces success to 19.8%, exposing a substantial mismatch in entry-state distributions. Full fine-tuning improves transition performance but degrades native shooting success from 77.93% to 54.82%, illustrating the trade-off between adaptation and preserving previously learned behavior. Our gated adapter avoids this trade-off in native execution by keeping the original student unchanged. Compared with per-transition adaptation, our shared adapter achieves the highest success rate on four of five transitions, although specialization benefits dribble→shoot. These results suggest that sharing adaptation parameters can provide competitive performance without separately modifying each skill policy.

    Qualitative comparison.

    Since TokenHSI* and SkillX* exhibit poor performance even under native skill initialization, we focus our qualitative comparison on three major transition strategies applied to our trained skills. Figure 4 illustrates a dribbling-to-shooting transition under three approaches. Direct switching produces a weak kick that fails to reach the goal. The STI-fine-tuned expert successfully scores but misses the commanded target by 0.9 m. In contrast, our shared adapter achieves a more accurate shot, with the ball reaching within 0.03 m of the target.

item.title: 视频基础模型其实是更好的「动作模型」：Motion prior 比专用动作模型更丰富也更通用 ｜ Video Models are Excellent Motion Models
item.description:
一句话：它们的优势不只在视觉真实感，还体现在动作的自然度与泛化上。

要点：

  • 主张很直接：视频基础模型已成为强大的动态视觉内容生成器，而作者认为它们**同时也成为了优秀的动作生成器**，其运动先验**比专用动作模型学到的更丰富、更通用**
  • 优势有两处被点名：一是**动作自然度**（不仅是画面真实感），二是（论文展开的另一维度，涉及泛化）
  • 换句话说，与其专门训一个动作模型，不如把视频模型当作 motion prior 来用

为什么值得看：如果这条成立，动作管线的起点会变：不必先有 mocap 数据集再训模型，而是直接借视频基础模型的运动先验再做适配。对缺少动作数据的团队，这可能是比「攒数据」更现实的路径。

中文摘要：这篇提出一个直接的主张：视频基础模型已经不只是强大的动态视觉内容生成器，它们同时成为了**优秀的动作生成器**，并且其运动先验比专门训练的动作模型更丰富、更通用。作者指出这种优势不仅体现在视觉真实感上，还体现在动作的自然度（以及泛化性）两个方面。若这一结论成立，动作生产的路径会发生改变：不必先拥有大规模动作捕捉数据再训练专用模型，而是可以把视频基础模型当作通用的运动先验，再做针对性适配。对缺少动作数据的团队，这提供了一条比「攒数据」更现实的路线。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

Video Models are Excellent Motion Models

Abstract

Video foundation models have emerged as powerful generators of dynamic visual content, exhibiting remarkable capabilities in synthesizing complex actions and interactions. We argue that these models have also become excellent motion generators, with motion priors that are richer and more general than those learned by dedicated motion models. Their advantage extends beyond visual realism and is manifested in two important aspects: motion naturalness, including coherent body coordination, physical plausibility, and realistic interactions with objects and the environment; and motion scope, encompassing a much broader range of activities and semantic coherence, particularly uncommon, complex, and compound actions. To investigate this position, we introduce a common evaluation framework that compares video and dedicated motion models through three complementary settings: text-only motion generation, reconstruction of video-generated motion from sparse keyframes, and video-based enrichment of motion-model outputs. By converting all outputs into a shared 3D skeletal representation, we evaluate motion naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical motion characteristics, and fidelity to motion constraints. Our results suggest that video foundation models can generate more natural and semantically meaningful movements, particularly for complex and compound actions. Moreover, we investigate motion-conditioned generation through loose skeletal control, finding that dedicated motion models do not consistently improve video-generated motion, while video models can enrich skeletal animations using sparse motion guidance. Our findings suggest a shift in the role of specialized motion models, from generating complete animations to guiding and controlling the richer motion capabilities already embedded in video foundation models.

Project Page:video-beats-motion.github.io

1 Introduction

Recent advances in video generation have brought us closer to the vision of generative world models that capture not only how the world looks, but also how it behaves and evolves over time [11]. Trained on large and diverse video datasets, modern video foundation models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in generating complex human activities, coordinated movements, and interactions between people, objects and the environment. These capabilities suggest that their learned representations extend beyond visual appearance, capturing useful knowledge about human motion and the relationships that govern human behavior. This raises an interesting question: can the motion knowledge embedded in video foundation models be used to generate more natural and semantically meaningful 3D human motion?

Dedicated generative motion models have also made significant progress in synthesizing realistic and controllable human movements from text descriptions, sparse keyframes, and other control signals [41, 13, 33]. By explicitly modeling skeletal poses and trajectories, they provide precise control over character animation. An important difference between motion and video models, however, lies in the scale and diversity of their training data.

Although motion models can benefit from larger training datasets, collecting diverse, high-quality, and semantically annotated 3D motion data remains challenging and expensive. In contrast, video data are substantially more abundant, allowing video foundation models to be trained on tens of thousands of hours of recordings covering a broader range of human activities, objects, and environments [54]. Although video and skeletal motion data are not directly comparable, the greater availability and diversity of video data may provide richer motion priors, particularly for uncommon and complex activities, human-object interactions, and compound actions that are less represented in structured motion datasets.

In this work, we argue that video foundation models have become stronger and more general motion generators than dedicated motion models, both in motion naturalness and the breadth of actions they can represent. First, video models have learned rich motion priors that capture not only human movement but also relationships between body parts, objects, and the environment. This knowledge enables more coherent and physically plausible movements, such as maintaining a consistent grasp when carrying a box, coordinating hand and foot placement when climbing a ladder, or combining actions, such as walking while drinking coffee and talking on a phone. Second, training on substantially larger and more diverse datasets expose video models to a broader range of activities and interactions, including those less represented in structured motion datasets. Importantly, our claim concerns the quality and semantic consistency of the underlying 3D motion, rather than the visual realism of generated videos. As illustrated in , video foundation models can generate richer, more natural, and semantically coherent 3D human motion than dedicated motion models given the same text prompt.

To investigate this position, we introduce a common evaluation framework that converts video- and motion-model outputs into a shared 3D skeletal representation. We examine three complementary experimental settings. First, text-only generation compares the ability of both model families to independently generate natural and semantically meaningful movements from the same prompt. Second, video-to-motion examines whether dedicated motion models can reconstruct or improve video-generated motion conditioned on a small set of keyframes. Third, motion-to-video investigates whether video models can enrich motion-model outputs under sparse skeletal guidance while retaining their intended motion structure. Together, these settings allow us to examine motion range, naturalness, and the complementary roles of video and motion models.

Our experiments provide evidence that video foundation models generate more natural and semantically meaningful movements, particularly for complex and compound actions. While dedicated motion models do not consistently improve video-generated motion through sparse-keyframe reconstruction, video models can enrich skeletal animations through loose control while preserving their original intent. We support these findings through semantic, perceptual, and quantitative motion evaluations. Our contributions offer a new perspective on video foundation models as motion generators, a unified evaluation framework, and empirical evidence of their richer motion priors. Our findings suggest a broader shift in motion generation, where video foundation models increasingly contribute rich semantic understanding and motion priors for generating natural and expressive animations, while dedicated motion models offer complementary capabilities for refining and controlling the generated motion.

2 Related Work

2.1 Human Motion Generation

Recent advances in generative models have significantly improved 3D human motion synthesis from natural language. Early approaches, e.g., TEMOS [29], MDM [41], and MotionDiffuse [49], established frameworks for text-to-motion generation, while T2M-GPT [48], MotionGPT [22], and MoMask [18] explored discrete motion representations and language-based generation. More recent methods, including Motion Mamba [51], BAMM [30], MotionLCM [14], and EMDM [56], have improved motion quality, efficiency, and controllability. K-Mask [1] further supports fine-grained body-part control, while CondMDI [13] enables flexible motion in-betweening from sparse keyframes. Kimodo [33] extends controllable motion generation through larger-scale training. These advances provide a strong foundation for comparing dedicated motion models with video foundation models.

Despite these advances, generating complex and compound actions remains challenging, particularly when multiple movements must be performed simultaneously.
