We measure the average Euclidean distance between corresponding generated and reference joints:

MPJPE=(100)/(|K|J)∑_t∈K∑ⱼ₌₁^J∥p̂_t,j-p_t,j∥₂.

(S12)

where J=22. MPJPE is reported in centimeters.

Procrustes-Aligned MPJPE (PA-MPJPE) ↓.

We additionally compute MPJPE after independently aligning each generated keyframe to its corresponding reference pose using an optimal similarity transformation, including rotation, translation, and uniform scaling. This reduces global alignment discrepancies and measures the residual joint-position differences. PA-MPJPE is reported in centimeters.

Joint Rotation Error (∘) ↓.

We evaluate rotational fidelity using the geodesic distance between generated and reference rotations:

d_R(R̂,R)=\cos⁻¹(clip((tr(R̂^⊤R)-1)/(2),-1,1)).

(S13)

We report the mean geodesic error across all 22 joints and matched keyframes, converted to degrees. We additionally report the mean error across the 21 non-root joints and the root orientation error separately.

Temporal Matching and Interpretation.

Only reference keyframes with valid corresponding frames in the generated sequence are evaluated; unmatched keyframes are excluded. Metrics are computed per sequence and then averaged with equal weight, with the numbers of matched and reference keyframes recorded separately.

Importantly, Experiments B and C do not impose equivalent constraints. Experiment B directly conditions skeletal motion on 3D poses, whereas Experiment C uses sparse 2D projections that do not uniquely specify depth or the complete 3D joint configuration. Furthermore, Experiment C introduces an additional video-to-3D reconstruction stage. Consequently, differences in fidelity may partly reflect projection ambiguity and reconstruction errors. These metrics measure structural consistency at selected keyframes rather than naturalness or preservation of the complete motion trajectory.

S1.4 Human Perceptual Evaluation

Study Setup. We conduct a blinded online perceptual study comparing V2M with Kimodo using pairs of 3D skeletal animations. Each pair is presented alongside the text description used to generate the motions. Both animations are rendered with neutral-colored avatars under identical visualization conditions, without identifying the underlying models. The video- and motion-model animations appear on both sides across the comparison set rather than consistently occupying the same position. A total of 43 participants completed the study, each evaluating 26 animation pairs. The selection and presentation order of the pairs vary across participants.

Pairwise Questions. For each pair, participants answer three questions: (i) “Which motion better matches the description?”, (ii) “Which motion looks more like a real person moving?”, and (iii) “Which motion has fewer visible errors?” These questions assess semantic alignment, perceived naturalness, and visible motion artifacts, respectively. The semantic question concerns how well the observed motion reflects the requested action, while the other two distinguish the overall impression of human movement from more localized errors, such as foot sliding, jitter, or implausible body poses. The questions are kept the same across all three experiments.

Action Coverage. To examine whether an animation performs the requested movements rather than only the dominant action, we also use a prompt-specific checklist for actions that can be evaluated separately. Participants assess the individual components of the description for each animation, without directly comparing the two models. For instance, a prompt asking a person to turn around and then wave is evaluated in terms of both movements. For compound prompts, an additional item assesses whether the movements occur in the required order or at the same time. This allows us to distinguish the presence of individual actions from their temporal coordination.

Preference Reporting and Scoring. For each pairwise question, participants select “Left”, “Right”, “About the same”, or “Cannot judge”. A preference for V2M is counted as a win and a preference for Kimodo as a loss. In the win/tie/loss (W/T/L) results reported in the main paper, “About the same” and “Cannot judge” are grouped in the non-preference category, reported as ties. Thus, the percentages are computed over all completed responses for each question; the displayed tie percentage is obtained after rounding the win and loss percentages so each row sums to 100%.

For the action checklist, participants indicate “Yes”, “Partly”, “No”, or “Cannot judge” for each component. We assign scores of 1, 0.5, and 0 to “Yes”, “Partly”, and “No”, respectively, and exclude “Cannot judge” from the corresponding average. We compute the action-completion score separately for video- and motion-model animations by averaging valid individual-action scores and reporting them as percentages. Temporal ordering and simultaneity are scored in the same way but reported separately from action completion. Incomplete submissions are excluded. Participants are not shown the original source motion as a reference; preservation of skeletal guidance is evaluated separately through quantitative keyframe fidelity.

item.title: 拼 3D 场景缺的不是资产，是「布局」：X-3DComposer 用前馈模型直接预测摆放 ｜ X-3DComposer: Feed-Forward 3D Scene Composition with Any Assets from Any Views
item.description:
一句话：3D 生成与 CAD 检索已经能供上资产，布局却仍缺通用解法。

要点：

  • 拆解清楚：要从图片组合出可编辑的 3D 场景，需要**每个物体一个资产 + 把它们摆好的布局**；资产已由 3D 生成与 CAD 检索解决
  • 布局却仍缺通用方案：场景生成方法把布局与生成**耦合**在一起，而姿态估计方法一次只处理一个物体，还需要真实尺寸的 CAD、深度或迭代精修
  • X-3DComposer 因此做一个**前馈模型**来直接预测布局，并支持「任意来源的资产、任意视角的输入」

为什么值得看：「资产已够、布局不够」这个判断很实：现在缺的是把一堆现成资产按图片摆好的能力。前馈预测布局比「生成式拼场景」更容易接进既有资产管线。

中文摘要：要从图片组合出一个可编辑的三维场景，需要两样东西：每个物体对应的资产，以及把它们摆放好的布局。如今三维生成与 CAD 检索已经能提供资产，但布局仍缺少通用解法——场景生成方法把布局与生成耦合在一起，姿态估计方法则一次只处理一个物体，并且需要真实尺寸的 CAD 模型、深度信息或迭代精修。X-3DComposer 因此提出一个前馈模型直接预测布局，并支持任意来源的资产与任意视角的输入。对已有资产库、需要快速把图片变成可编辑场景的团队，这种「只补布局」的做法更容易接进现有管线。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

X-3DComposer: Feed-Forward 3D Scene Composition
with Any Assets from Any Views

Abstract

Composing an editable 3D scene from images requires an asset for each object and a layout that places the assets. 3D generation and CAD retrieval now supply the assets, but layout still lacks a general solution: scene generation methods couple it with generation, and pose estimators handle one object at a time and need true-size CAD models, depth, or iterative refinement. We present X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that predicts the layout separately from asset generation. Given one or more images of a scene, the object masks, and an asset for each object from any source, it jointly predicts the rotation, translation, and per-axis scale of all objects in a single forward pass of about one second. The key idea is to treat objects as views: renders of the assets are processed together with the scene images by a multi-view geometry model adapted from VGGT-Ω, and each object pose follows in closed form from the cameras predicted for its renders. Camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth are optional inputs. When the meshes produced by five scene generation methods are kept fixed and only their layout is replaced, the layouts of X-3DComposer are more accurate than the native layouts of these methods. Compared with the stand-alone layout model SceneMaker, it reduces the scene-level Chamfer distance by 52% on IndoorMix, our test set from six indoor datasets, and by 28% on 3D-FUTURE.

1 Introduction

Composing an editable 3D scene of separate objects from one or more images is needed in content creation, embodied AI, and robot manipulation. Such a scene consists of a 3D asset for each object and the pose and scale of each asset. Assets are increasingly easy to obtain. 3D generators [52, 5] produce high-quality meshes from images, and CAD retrieval can provide exact or similar CAD models. This paper studies the other half of the problem, scene layout: given the assets, estimate the pose and scale of each one so that the composed scene matches the images.

Existing methods fall into three groups (Fig.1). The first group consists of scene generation methods [18, 31, 5, 27, 50], which output a layout together with the object geometry. This layout is a by-product of generation and cannot be applied to assets from other sources. The second group takes a CAD model as given. Object pose estimators [49, 25] handle one object at a time, assume a true-size CAD model, often require depth, and refine each pose by render-and-compare. CAD alignment methods [12] also estimate scale, but they too treat each detected object independently. The third group consists of stand-alone layout models [39, 28, 56], which separate layout from generation but rely on iterative sampling, dense correspondences, or per-scene optimization; most accept only a single image.

A general layout method should accept assets from any source and place all objects jointly, in a single forward pass, from one or more views. None of the methods above meets all of these requirements. Multi-view geometry models [43, 44] already do this for cameras: they predict the cameras of any number of views in a common frame at once. We observe that layout can be cast as the same task by treating objects as views. We render each asset from a few viewpoints with known cameras in its own frame and feed the renders to a multi-view geometry model together with the scene images. The model predicts a camera for every view in a common scene frame. Each render camera is then known in the asset frame and predicted in the scene frame, and the object pose follows from the two in closed form. All objects are thus placed jointly, without sampling or optimization, and since the model needs only renders of an asset, it applies to any asset. Predicting a camera for each view is also the pretraining task of these models, which lets us start from the pretrained VGGT-Ω[44], keep its architecture, and add few parameters.

Whole scenes raise further difficulties. The model must know which object each render belongs to, even when objects look identical, so each object is assigned an identity embedding that links its masks, its crops from the scene images, and its renders. Generated or retrieved assets often differ in proportions from the real objects, and we therefore predict one scale per axis. The input also varies from one image to several, with or without camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth. We treat these as optional geometric conditions. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We present X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that predicts the layout of all objects (rotation, translation, and per-axis scale) in a single forward pass of about one second, given any number of scene images and assets from any source.

  • •

    We extend camera-based pose prediction [4, 37] from single objects to whole scenes: the crops and renders of all objects are fed as extra views to a multi-view geometry model adapted from VGGT-Ω, with identity embeddings and optional geometric conditions, and the object poses are read out in closed form from the predicted cameras.

  • •

    With the meshes fixed and only the layout changed, our layouts are more accurate than the native layouts of five scene generation methods, and our scene-level Chamfer distance is 52% lower than that of SceneMaker [39] on our IndoorMix test set and 28% lower on 3D-FUTURE.

    • 2 Related Work

    Compositional 3D scene generation and reconstruction.

    One line of work generates the geometry of several objects together with their layout. MIDI [18] and SceneGen [31] generate all objects of a scene jointly, while SAM 3D [5] and its multi-view extension MV-SAM3D [27] generate a mesh for each object and predict its rotation, translation, and scale. FIRE3D [50] also outputs the objects together with their layout. Such a layout applies only to the assets generated with it. Our model does not depend on a particular generator. Another line of work first obtains the assets and then solves for the layout. CAST [54] places each generated object in the scene point cloud with an alignment model and refines the poses by optimization under physics constraints. Given a single image, SceneMaker [39] samples the object poses iteratively from a pose model conditioned on object geometry. Mira-Scene [41] and Easy-3Dfy [56] solve for the transformation from dense correspondences between the object and an estimated point cloud, and Lucida [36] adjusts the poses iteratively with a vision-language model. SPOON [28] handles uncalibrated multi-view input by guiding the pose sampling of SAM 3D with a VGGT-Ω reconstruction, followed by per-scene optimization. Pano3DComposer [37] feeds object crops and asset renders to VGGT and predicts a transformation with per-axis scale for each object separately, from panoramic input. These methods handle one object at a time or rely on iterative procedures, whereas our model places all objects in a single forward pass.

    CAD alignment and object pose estimation.

    Single-image CAD alignment methods [24, 12, 11] retrieve a CAD model for each detected object and align it to the image, and recent methods [1, 7] solve for pose and scale from feature correspondences between the image and the CAD model. Methods for 6-DoF pose estimation of novel objects assume a true-size CAD model. MegaPose [25] and FoundationPose [49] use render-and-compare, GigaPose [33] uses templates and feature correspondences, and AlignPose [32] refines poses over multiple views. Closest to our approach is PoseGAM [4]. Initialized from VGGT, it treats renders of the CAD model as views with known cameras, regresses the camera of the query image, and derives the 6-DoF object pose from it. In contrast, we place all objects jointly and predict per-axis scales, and thus need no true-size CAD models.

    Multi-view geometry models.

    DUSt3R [47] and MASt3R [26] regress point maps directly from image pairs, and VGGT [43] predicts the cameras, depth, and point maps of multiple images in a single forward pass. Later models such as π³[48], Depth Anything 3 [29], and VGGT-Ω[44] follow the same paradigm. Pow3R [19], MapAnything [21], and OmniVGGT [34] additionally accept camera intrinsics, camera poses, or depth as optional inputs. These models reconstruct the scene as a whole and have no notion of individual objects; we keep their task and optional conditions and add objects as extra views.

    3 Method

    Figure2 gives an overview of X-3DComposer; details are in the supplementary material.

    3.1 Problem Definition

    The required input consists of S≥1 images of a scene, the scene views{Iⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^S; the masks Mᵢ of the N target objects in these views; and one 3D asset Aᵢ per object. An asset is a mesh, usually textured, from a CAD library, a retrieval system, or a 3D generator. It need not match its object exactly; the same category and a similar shape suffice. From these inputs, our method predicts the layout of all objects,

    {(Rᵢ,tᵢ,sᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^N=F({Iⱼ}, {Mᵢ}, {Aᵢ}; K,P,D),

    		(1)

    where K, P, and D are optional geometric conditions described below. For each object i, the layout specifies a rotation Rᵢ∈SO(3), a translation tᵢ∈ℝ³, and a per-axis scale sᵢ∈ℝ³_>0, nine degrees of freedom in total. A point p on the asset is mapped to the scene point

    x=Rᵢ diag(sᵢ) p+tᵢ.

    		(2)

    Frames and geometric conditions.

    Each asset is first normalized: it is translated so that its bounding box is centered at the origin and scaled uniformly so that the longest side of the box is 1. This defines its asset frame. The output poses are expressed in the scene frame, the camera frame of the first scene view (Fig.3). The scene views may come with three optional geometric conditions: intrinsics K, the camera pose Pⱼ of each view relative to the first one (collectively P), and depth D. They may be measured, for example by an RGB-D sensor or SLAM, or estimated by other models. A camera pose is the rigid transformation from the camera frame to a reference frame; the superscripts R and o, as in Pⱼ^R and Pⱼᵒ, denote the rotation and camera center of a pose. If the input fixes a unit of length through depth or camera poses, the output is in that unit; otherwise it is in normalized units, in which the mean distance from the scene points to the first camera is 1.

    3.2 Objects as Views

    Background: multi-view geometry models.

    VGGT-Ω[44], the successor to VGGT [43], predicts a camera and a depth map for every input image in a single forward pass, with all cameras expressed in the camera frame of the first image. Each image is encoded into patch tokens by a DINO encoder, and one camera token and several register tokens are prepended. The tokens of all images pass through alternating frame-attention and global-attention blocks. A camera head then regresses the camera of each image from its camera token, and a dense head predicts depth.

    Representing objects as views.

    We do not feed the asset geometry to the model. Instead, we render each asset and treat the renders as extra views. The pretrained model already takes images as input, so its ability to relate views carries over to relating an asset to the scene, and no 3D encoder has to be trained from scratch.

    Three types of views.

    The model takes three types of views as input (Fig.2):

  • •

    Scene views: the S scene images.

  • •

    Object crops: c square regions around each object, cut from the full-resolution scene images. Scene views are downsampled before entering the model, and the crops restore the detail that small objects lose.

  • •

    Asset renders: M images of each asset rendered in its asset frame. The camera pose of the m-th render of object i, L_i,m=[L^R_i,m|Lᵒ_i,m], and its intrinsics are known by construction.

    • Views of all types are processed alike, and the camera head predicts a camera for each. The masks are not fed to the model as images; they determine where the identity embeddings of the objects are added (Sec.3.3).

    Pose readout.

    The readout converts the predicted render cameras into object poses. Let q=diag(sᵢ) p be the coordinates in the scaled asset frame, where Eq.2 becomes the rigid transformation x=Rᵢq+tᵢ. In this frame, the camera of the m-th render is

    V_i,m=[ L^R_i,m | diag(sᵢ) Lᵒ_i,m ],

    		(3)

    that is, its orientation is unchanged and its center is scaled together with the asset (Fig.3b). For an isotropic scale this is exact; for an anisotropic scale it is a convention, which the training labels and the readout both follow. The model predicts the camera of each render in the scene frame, P̂_i,m=[P̂^R_i,m|P̂ᵒ_i,m], expressed relative to the predicted camera of the first scene view. Since V_i,m and P̂_i,m describe the same camera in the scaled asset frame and in the scene frame, each render gives a rigid pose of the object in closed form:

    [ R_i,m|t_i,m ] = P̂_i,m V_i,m⁻¹,

    		(4)

    or, explicitly, R_i,m=P̂^R_i,m(L^R_i,m)^⊤ and t_i,m=P̂ᵒ_i,m-R_i,m diag(sᵢ) Lᵒ_i,m.

    Fusion over renders.

    We average the M pose candidates (R_i,m,t_i,m) given by Eq.4 into the fused pose: the translation tᵢ is the mean of the candidate translations, and the rotation Rᵢ is the mean of the candidate rotation matrices, projected back onto SO(3) by SVD. The scale is computed before the poses, since the candidates depend on it. The model outputs a per-axis log-scale ℓ_i,m for each render (Sec.3.3), and the object scale is sᵢ=\exp(1/M∑ₘℓ_i,m), used for all render cameras of object i in Eq.3. If the input fixes a unit of length, we estimate one global factor that converts normalized units to this unit and multiply all tᵢ and sᵢ by it. The readout involves no test-time optimization and does not use the crops.

    3.3 Network

    Backbone and trainable parameters.

    We build on VGGT-Ω and keep its architecture. The trainable parameters (Fig.2) are (i) the output branch of the camera head, (ii) LoRA [17] on the query and value projections of the frame- and global-attention blocks and of the attention blocks in the camera head, and (iii) the condition encoders and identity embeddings introduced below; all other weights are frozen. The output layers of the new modules are zero-initialized, so training starts from the output of the pretrained backbone. The camera head outputs a 9-dimensional camera encoding per view. We add three dimensions for the per-axis log-scale ℓ, used only for the renders.

    Identity embeddings.

    Identical objects cannot be told apart by appearance, so each crop and render must be tied to its object explicitly. We keep a set of learnable identity embeddings and assign one of them, eᵢ, at random to each object of a scene. An embedding thus only distinguishes the objects within a scene and carries no other meaning. In every view, the identity vector of patch u is the sum of the embeddings of the objects whose masks overlap the patch, weighted by the overlap:

    zᵤ=∑ᵢ₌₁^Nα_i,u eᵢ,

    		(5)

    where α_i,u∈[0,1] is the fraction of the patch covered by the mask of object i, so that zᵤ is zero on the background. In scene views and crops, the masks are those given as input; in a render, the mask is the foreground of the rendered asset. After a linear projection, zᵤ is added to the values of every attention block and, in the global-attention blocks, also to the queries and keys.

    Condition encoders.

    For a view with intrinsics and a camera pose, the camera parameters are encoded by an MLP and added to the camera token, and the Plücker ray of each pixel is embedded by a convolution and added to the patch tokens. With intrinsics only, the rays are computed in the view’s own camera frame. A depth map is embedded by a second convolution and added to the patch tokens. The render cameras L_i,m are always known and are encoded in the same way, in the asset frame.

    3.4 Training

    Training uses the ground-truth cameras and depth of the scene, as well as the ground-truth pose and scale (Rᵢ^*,tᵢ^*,sᵢ^*) of every object. As in the backbone, all targets are expressed in the normalized units of Sec.3.1.

    Supervision of cameras, scales, and poses.

    Scene views keep the losses of the backbone. Renders use the same camera loss, with the label P^*_i,m=[Rᵢ^*|tᵢ^*] V^*_i,m, where V^*_i,m is built from the ground-truth scale as in Eq.3. Each log-scale ℓ_i,m is supervised with an L1 loss against \logsᵢ^*. Crops are supervised with auxiliary camera and depth losses.

    The camera loss treats each render separately and does not directly constrain the pose that is finally read out. We therefore also compute the pose candidates differentiably with Eq.4 and compare two poses of object i by

    dᵢ(R,t;R^′,t^′) = (\lVertt-t^′\rVert₂)/(\lVertsᵢ^*\rVert₂) + (\lVertR-R^′\rVert_F)/(√2).

    		(6)

    The translation term is divided by the object size \lVertsᵢ^*\rVert₂ and is thus independent of the unit of length. We penalize dᵢ between every candidate and the ground truth, between the fused pose and the ground truth, and between every candidate and the fused pose.

    Symmetry, grounding, and physics.

    Objects that are symmetric about the vertical axis, such as round tables and vases, have several equally correct poses. We detect such symmetries for each asset offline and train with the equivalent label closest to the current prediction. A grounding head, used only in training, takes the camera token of each crop and render and predicts which scene-view patches its object occupies. This encourages the model to link crops and renders to their objects in the scene. We also apply two physics constraints to the layout that is read out, penalizing penetration between objects and the offset of floor-supported objects from the floor.

    Training data and sampling.

    Training requires scenes with 9-DoF object annotations. We combine several sources in a common format: synthetic indoor scenes [9, 10, 22, 57, 23, 51, 35], real scans from ScanNet++ [55] with annotated CAD models [38, 3], and single-view images [40, 10]. We oversample scenes that contain several instances of the same asset, so that the model must rely on the identity embeddings to tell them apart. We also randomly replace the asset of an object with an asset of similar shape from the same category and adjust the labels accordingly, which mimics assets that do not exactly match the object. Since the geometric conditions are optional at inference, each training sample is given a random subset of them. The numbers of scene views, objects, and renders per object are also drawn at random, so one model covers all input settings.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Test data.

    Our main test set, IndoorMix, merges held-out scenes from six indoor datasets: InternScenes [57], MolmoSpaces [23], SAGE [51], SceneSmith [35], 3D-FRONT [9], and the real scans of ScanNet++ [55]. We also report results on the 3D-FUTURE [10] test set of SceneGen [31], an existing benchmark of rendered single-view indoor scenes. Details of the test data, results per dataset, and more qualitative results are given in the supplementary material.

    Metrics and alignment.

    We use the metrics of MIDI [18]: the scene-level Chamfer distance (CD-S), F-score (F-S), and bounding-box IoU (IoU-B), and, in Table1, the object-level CD-O and F-O. The methods compared on generated assets (Table1) output layouts in different frames. We follow MIDI and normalize the predicted and the ground-truth scene separately before registering them with a single rigid ICP [2]. These metrics therefore measure the relative layout of the objects. CD-S, a mean over scenes of squared distances, is sensitive to a few scenes with large errors; F-S and IoU-B are less so. With ground-truth CAD models (Tables2, 3 and 4), every method outputs poses in the camera frame of the first scene view, where we compare them without ICP, aligning only the scale of each scene. In all tables, CD values are multiplied by 10³, F-scores are in percent, and the best result is in bold (Tables3 and 4: second best underlined).

    Inputs and implementation.

    All methods that take object masks use the same ground-truth masks. Unless a method specifies its own estimator, estimated geometric conditions come from MoGe-2 [46] for single-view input and from Depth Anything 3 [29] for multi-view input. Our model uses the 1B-parameter VGGT-Ω with rank-32 LoRA and is trained with AdamW [30] on 8 GPUs for about 200k steps. At inference, we use M=4 renders per object.

    4.2 Layout Prediction for Generated Assets

    This experiment tests whether a stand-alone layout model places a set of assets more accurately than the method that generated them. We use five scene generation methods: MIDI [18], SceneGen [31], FIRE3D [50], SAM 3D [5], and MV-SAM3D [27]. MIDI, SceneGen, and SAM 3D take a single view, MV-SAM3D takes several views, and FIRE3D supports both. Each method generates the meshes of all objects in the scene views, together with its native layout. We then place the same meshes with our model and with the public pose model of SceneMaker [39], which reports state-of-the-art pose accuracy and takes only a single view.

    Results.

    In Table1, our layouts are more accurate than SceneMaker’s in every single-view group and, with one exception, more accurate than the native layouts in every group and metric: in the FIRE3D group on 3D-FUTURE, the F-S of the native layout is 0.08 points higher. The gain is largest for MIDI and SceneGen, whose native layouts have large errors, but there is also a gain for SAM 3D, whose native layout is already fairly accurate. Averaged over the four single-view groups, our CD-S is 52% lower than that of SceneMaker on IndoorMix and 28% lower on 3D-FUTURE. With multi-view input, our layouts improve on the native layouts of FIRE3D and MV-SAM3D in all metrics, most clearly for MV-SAM3D (CD-S 1.61 vs. 6.38). Our model receives no geometric conditions in this comparison, whereas FIRE3D, SAM 3D, MV-SAM3D, and SceneMaker all use estimated depth. The gain therefore does not come from a better depth estimator. In Fig.4, when objects occlude one another or are cut off by the image border, the baselines place them in the wrong position or orientation, while our layouts stay close to the ground truth.

    4.3 Layout Prediction for GT CAD Models

    When the asset is the ground-truth CAD model of the object, our task coincides with object pose estimation. We compare with FoundationPose [49], PoseGAM [4], and the multi-view AlignPose [32]. Since these methods require true-size CAD models, all methods receive the ground-truth CAD models at their true size, and our model uses the given size in place of its predicted scale.

    Results.

    Among the methods that use no ground-truth conditions (upper block of Table2; examples in Fig.5), our model without conditions is the most accurate in all three settings. PoseGAM, the only baseline without depth, has much larger errors. With the same estimated conditions as the baselines, our F-S and IoU-B are also higher than those of FoundationPose and AlignPose. Our CD-S is lower than or on par with that of FoundationPose. With K+P+D, however, it is far higher than without conditions (75.95 vs. 0.85) and slightly above that of AlignPose. Inaccurate estimated camera poses mislead the model. Ground-truth poses give its lowest CD-S (0.52). Here, estimated conditions do not improve our results and can degrade them, whereas ground-truth ones improve them. With ground-truth conditions (lower block), FoundationPose reaches a higher IoU-B on IndoorMix, as its render-and-compare gains more from accurate depth than our model does. Our F-S under the same conditions is on par or higher.

    4.4 Layout Prediction from Panoramic Input

    We compare with Pano3DComposer [37] on 42 3D-FRONT houses that are in the training data of neither method, with one or two panoramas of the same room as input. For our model, each panorama is split into six perspective views, whose intrinsics and relative camera poses within the panorama follow from the projection and can be given as conditions. In Table3, our model is more accurate for both input types, even without conditions. Adding the intrinsics and camera poses derived from a single panorama improves our results further.

    4.5 Ablations and Analysis

    Design choices.

    All variants in Table4 are trained on 3D-FRONT with the same shortened schedule and evaluated there with ground-truth intrinsics and depth. Trained from random initialization, the model fails under this schedule (single-view F-S 40.7 vs. 90.8). Without identity embeddings, and hence without the masks, F-S falls to 71.7: the embeddings are needed to tie crops and renders to their objects in general, not only when objects look identical. The object crops give a smaller but consistent gain (single-view CD-S 9.49 vs. 11.88). The grounding head helps with multi-view input (CD-S 3.92 vs. 4.94) and has a mixed effect with single-view input. Without the physics constraints, the scene metrics are slightly better, but the percentage of penetrating objects rises from 7.9% to 10.1%.

    Mismatched assets and identical objects.

    Assets from retrieval or generation rarely match the object exactly, and a scene may contain identical objects. We test both cases in Fig.6. Re-texturing an asset barely changes the predicted pose (a), and replacing it with another asset of the same category makes the model adapt the pose to the new shape (b). For two identical objects, swapping their identity embeddings swaps the two assets (c), which shows that the model follows the identity embeddings.

    Views, renders, and runtime.

    More scene views improve accuracy at little extra cost. From one to eight views, the time per scene grows by less than 0.2 s. More renders per object raise F-S and IoU-B slightly (see the supplementary material). In Table5, our model takes about 1 s per scene, and the three baselines take 5.8–7.5 s.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that composes a 3D scene from given assets by predicting their layout. Its key idea is to treat objects as views: with asset renders as extra views, layout becomes camera prediction, a task that pretrained multi-view geometry models already solve well. Our experiments show that layout need not be tied to asset generation. On the same meshes, our layouts are more accurate than the native layouts of five scene generation methods. Without depth input, our scene-level Chamfer distance is 52% lower than that of SceneMaker on IndoorMix and 28% lower on 3D-FUTURE. As the model needs only asset renders, it can be combined with any generator or retrieval system. Our model has limitations. It requires object masks as input and is trained and tested only on indoor scenes. It is also sensitive to inaccurate geometric conditions, and its physics constraints reduce penetration without guaranteeing physically plausible layouts. Predicting the masks within the model and extending it to other scene types are left for future work.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    Section and equation numbers, Tables 1–5, and Figures 1–6 refer to the main paper, and the tables follow its conventions.

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    Backbone.

    The backbone is the 1B-parameter VGGT-Ω model. It has a token width of 1024 and alternates 24 frame-attention blocks with 24 global-attention blocks; five of the global-attention blocks attend only to the camera and register tokens. As in the original model, the resolution of a scene view depends on its aspect ratio, and every scene view has about 416² pixels (for example, 416×416 or 304×560). For frame attention, views are batched by resolution.

    New modules.

    The ray encoder is a convolution of stride 16 on the 6-channel Plücker rays, followed by a linear layer that maps to the token width. For a view with intrinsics but no camera pose, two learnable “camera pose unknown” vectors are added, one to its camera token and the other to each of its patch tokens. The depth encoder is a second convolution of stride 16, applied to the logarithm of the normalized depth and a validity mask. The camera encoder is an MLP that maps the field of view and the world-to-camera rotation (as a quaternion) and translation to the token width. There are 64 identity embeddings of dimension 64, so one forward pass handles at most 64 objects. In addition to the patch-wise identity vectors of Eq.5, the camera token of each crop and render receives the embedding of its object. The output layers of the ray and camera encoders, the two “camera pose unknown” vectors, the linear projections of the identity vectors, and the three log-scale outputs added to the camera head are zero-initialized. The convolution of the depth encoder has no bias and starts from small random weights; it adds nothing to the tokens of views without depth input.

    Frames and geometric conditions.

    In the asset frame, +Y points up, and coordinates have no physical unit. The scale sᵢ and the translation tᵢ share one unit of length, which can be fixed only by depth or by camera poses with a nonzero baseline. Camera poses and depth are accepted only together with intrinsics, so there are five combinations of conditions: K+P+D, K+P, K+D, K, and none.

    Normalization and metric-scale recovery.

    Let X be the ground-truth scene points (in the frame of the first camera) and oⱼ the camera center of scene view j (o₁=0). The training targets are divided by g, and, following OmniVGGT [34], the input depth and camera centers are normalized separately:

    \begingatheredg=(1)/(|X|)∑_x∈X\lVertx\rVert₂, D̃=D/mean(D), õⱼ=oⱼ/β, β=1/S-1∑ⱼ₌₂^S\lVertoⱼ\rVert₂,\endgathered

    		(7)

    with β=1 if S=1 or if all camera centers coincide. At inference, the global factor of Sec.3.2, denoted here by λ, is λ_D if depth is given, and otherwise λ_P if camera poses of several views are given:

    λ_D=median(D/D̂), λ_P=(∑_j≥2\lVertoⱼ\rVert₂ \lVertôⱼ\rVert₂)/(∑_j≥2\lVertôⱼ\rVert₂²),

    		(8)
item.content:encoded:
一句话：3D 生成与 CAD 检索已经能供上资产，布局却仍缺通用解法。

要点：

  • 拆解清楚：要从图片组合出可编辑的 3D 场景，需要**每个物体一个资产 + 把它们摆好的布局**；资产已由 3D 生成与 CAD 检索解决
  • 布局却仍缺通用方案：场景生成方法把布局与生成**耦合**在一起，而姿态估计方法一次只处理一个物体，还需要真实尺寸的 CAD、深度或迭代精修
  • X-3DComposer 因此做一个**前馈模型**来直接预测布局，并支持「任意来源的资产、任意视角的输入」

为什么值得看：「资产已够、布局不够」这个判断很实：现在缺的是把一堆现成资产按图片摆好的能力。前馈预测布局比「生成式拼场景」更容易接进既有资产管线。

中文摘要：要从图片组合出一个可编辑的三维场景，需要两样东西：每个物体对应的资产，以及把它们摆放好的布局。如今三维生成与 CAD 检索已经能提供资产，但布局仍缺少通用解法——场景生成方法把布局与生成耦合在一起，姿态估计方法则一次只处理一个物体，并且需要真实尺寸的 CAD 模型、深度信息或迭代精修。X-3DComposer 因此提出一个前馈模型直接预测布局，并支持任意来源的资产与任意视角的输入。对已有资产库、需要快速把图片变成可编辑场景的团队，这种「只补布局」的做法更容易接进现有管线。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

X-3DComposer: Feed-Forward 3D Scene Composition
with Any Assets from Any Views

Abstract

Composing an editable 3D scene from images requires an asset for each object and a layout that places the assets. 3D generation and CAD retrieval now supply the assets, but layout still lacks a general solution: scene generation methods couple it with generation, and pose estimators handle one object at a time and need true-size CAD models, depth, or iterative refinement. We present X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that predicts the layout separately from asset generation. Given one or more images of a scene, the object masks, and an asset for each object from any source, it jointly predicts the rotation, translation, and per-axis scale of all objects in a single forward pass of about one second. The key idea is to treat objects as views: renders of the assets are processed together with the scene images by a multi-view geometry model adapted from VGGT-Ω, and each object pose follows in closed form from the cameras predicted for its renders. Camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth are optional inputs. When the meshes produced by five scene generation methods are kept fixed and only their layout is replaced, the layouts of X-3DComposer are more accurate than the native layouts of these methods. Compared with the stand-alone layout model SceneMaker, it reduces the scene-level Chamfer distance by 52% on IndoorMix, our test set from six indoor datasets, and by 28% on 3D-FUTURE.

1 Introduction

Composing an editable 3D scene of separate objects from one or more images is needed in content creation, embodied AI, and robot manipulation. Such a scene consists of a 3D asset for each object and the pose and scale of each asset. Assets are increasingly easy to obtain. 3D generators [52, 5] produce high-quality meshes from images, and CAD retrieval can provide exact or similar CAD models. This paper studies the other half of the problem, scene layout: given the assets, estimate the pose and scale of each one so that the composed scene matches the images.

Existing methods fall into three groups (Fig.1). The first group consists of scene generation methods [18, 31, 5, 27, 50], which output a layout together with the object geometry. This layout is a by-product of generation and cannot be applied to assets from other sources. The second group takes a CAD model as given. Object pose estimators [49, 25] handle one object at a time, assume a true-size CAD model, often require depth, and refine each pose by render-and-compare. CAD alignment methods [12] also estimate scale, but they too treat each detected object independently. The third group consists of stand-alone layout models [39, 28, 56], which separate layout from generation but rely on iterative sampling, dense correspondences, or per-scene optimization; most accept only a single image.

A general layout method should accept assets from any source and place all objects jointly, in a single forward pass, from one or more views. None of the methods above meets all of these requirements. Multi-view geometry models [43, 44] already do this for cameras: they predict the cameras of any number of views in a common frame at once. We observe that layout can be cast as the same task by treating objects as views. We render each asset from a few viewpoints with known cameras in its own frame and feed the renders to a multi-view geometry model together with the scene images. The model predicts a camera for every view in a common scene frame. Each render camera is then known in the asset frame and predicted in the scene frame, and the object pose follows from the two in closed form. All objects are thus placed jointly, without sampling or optimization, and since the model needs only renders of an asset, it applies to any asset. Predicting a camera for each view is also the pretraining task of these models, which lets us start from the pretrained VGGT-Ω[44], keep its architecture, and add few parameters.

Whole scenes raise further difficulties. The model must know which object each render belongs to, even when objects look identical, so each object is assigned an identity embedding that links its masks, its crops from the scene images, and its renders. Generated or retrieved assets often differ in proportions from the real objects, and we therefore predict one scale per axis. The input also varies from one image to several, with or without camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth. We treat these as optional geometric conditions. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We present X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that predicts the layout of all objects (rotation, translation, and per-axis scale) in a single forward pass of about one second, given any number of scene images and assets from any source.

  • •

    We extend camera-based pose prediction [4, 37] from single objects to whole scenes: the crops and renders of all objects are fed as extra views to a multi-view geometry model adapted from VGGT-Ω, with identity embeddings and optional geometric conditions, and the object poses are read out in closed form from the predicted cameras.

  • •

    With the meshes fixed and only the layout changed, our layouts are more accurate than the native layouts of five scene generation methods, and our scene-level Chamfer distance is 52% lower than that of SceneMaker [39] on our IndoorMix test set and 28% lower on 3D-FUTURE.

    • 2 Related Work

    Compositional 3D scene generation and reconstruction.

    One line of work generates the geometry of several objects together with their layout. MIDI [18] and SceneGen [31] generate all objects of a scene jointly, while SAM 3D [5] and its multi-view extension MV-SAM3D [27] generate a mesh for each object and predict its rotation, translation, and scale. FIRE3D [50] also outputs the objects together with their layout. Such a layout applies only to the assets generated with it. Our model does not depend on a particular generator. Another line of work first obtains the assets and then solves for the layout. CAST [54] places each generated object in the scene point cloud with an alignment model and refines the poses by optimization under physics constraints. Given a single image, SceneMaker [39] samples the object poses iteratively from a pose model conditioned on object geometry. Mira-Scene [41] and Easy-3Dfy [56] solve for the transformation from dense correspondences between the object and an estimated point cloud, and Lucida [36] adjusts the poses iteratively with a vision-language model. SPOON [28] handles uncalibrated multi-view input by guiding the pose sampling of SAM 3D with a VGGT-Ω reconstruction, followed by per-scene optimization. Pano3DComposer [37] feeds object crops and asset renders to VGGT and predicts a transformation with per-axis scale for each object separately, from panoramic input. These methods handle one object at a time or rely on iterative procedures, whereas our model places all objects in a single forward pass.

    CAD alignment and object pose estimation.

    Single-image CAD alignment methods [24, 12, 11] retrieve a CAD model for each detected object and align it to the image, and recent methods [1, 7] solve for pose and scale from feature correspondences between the image and the CAD model. Methods for 6-DoF pose estimation of novel objects assume a true-size CAD model. MegaPose [25] and FoundationPose [49] use render-and-compare, GigaPose [33] uses templates and feature correspondences, and AlignPose [32] refines poses over multiple views. Closest to our approach is PoseGAM [4]. Initialized from VGGT, it treats renders of the CAD model as views with known cameras, regresses the camera of the query image, and derives the 6-DoF object pose from it. In contrast, we place all objects jointly and predict per-axis scales, and thus need no true-size CAD models.

    Multi-view geometry models.

    DUSt3R [47] and MASt3R [26] regress point maps directly from image pairs, and VGGT [43] predicts the cameras, depth, and point maps of multiple images in a single forward pass. Later models such as π³[48], Depth Anything 3 [29], and VGGT-Ω[44] follow the same paradigm. Pow3R [19], MapAnything [21], and OmniVGGT [34] additionally accept camera intrinsics, camera poses, or depth as optional inputs. These models reconstruct the scene as a whole and have no notion of individual objects; we keep their task and optional conditions and add objects as extra views.

    3 Method

    Figure2 gives an overview of X-3DComposer; details are in the supplementary material.

    3.1 Problem Definition

    The required input consists of S≥1 images of a scene, the scene views{Iⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^S; the masks Mᵢ of the N target objects in these views; and one 3D asset Aᵢ per object. An asset is a mesh, usually textured, from a CAD library, a retrieval system, or a 3D generator. It need not match its object exactly; the same category and a similar shape suffice. From these inputs, our method predicts the layout of all objects,

    {(Rᵢ,tᵢ,sᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^N=F({Iⱼ}, {Mᵢ}, {Aᵢ}; K,P,D),

    		(1)

    where K, P, and D are optional geometric conditions described below. For each object i, the layout specifies a rotation Rᵢ∈SO(3), a translation tᵢ∈ℝ³, and a per-axis scale sᵢ∈ℝ³_>0, nine degrees of freedom in total. A point p on the asset is mapped to the scene point

    x=Rᵢ diag(sᵢ) p+tᵢ.

    		(2)

    Frames and geometric conditions.

    Each asset is first normalized: it is translated so that its bounding box is centered at the origin and scaled uniformly so that the longest side of the box is 1. This defines its asset frame. The output poses are expressed in the scene frame, the camera frame of the first scene view (Fig.3). The scene views may come with three optional geometric conditions: intrinsics K, the camera pose Pⱼ of each view relative to the first one (collectively P), and depth D. They may be measured, for example by an RGB-D sensor or SLAM, or estimated by other models. A camera pose is the rigid transformation from the camera frame to a reference frame; the superscripts R and o, as in Pⱼ^R and Pⱼᵒ, denote the rotation and camera center of a pose. If the input fixes a unit of length through depth or camera poses, the output is in that unit; otherwise it is in normalized units, in which the mean distance from the scene points to the first camera is 1.

    3.2 Objects as Views

    Background: multi-view geometry models.

    VGGT-Ω[44], the successor to VGGT [43], predicts a camera and a depth map for every input image in a single forward pass, with all cameras expressed in the camera frame of the first image. Each image is encoded into patch tokens by a DINO encoder, and one camera token and several register tokens are prepended. The tokens of all images pass through alternating frame-attention and global-attention blocks. A camera head then regresses the camera of each image from its camera token, and a dense head predicts depth.

    Representing objects as views.

    We do not feed the asset geometry to the model. Instead, we render each asset and treat the renders as extra views. The pretrained model already takes images as input, so its ability to relate views carries over to relating an asset to the scene, and no 3D encoder has to be trained from scratch.

    Three types of views.

    The model takes three types of views as input (Fig.2):

  • •

    Scene views: the S scene images.

  • •

    Object crops: c square regions around each object, cut from the full-resolution scene images. Scene views are downsampled before entering the model, and the crops restore the detail that small objects lose.

  • •

    Asset renders: M images of each asset rendered in its asset frame. The camera pose of the m-th render of object i, L_i,m=[L^R_i,m|Lᵒ_i,m], and its intrinsics are known by construction.

    • Views of all types are processed alike, and the camera head predicts a camera for each. The masks are not fed to the model as images; they determine where the identity embeddings of the objects are added (Sec.3.3).

    Pose readout.

    The readout converts the predicted render cameras into object poses. Let q=diag(sᵢ) p be the coordinates in the scaled asset frame, where Eq.2 becomes the rigid transformation x=Rᵢq+tᵢ. In this frame, the camera of the m-th render is

    V_i,m=[ L^R_i,m | diag(sᵢ) Lᵒ_i,m ],

    		(3)

    that is, its orientation is unchanged and its center is scaled together with the asset (Fig.3b). For an isotropic scale this is exact; for an anisotropic scale it is a convention, which the training labels and the readout both follow. The model predicts the camera of each render in the scene frame, P̂_i,m=[P̂^R_i,m|P̂ᵒ_i,m], expressed relative to the predicted camera of the first scene view. Since V_i,m and P̂_i,m describe the same camera in the scaled asset frame and in the scene frame, each render gives a rigid pose of the object in closed form:

    [ R_i,m|t_i,m ] = P̂_i,m V_i,m⁻¹,

    		(4)

    or, explicitly, R_i,m=P̂^R_i,m(L^R_i,m)^⊤ and t_i,m=P̂ᵒ_i,m-R_i,m diag(sᵢ) Lᵒ_i,m.

    Fusion over renders.

    We average the M pose candidates (R_i,m,t_i,m) given by Eq.4 into the fused pose: the translation tᵢ is the mean of the candidate translations, and the rotation Rᵢ is the mean of the candidate rotation matrices, projected back onto SO(3) by SVD. The scale is computed before the poses, since the candidates depend on it. The model outputs a per-axis log-scale ℓ_i,m for each render (Sec.3.3), and the object scale is sᵢ=\exp(1/M∑ₘℓ_i,m), used for all render cameras of object i in Eq.3. If the input fixes a unit of length, we estimate one global factor that converts normalized units to this unit and multiply all tᵢ and sᵢ by it. The readout involves no test-time optimization and does not use the crops.

    3.3 Network

    Backbone and trainable parameters.

    We build on VGGT-Ω and keep its architecture. The trainable parameters (Fig.2) are (i) the output branch of the camera head, (ii) LoRA [17] on the query and value projections of the frame- and global-attention blocks and of the attention blocks in the camera head, and (iii) the condition encoders and identity embeddings introduced below; all other weights are frozen. The output layers of the new modules are zero-initialized, so training starts from the output of the pretrained backbone. The camera head outputs a 9-dimensional camera encoding per view. We add three dimensions for the per-axis log-scale ℓ, used only for the renders.

    Identity embeddings.

    Identical objects cannot be told apart by appearance, so each crop and render must be tied to its object explicitly. We keep a set of learnable identity embeddings and assign one of them, eᵢ, at random to each object of a scene. An embedding thus only distinguishes the objects within a scene and carries no other meaning. In every view, the identity vector of patch u is the sum of the embeddings of the objects whose masks overlap the patch, weighted by the overlap:

    zᵤ=∑ᵢ₌₁^Nα_i,u eᵢ,

    		(5)

    where α_i,u∈[0,1] is the fraction of the patch covered by the mask of object i, so that zᵤ is zero on the background. In scene views and crops, the masks are those given as input; in a render, the mask is the foreground of the rendered asset. After a linear projection, zᵤ is added to the values of every attention block and, in the global-attention blocks, also to the queries and keys.

    Condition encoders.

    For a view with intrinsics and a camera pose, the camera parameters are encoded by an MLP and added to the camera token, and the Plücker ray of each pixel is embedded by a convolution and added to the patch tokens. With intrinsics only, the rays are computed in the view’s own camera frame. A depth map is embedded by a second convolution and added to the patch tokens. The render cameras L_i,m are always known and are encoded in the same way, in the asset frame.

    3.4 Training

    Training uses the ground-truth cameras and depth of the scene, as well as the ground-truth pose and scale (Rᵢ^*,tᵢ^*,sᵢ^*) of every object. As in the backbone, all targets are expressed in the normalized units of Sec.3.1.

    Supervision of cameras, scales, and poses.

    Scene views keep the losses of the backbone. Renders use the same camera loss, with the label P^*_i,m=[Rᵢ^*|tᵢ^*] V^*_i,m, where V^*_i,m is built from the ground-truth scale as in Eq.3. Each log-scale ℓ_i,m is supervised with an L1 loss against \logsᵢ^*. Crops are supervised with auxiliary camera and depth losses.

    The camera loss treats each render separately and does not directly constrain the pose that is finally read out. We therefore also compute the pose candidates differentiably with Eq.4 and compare two poses of object i by

    dᵢ(R,t;R^′,t^′) = (\lVertt-t^′\rVert₂)/(\lVertsᵢ^*\rVert₂) + (\lVertR-R^′\rVert_F)/(√2).

    		(6)

    The translation term is divided by the object size \lVertsᵢ^*\rVert₂ and is thus independent of the unit of length. We penalize dᵢ between every candidate and the ground truth, between the fused pose and the ground truth, and between every candidate and the fused pose.

    Symmetry, grounding, and physics.

    Objects that are symmetric about the vertical axis, such as round tables and vases, have several equally correct poses. We detect such symmetries for each asset offline and train with the equivalent label closest to the current prediction. A grounding head, used only in training, takes the camera token of each crop and render and predicts which scene-view patches its object occupies. This encourages the model to link crops and renders to their objects in the scene. We also apply two physics constraints to the layout that is read out, penalizing penetration between objects and the offset of floor-supported objects from the floor.

    Training data and sampling.

    Training requires scenes with 9-DoF object annotations. We combine several sources in a common format: synthetic indoor scenes [9, 10, 22, 57, 23, 51, 35], real scans from ScanNet++ [55] with annotated CAD models [38, 3], and single-view images [40, 10]. We oversample scenes that contain several instances of the same asset, so that the model must rely on the identity embeddings to tell them apart. We also randomly replace the asset of an object with an asset of similar shape from the same category and adjust the labels accordingly, which mimics assets that do not exactly match the object. Since the geometric conditions are optional at inference, each training sample is given a random subset of them. The numbers of scene views, objects, and renders per object are also drawn at random, so one model covers all input settings.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Test data.

    Our main test set, IndoorMix, merges held-out scenes from six indoor datasets: InternScenes [57], MolmoSpaces [23], SAGE [51], SceneSmith [35], 3D-FRONT [9], and the real scans of ScanNet++ [55]. We also report results on the 3D-FUTURE [10] test set of SceneGen [31], an existing benchmark of rendered single-view indoor scenes. Details of the test data, results per dataset, and more qualitative results are given in the supplementary material.

    Metrics and alignment.

    We use the metrics of MIDI [18]: the scene-level Chamfer distance (CD-S), F-score (F-S), and bounding-box IoU (IoU-B), and, in Table1, the object-level CD-O and F-O. The methods compared on generated assets (Table1) output layouts in different frames. We follow MIDI and normalize the predicted and the ground-truth scene separately before registering them with a single rigid ICP [2]. These metrics therefore measure the relative layout of the objects. CD-S, a mean over scenes of squared distances, is sensitive to a few scenes with large errors; F-S and IoU-B are less so. With ground-truth CAD models (Tables2, 3 and 4), every method outputs poses in the camera frame of the first scene view, where we compare them without ICP, aligning only the scale of each scene. In all tables, CD values are multiplied by 10³, F-scores are in percent, and the best result is in bold (Tables3 and 4: second best underlined).

    Inputs and implementation.

    All methods that take object masks use the same ground-truth masks. Unless a method specifies its own estimator, estimated geometric conditions come from MoGe-2 [46] for single-view input and from Depth Anything 3 [29] for multi-view input. Our model uses the 1B-parameter VGGT-Ω with rank-32 LoRA and is trained with AdamW [30] on 8 GPUs for about 200k steps. At inference, we use M=4 renders per object.

    4.2 Layout Prediction for Generated Assets

    This experiment tests whether a stand-alone layout model places a set of assets more accurately than the method that generated them. We use five scene generation methods: MIDI [18], SceneGen [31], FIRE3D [50], SAM 3D [5], and MV-SAM3D [27]. MIDI, SceneGen, and SAM 3D take a single view, MV-SAM3D takes several views, and FIRE3D supports both. Each method generates the meshes of all objects in the scene views, together with its native layout. We then place the same meshes with our model and with the public pose model of SceneMaker [39], which reports state-of-the-art pose accuracy and takes only a single view.

    Results.

    In Table1, our layouts are more accurate than SceneMaker’s in every single-view group and, with one exception, more accurate than the native layouts in every group and metric: in the FIRE3D group on 3D-FUTURE, the F-S of the native layout is 0.08 points higher. The gain is largest for MIDI and SceneGen, whose native layouts have large errors, but there is also a gain for SAM 3D, whose native layout is already fairly accurate. Averaged over the four single-view groups, our CD-S is 52% lower than that of SceneMaker on IndoorMix and 28% lower on 3D-FUTURE. With multi-view input, our layouts improve on the native layouts of FIRE3D and MV-SAM3D in all metrics, most clearly for MV-SAM3D (CD-S 1.61 vs. 6.38). Our model receives no geometric conditions in this comparison, whereas FIRE3D, SAM 3D, MV-SAM3D, and SceneMaker all use estimated depth. The gain therefore does not come from a better depth estimator. In Fig.4, when objects occlude one another or are cut off by the image border, the baselines place them in the wrong position or orientation, while our layouts stay close to the ground truth.

    4.3 Layout Prediction for GT CAD Models

    When the asset is the ground-truth CAD model of the object, our task coincides with object pose estimation. We compare with FoundationPose [49], PoseGAM [4], and the multi-view AlignPose [32]. Since these methods require true-size CAD models, all methods receive the ground-truth CAD models at their true size, and our model uses the given size in place of its predicted scale.

    Results.

    Among the methods that use no ground-truth conditions (upper block of Table2; examples in Fig.5), our model without conditions is the most accurate in all three settings. PoseGAM, the only baseline without depth, has much larger errors. With the same estimated conditions as the baselines, our F-S and IoU-B are also higher than those of FoundationPose and AlignPose. Our CD-S is lower than or on par with that of FoundationPose. With K+P+D, however, it is far higher than without conditions (75.95 vs. 0.85) and slightly above that of AlignPose. Inaccurate estimated camera poses mislead the model. Ground-truth poses give its lowest CD-S (0.52). Here, estimated conditions do not improve our results and can degrade them, whereas ground-truth ones improve them. With ground-truth conditions (lower block), FoundationPose reaches a higher IoU-B on IndoorMix, as its render-and-compare gains more from accurate depth than our model does. Our F-S under the same conditions is on par or higher.

    4.4 Layout Prediction from Panoramic Input

    We compare with Pano3DComposer [37] on 42 3D-FRONT houses that are in the training data of neither method, with one or two panoramas of the same room as input. For our model, each panorama is split into six perspective views, whose intrinsics and relative camera poses within the panorama follow from the projection and can be given as conditions. In Table3, our model is more accurate for both input types, even without conditions. Adding the intrinsics and camera poses derived from a single panorama improves our results further.

    4.5 Ablations and Analysis

    Design choices.

    All variants in Table4 are trained on 3D-FRONT with the same shortened schedule and evaluated there with ground-truth intrinsics and depth. Trained from random initialization, the model fails under this schedule (single-view F-S 40.7 vs. 90.8). Without identity embeddings, and hence without the masks, F-S falls to 71.7: the embeddings are needed to tie crops and renders to their objects in general, not only when objects look identical. The object crops give a smaller but consistent gain (single-view CD-S 9.49 vs. 11.88). The grounding head helps with multi-view input (CD-S 3.92 vs. 4.94) and has a mixed effect with single-view input. Without the physics constraints, the scene metrics are slightly better, but the percentage of penetrating objects rises from 7.9% to 10.1%.

    Mismatched assets and identical objects.

    Assets from retrieval or generation rarely match the object exactly, and a scene may contain identical objects. We test both cases in Fig.6. Re-texturing an asset barely changes the predicted pose (a), and replacing it with another asset of the same category makes the model adapt the pose to the new shape (b). For two identical objects, swapping their identity embeddings swaps the two assets (c), which shows that the model follows the identity embeddings.

    Views, renders, and runtime.

    More scene views improve accuracy at little extra cost. From one to eight views, the time per scene grows by less than 0.2 s. More renders per object raise F-S and IoU-B slightly (see the supplementary material). In Table5, our model takes about 1 s per scene, and the three baselines take 5.8–7.5 s.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented X-3DComposer, a feed-forward model that composes a 3D scene from given assets by predicting their layout. Its key idea is to treat objects as views: with asset renders as extra views, layout becomes camera prediction, a task that pretrained multi-view geometry models already solve well. Our experiments show that layout need not be tied to asset generation. On the same meshes, our layouts are more accurate than the native layouts of five scene generation methods. Without depth input, our scene-level Chamfer distance is 52% lower than that of SceneMaker on IndoorMix and 28% lower on 3D-FUTURE. As the model needs only asset renders, it can be combined with any generator or retrieval system. Our model has limitations. It requires object masks as input and is trained and tested only on indoor scenes. It is also sensitive to inaccurate geometric conditions, and its physics constraints reduce penetration without guaranteeing physically plausible layouts. Predicting the masks within the model and extending it to other scene types are left for future work.
