一句话：短时接触或共享运动并不足以证明物体持续刚性相连。

要点：

  • 任务要求：忠实的 4D 重建应同时捕捉物体的**形状与运动，即使它们离开视野**
  • 现有做法与其风险：依靠局部空间与运动关联来保留已观测几何、并在遮挡期延展运动；但**把短时接触或共享运动当作持久刚性的充分证据，会引入错误的运动约束**，从而扭曲整体重建
  • PRC4D 因此引入**物理关系约束**来判断哪些「连接」是真的、应当持续，哪些只是瞬时接触

为什么值得看：重建里最容易犯的错就是把「刚才挨着」当成「焊在一起」。用物理关系（接触、支撑、约束）来判断持续性，是把物理常识接进几何重建——对把实拍内容转成可仿真场景的管线尤其重要。

中文摘要：一次忠实的 4D 重建应当同时捕捉物体的形状与运动，即使这些物体曾经离开视野。现有方法依靠局部的空间关联与运动关联来保留已经观测到的几何，并在遮挡期间外延运动；但作者指出，把短时接触或共享运动当作「持久刚性连接」的充分证据，会引入错误的运动约束，从而扭曲整体重建结果。PRC4D 因此引入物理关系约束，用来区分哪些连接是真实且应当持续的、哪些只是瞬时接触，从而在遮挡与重新出现的过程中保持重建的物理合理性。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

PRC4D: Physical Relation-Constrained Persistent 4D Reconstruction

Abstract

A faithful 4D reconstruction should capture both the shape and motion of objects, even when they disappear from view. Existing methods preserve previously observed geometry and extend motion through occlusion using local spatial and motion associations. However, treating short-term contact or shared motion as sufficient evidence of persistent rigidity can introduce incorrect motion constraints and distort overall reconstruction. To address this limitation, we present PRC4D, a physical relation-constrained framework that identifies reliable rigid relations and uses them to maintain spatial consistency through occlusion. PRC4D combines 3D contact and relative motion consistency with sequence-level verification to distinguish persistent couplings from transient interactions. The resulting graph guides observed-pose refinement and motion propagation from visible to occluded components without altering reconstructed geometry. Experiments on diverse real-world multi-object sequences and controlled occlusion simulations demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy, reduced relative pose errors, and more consistent object configurations under changing visibility.

††footnotetext: ∗ Co-first authors.  † Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Monocular videos provide only partial observations of dynamic scenes, leaving the motion of occluded objects uncertain. Recent advances in monocular 4D reconstruction have improved geometric recovery and motion estimation through visual correspondences [3, 11, 37] and structured motion representations [42, 40, 17]. In particular, 4D Primitive-Mâché (4DPM) [22] accumulates previously observed geometry as 3D primitives and extends their motion through occlusion, enabling persistent reconstruction beyond the currently visible scene.

However, approaches that infer occluded motion from local spatial and motion associations can mistake transient interactions for persistent rigid couplings. Components may remain in contact while undergoing relative motion, as in articulated structures [27, 18, 9], or briefly move together before separating. Treating these associations as fixed rigid relations can introduce incorrect motion constraints and distort relative object poses. The central challenge is therefore not simply to propagate object motion, but to determine which physical relations provide reliable constraints over time.

To address this limitation, we present PRC4D, a physical relation-constrained framework for persistent 4D reconstruction. We infer candidate rigid couplings from 3D contact and relative motion consistency, then verify their persistence using sequence-level evidence and graph-level consistency. The verified relations form a temporal physical-relation graph that identifies which reconstructed components remain rigidly coupled.

The verified graph constrains both observed and occluded motion. For observed components, we refine their poses to reduce deviations from the relative configurations of their rigid groups. When a component becomes occluded, we propagate motion from a visible member of the same group, maintaining the relative configuration as visibility changes (Fig. 1).

We evaluate PRC4D on diverse real-world multi-object sequences and demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy. To further assess its robustness to occlusion, we construct OmniGibson-Occlusion, a controlled synthetic benchmark that provides ground-truth geometry and motion throughout both visible and occluded intervals. PRC4D achieves the highest mean reconstruction F-score among the compared methods on both benchmarks, with controlled occlusion experiments additionally showing reduced relative pose errors and more consistent object configurations.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a temporal physical-relation graph that distinguishes persistent rigid couplings from transient interactions by combining geometric and motion evidence with sequence-level verification.

  • •

    We develop a relation-constrained reconstruction framework that uses the same verified relations to refine observed component poses and propagate motion through occlusion.

  • •

    We construct OmniGibson-Occlusion, a synthetic benchmark with ground-truth geometry and motion throughout occlusion, enabling controlled evaluation of reconstruction robustness under changing visibility.

  • •

    We demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy on real-world and synthetic benchmarks, with controlled occlusion experiments showing reduced relative pose errors and more consistent object configurations.

    • 2 Related Work

    Monocular 4D Reconstruction.

    Recent advances in monocular 4D reconstruction have improved the recovery of dynamic scene geometry and motion through geometric priors [34, 14, 29, 36, 23], temporal correspondences [3, 11, 7, 30], and structured motion representations [40, 43, 26, 25, 1, 21]. Optimization-based approaches, such as Shape of Motion [31] and C4D [33], integrate long-range correspondences and geometric constraints to recover coherent 3D motion. Meanwhile, feed-forward methods, including POMATO [41], St4RTrack [4], and D4RT [39], jointly estimate spatiotemporal geometry and motion from video. However, temporal correspondences and motion regularization do not necessarily enforce constant relative transformations between distinct components that move rigidly together. Our method addresses this by inferring persistent rigid relations from reconstructed geometry and motion, and using them as explicit cross-component SE(3) constraints for pose refinement.

    Occlusion-Aware and Persistent 4D Reconstruction.

    Occlusion-aware 4D reconstruction has been explored through spatiotemporal reasoning, geometric completion, and persistent scene representations [20, 32, 8]. Recent approaches, such as Complet4R [35] and COM4D [5], leverage information across observations to reconstruct geometry beyond the current view and recover compositional 4D scenes. 4DPM [22] further enables persistent reconstruction by accumulating previously observed geometry and extending object motion through occlusion using spatial contact and motion similarity. However, such local associations do not necessarily establish persistent rigid couplings across a sequence. Our method addresses this limitation through sequence-level relation verification and relation-constrained pose refinement and motion propagation.

    Rigid Motion Constraints and Relational Reconstruction.

    Geometric and relational constraints provide additional structure for reconstructing dynamic scenes from ambiguous visual observations [2, 12, 24]. MoSca [13] represents scene deformation using sparse motion scaffolds, enforcing local rigidity and smoothness to recover coherent motion. Beyond deformation regularization, CARI4D [38] reasons about human-object contacts and incorporates them into joint pose optimization to improve spatial and temporal alignment. Relational reasoning has also been explored in HAT-4D [16], which constructs an interaction knowledge graph to guide multi-object scene composition and memory-guided 4D generation. These approaches demonstrate the value of motion and interaction constraints for dynamic reconstruction. Our work focuses on verifying the temporal persistence of rigid relations between reconstructed scene components and using them to constrain both observed and occluded motion.

    3 Method

    3.1 Problem Formulation and Overview

    Given a monocular RGB video I={Iₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, our goal is to reconstruct a dynamic scene while preserving coherent spatial configurations across changing visibility, including occlusion.

    We obtain an initial primitive-based reconstruction using 4D Primitive-Mâché (4DPM) [22], which recovers scene geometry and estimates component motion from visual correspondences. Let O={Oᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N denote the reconstructed scene components, each associated with 3D geometry and estimated poses T̃ᵢᵗ∈SE(3) at observed keyframes in a common coordinate frame. Although the reconstructed geometry persists, independently estimated component poses may violate the relative configurations of components that move rigidly together.

    To address this inconsistency, we construct a temporal physical-relation graph G=(V,𝔼), where nodes represent reconstructed components and edges encode inferred persistent rigid relations. For a rigidly coupled parent-child pair (p,c)∈𝔼, we seek poses satisfying

    (Tₚᵗ)⁻¹T_cᵗ≈T̄_pc,

    		(1)

    where T̄_pc∈SE(3) denotes their reference relative transformation.

    Our framework infers persistent relations from geometric and temporal evidence, then uses the resulting graph to refine observed component poses and propagate motion to occluded components through their visible rigid partners. The refined motions are applied to the original 3D primitives without modifying their geometry (Fig. 2).

    3.2 Temporal Physical-Relation Graph

    Geometric Contact Evidence.

    We first identify potential rigid couplings using the accumulated 3D geometry of reconstructed components. Candidate pairs are selected based on overlap between expanded oriented bounding boxes (OBBs), followed by geometric contact evaluation using voxelized surfaces at jointly observed keyframes. Contact is measured by the proportion of surface voxels within a spatial neighborhood of the other component. Temporal hysteresis aggregates noisy observations into continuous contact intervals. These intervals provide evidence of physical contact, but do not by themselves establish rigid coupling.

    Rigid Motion Consistency.

    We further examine whether contacting components exhibit consistent motion. Following the 4DPM convention, we define the motion increment of component i as Dᵢᵗ=(Uᵢᵗ)⁻¹Uᵢᵗ⁻¹, where Uᵢᵗ denotes its original transform. For a candidate relation from child i to parent j, let (τᵢⱼᵗ,φᵢⱼᵗ) denote the translational and rotational components of Log_SE(3)((Dⱼᵗ)⁻¹Dᵢᵗ). We compute the normalized motion discrepancy as

    εᵢⱼᵗ=\max((∥τᵢⱼᵗ∥)/(\max(αsᵢ,b)),(∥φᵢⱼᵗ∥)/(2β)),

    		(2)

    where sᵢ is the component size, α and b control translation tolerance, and β controls angular tolerance.

    Motion consistency is evaluated only at transitions with measurable motion, since shared stillness does not provide evidence of rigid coupling. Contact intervals with consistent informative motion and bounded relative translation drift form candidate rigid relations.

    Sequence-Level Persistence Reasoning.

    Local contact and motion consistency provide evidence of rigid coupling, but may also arise from transient interactions. We therefore verify candidate relations across the complete sequence by examining evidence that contradicts persistent rigidity.

    For each candidate pair (i,j), we examine contradictory evidence from separated fixed-contact episodes and independent motion beyond the supporting interval. We additionally measure relative translation drift at jointly observed keyframes as

    dᵢⱼᵗ=(∥pᵢⱼᵗ-pᵢⱼ^ref∥₂)/(sᵢ),

    		(3)

    where pᵢⱼᵗ=trans((T̃ⱼᵗ)⁻¹T̃ᵢᵗ) denotes the relative translation, and pᵢⱼ^ref is its median over the early half of the final supporting interval. When this interval extends to the last joint observation, sustained terminal drift indicates a possible violation of fixed rigidity. Missing observations alone do not invalidate a relation, since occlusion does not imply relation termination.

    We further exploit graph-level consistency to resolve ambiguities remaining after pairwise temporal verification. Relations with sufficient motion evidence and no temporal contradictions first establish trusted rigid groups. Remaining candidates are evaluated against these groups, allowing consistent relations to reinforce or extend existing groups while rejecting connections between independently established trusted groups.

    Relations with separated fixed-contact episodes are classified as transient. For candidates exhibiting independent motion or terminal drift, we examine redundant support from distinct neighbors within the same trusted group. Sufficient support can retain these uncertain relations, while unsupported candidates are rejected. This prevents isolated noisy observations from breaking otherwise consistent rigid assemblies.

    The resulting persistent rigid-relation graph provides shared constraints for pose refinement and motion propagation through occlusion.

    3.3 Graph-Constrained Pose Refinement

    Reference Relative Configuration.

    For each persistent rigid relation between parent p and child c, we estimate a reference transformation T̄_pc by robustly averaging (T̃ₚᵗ)⁻¹T̃_cᵗ over jointly observed keyframes within its supporting interval. We employ Huber-weighted averaging in SE(3) to reduce the influence of noisy estimates, establishing a reference configuration for subsequent refinement.

    Relation-Constrained Optimization.

    We refine observed component poses by enforcing consistent relative configurations while preserving the initial visual pose estimates. At keyframe t, let 𝔼ₜ denote the active persistent relations whose endpoints are jointly observed, and ℂₜ their child components. We optimize the poses of ℂₜ, keeping other components fixed to their initial estimates. A parent remains anchored unless it is itself a child of another active relation.

    We define the scale-normalized residual rᵢ(A,B)=Sᵢ⁻¹q(A⁻¹B), where q stacks the relative translation and SO(3) rotation logarithm, and Sᵢ balances their scales. We solve

    \min_{Tᵢᵗ}_i∈ℂₜ∑_i∈ℂₜL(√λₒ rᵢ(T̃ᵢᵗ,Tᵢᵗ))(4)
    +∑_(p,c)∈𝔼ₜL(√λᵣ r_c(T̄_pc,(Tₚᵗ)⁻¹T_cᵗ)),

    where L denotes the element-wise robust soft-L₁ penalty. The observation term maintains fidelity to the initial pose estimates, while the relation term penalizes deviations from persistent rigid configurations. We denote the optimized poses by T̂ᵢᵗ, retaining T̂ᵢᵗ=T̃ᵢᵗ for components not optimized. Optimization is performed independently at each observed keyframe without explicit temporal smoothing.

    Gauge-Consistent Motion Correction.

    Since 4DPM represents primitive motion in component-specific gauge frames, the refined poses must be transferred without altering the original reference geometry. Let aᵢ denote the first observed keyframe of component i. We compute an anchor-relative correction

    Hᵢᵗ=[T̂ᵢᵗ(T̂ᵢ^aᵢ)⁻¹][T̃ᵢᵗ(T̃ᵢ^aᵢ)⁻¹]⁻¹.

    		(5)

    This correction preserves the initial configuration (Hᵢ^aᵢ=I) while updating the component’s relative motion. We transfer the corrected motion to the original 4DPM transformations, preserving the geometry and internal structure of the reconstructed primitives.

    3.4 Graph-Guided Motion Propagation

    Occlusion-Aware Relation Activation.

    The inferred persistent rigid relations enable motion propagation from visible components to their occluded rigid partners. At each keyframe, we construct active rigid groups from the verified physical-relation graph. A relation remains active during occlusion if its most recent joint observation supports rigid coupling, while contradictory reobservations prevent further propagation through that relation. For each occluded component, we select a visible driver within its active rigid group, prioritizing relations with stronger geometric and temporal evidence.

    Relative Motion Propagation.

    Given an occluded component h and its visible driver d, we transfer the driver’s motion relative to a jointly observed anchor keyframe a:

    Tₕ^t,*=T_d^t,*(T_d^a,*)⁻¹Tₕ^a,*,

    		(6)

    where T^t,* denotes a refined or propagated component pose. This transfers the driver’s anchor-to-current motion to the occluded component, preserving their reference relative configuration. Upon reappearance, observed components use their refined poses rather than propagated estimates. If no valid driver is available, the component is not propagated.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Evaluation Protocol

    OmniGibson-Occlusion Benchmark.

    We construct OmniGibson-Occlusion using the OmniGibson simulator [15], a synthetic benchmark of six sequences covering diverse occlusion conditions (Fig. S2). The refrigerator and drawer sequences involve rotational and translational motion, respectively, while Tray examines temporary occlusion followed by reappearance. Storage Box evaluates complete occlusion of objects moving rigidly with their container. Metric ground-truth geometry and motion remain available throughout each sequence.

    Multi-Object Benchmark.

    We also evaluate on the real-world Multi-Object benchmark introduced by 4DPM [22], comprising seven sequences involving object manipulation and multi-object interactions. The dataset was captured using four synchronized cameras, with a single monocular RGB stream used as input and multi-view reconstructions providing pseudo-ground-truth geometry.

    Reconstruction Evaluation.

    We compare against π³[36], St4RTrack [4], POMATO [41], TraceAny [19], D4RT  [39], and 4DPM [22] on both benchmarks. Following 4DPM, π³ (Last-view Oracle) uses only the final-frame pointmap, while π³ aggregates pointmaps without motion compensation. We warp reconstructed observations to the final keyframe and aggregate them into a point cloud. A separate Umeyama [28] Sim(3) alignment is estimated between each method’s final-keyframe pointmap and the corresponding ground-truth geometry. We report precision, recall, and F-score at a 1 cm distance threshold on dynamic scene geometry, averaged across sequences.

    Relative Pose Evaluation.

    We evaluate object-level relative pose errors on OmniGibson-Occlusion using metric ground truth. Reconstructed components are associated with ground-truth instances and aggregated to estimate object-level poses through Kabsch alignment [10]. We evaluate moving objects relative to their supporting or enclosing structures, excluding the structures themselves. Final-keyframe translation and rotation errors are reported in centimeters and degrees.

    Rigid-Relation Evaluation.

    We evaluate inferred fixed relations on OmniGibson-Occlusion against ground-truth rigid-coupling annotations. Articulated connections and temporary co-motion are not considered fixed rigid relations. Ground-truth annotations are used solely for evaluation. We compute relation precision, recall, and F1 from pooled TP, FP, and FN across six sequences, containing 17 ground-truth positive relations.

    Implementation.

    We adopt the 4DPM visual frontend and extend its reconstruction backend with physical-relation inference, pose refinement, and motion propagation. All module ablations in Tab. 3 share the same initial reconstruction, while graph-based variants use identical inferred relations. For Tab. 4, we evaluate temporal smoothing configurations across three window sizes and four blending strengths, reporting the one with the highest reconstruction F-score. The 4DPM grouping baseline converts its original motion-extension associations into rigid relations and applies the same refinement and propagation modules. The graph ablation in Tab. 5 varies persistence classification while keeping refinement and propagation unchanged. All experiments use a single NVIDIA L40S GPU. Detailed algorithmic procedures, implementation parameters, and runtime analysis are provided in the supplementary material.

    4.2 Persistent Reconstruction under Occlusion

    Geometry Persistence and Spatial Consistency.

    Tab. 1 reveals the distinction between preserving observed geometry and maintaining its correct spatial configuration. While the last-view π³ lacks previously observed geometry, aggregating unaligned observations introduces spatial inconsistencies. 4DPM preserves accumulated geometry, but independently estimated component motions can still distort its configuration. Our method improves F-score across all six scenes without modifying the underlying primitives, highlighting the importance of consistent object motion.

    Reconstruction under Changing Visibility.

    Fig. 3 illustrates temporary occlusion and reappearance in Tray, and complete occlusion during rigid motion in Storage Box. The latter requires hidden components to follow the motion of their visible rigid partner. Our inferred relations preserve coherent relative configurations across these changing visibility conditions.

    4.3 Multi-Object Reconstruction and Physical Relations

    Reconstruction under Complex Motion.

    Tab. 2 evaluates our method under diverse real-world object motions. Unlike the consistent improvements observed in synthetic occlusion scenarios, the gains vary across multi-object sequences. The larger improvements in MultiObj2 and Spin2 contrast with the unchanged result in MultiObj1 and the degradation in BallPush. This suggests that physical-relation constraints are beneficial when persistent rigid couplings can be identified and visual observations become incomplete or unreliable, rather than acting as a general regularizer for arbitrary object motion. Additional quantitative and qualitative results on HO3D [6] are provided in the supplementary material.

    Persistent and Transient Interactions.

    Fig. 4 illustrates the distinction between persistent rigid couplings and temporary interactions in a real-world sequence. Objects may exhibit contact or similar motion over a short interval without remaining rigidly attached. Enforcing such relations throughout the sequence would incorrectly constrain their subsequent independent motions. Our method therefore applies pose refinement and motion propagation only to relations verified as persistent, while excluding transient interactions from the reconstruction constraints.

    4.4 Analysis of Physical Relation Constraints

    Roles of Pose Refinement and Propagation.

    Tab. 3 examines the individual contributions of pose refinement and graph-guided motion propagation. Replacing 4DPM’s original motion extension with graph-guided propagation yields a larger improvement than applying pose refinement alone. This suggests that persistent physical relations provide more reliable motion transfer through occlusion than the original motion grouping. Pose refinement further improves reconstruction by correcting inconsistent observed poses. Combining both modules achieves the highest F-score and recall, maintaining coherent object configurations across changing visibility.

    Temporal Smoothness versus Relational Constraints.

    Tab. 4 investigates whether temporal smoothing or 4DPM grouping can substitute for persistent physical relations. Independent temporal smoothing reduces relative pose errors but degrades reconstruction F-score, indicating that smoother individual trajectories do not necessarily yield more accurate scene reconstructions. The complete evaluation across all smoothing configurations is reported in the supplementary material.

    We further replace our inferred relations with the original 4DPM motion-extension groups while retaining the same refinement and propagation modules. Despite improving rotational accuracy, this alternative increases translation error and reduces reconstruction F-score. This suggests that enforcing rigid constraints alone is insufficient when the underlying component associations are unreliable. Together, these results highlight the importance of identifying reliable physical relations, rather than merely smoothing or coupling component motions.

    Importance of Persistent Relation Verification.

    Tab. 5 shows that locally plausible rigid relations can degrade reconstruction when enforced without sufficient verification. Temporal verification and graph-level consistency checks progressively reduce false-positive relations from four to one, while correctly identifying all 17 evaluated ground-truth rigid relations. These improvements increase relation precision from 80.95% to 94.44%, accompanied by substantial reconstruction gains. The results demonstrate that the reliability of inferred relations is critical when using them as persistent motion constraints.

    5 Limitations

    Our method inherits the piecewise-rigid assumption of 4DPM and cannot model complex non-rigid deformations. Relation inference depends on initial geometry and motion estimates, potentially coupling unattached components with similar motion. Although articulated components can be reconstructed independently, our constraints only handle persistent fixed couplings. Finally, motion propagation requires a visible rigid partner, and sequence-level verification requires the full video, limiting incremental reconstruction.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented PRC4D, a framework that leverages persistent rigid relations to maintain spatial consistency across changing visibility. By verifying physical relations through geometric and temporal evidence, our method refines observed component poses and propagates motion through occlusion without altering the underlying geometry. Experiments on synthetic occlusion and real-world multi-object benchmarks demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy. Our ablations further highlight that reliable relation verification is essential to prevent incorrect motion constraints from degrading persistent reconstruction.

    LLM Usage Statement

    OpenAI’s ChatGPT was used to assist with manuscript, language editing, and improving the clarity and organization of technical explanations. It was also used to discuss research framing, experimental design, and the interpretation of ablation results. Anthropic’s Claude was used to assist with the design, generation, and refinement of research figure. The authors reviewed the generated suggestions and retain full responsibility for all technical claims, experimental results, and scientific conclusions.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    1 Implementation Details

    Algorithm overview.

    Alg. A1 summarizes the detailed PRC4D pipeline, from rigid-relation inference to pose refinement and motion propagation. Temporal verification distinguishes transient contacts from ambiguous motion evidence, while graph-level consistency resolves uncertain relations using trusted rigid groups and redundant support.

    Parameter settings.

    Tab. S1 reports the key settings used for the quantitative evaluations. The child of a candidate pair is chosen as the component with the smaller median OBB volume, and its size s is the median OBB diagonal. Lengths are expressed in reconstruction units unless scaled by s; the voxel size is expressed relative to the median point spacing. The parameters α, b, and β correspond to the motion-consistency criterion in Eq. (2) of the main paper. For observed keyframes, we estimate a robust reference relative transformation for each verified relation and optimize component poses using the observation and relation terms in Eq. (4). For occluded components, motion is propagated from a visible rigid partner when one is available, while the original primitive geometry remains unchanged.

    2 Additional Results on HO3D

    Evaluation protocol.

    HO3D contains real-world hand-object interaction sequences involving object manipulation, partial occlusion, and changing visibility. We evaluate 85 clips of 150 frames from seven sequences using camera 0, following the reconstruction protocol in the main paper.

    Quantitative results.

    Tab. S6 evaluates PRC4D on real-world hand-object interactions beyond the main benchmarks. PRC4D improves reconstruction F-score over 4DPM across all seven sequences, while preserving the original geometry. These results suggest that relation-constrained motion correction can improve spatial consistency in different real-world settings.

    Qualitative comparisons.

    Fig. S1 illustrates how PRC4D maintains consistent configurations of separately reconstructed components during hand-object interactions. By preserving persistent rigid relations while excluding transient contacts, PRC4D reduces component-level pose inconsistencies observed in 4DPM, even when the components remain visible.

    3 Scene-wise Ablation Studies

    Pose refinement and propagation.

    Tab. S2 shows that the two modules contribute differently across scenes. Graph-guided propagation is particularly effective in Tray and Storage Box, where occluded components must follow visible rigid partners. Pose refinement improves reconstruction in scenes such as Fridge1 and Drawer1 by correcting observed component configurations. Combining both modules yields the best overall performance, although their benefits vary by scene.

    Relation verification and graph consistency.

    Tab. S3 demonstrates the importance of rejecting unreliable rigid relations. In Fridge1, Fridge2, and Storage Box, locally plausible but incorrect relations substantially degrade reconstruction. Temporal verification removes contradictory relations, while graph-level consistency further rejects incompatible couplings. These results show that reliable relation selection is essential for maintaining coherent component configurations.

    Among 25 initially annotated relation candidates, we exclude five without reconstructed endpoints and three that do not meet the fixed-coupling evaluation criteria. The remaining 17 relations are used for evaluation, with metrics computed from pooled TP, FP, and FN.

    4 Temporal Smoothing Baseline

    Tab. S4 evaluates temporal smoothing across 12 parameter configurations. Although smoothing can reduce relative pose errors, all tested configurations degrade reconstruction F-score compared with 4DPM. This suggests that improving temporal smoothness alone is insufficient for reliable reconstruction, highlighting the importance of enforcing persistent relations between components.

    5 Additional OmniGibson-Occlusion Visualizations

    Figs. S3 and S4 further illustrate the importance of maintaining relative object configurations under occlusion. While 4DPM preserves previously observed geometry, its estimated component motions can lead to inconsistent object placements. PRC4D maintains spatial consistency through verified rigid relations across both rotational and translational motions. The dashed reference boxes visualize relative configuration drift rather than absolute pose errors.

    6 Runtime Analysis

    Runtime breakdown.

    Tab. S5 shows that the additional computational cost of PRC4D is dominated by physical-relation graph construction, particularly geometric contact evaluation between reconstructed components. In contrast, pose refinement and graph-guided motion propagation incur relatively little overhead. This identifies efficient relation inference as the main opportunity for reducing runtime.

item.title: 流式重建的空间 KV 缓存随场景无限涨：STAC++ 用八叉树做自适应分辨率的空间记忆 ｜ STAC++: Plug-and-Play Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Aware Cache Compression for Streaming 3D Reconstruction
item.description:
一句话：流式 3D 重建要在有限显存下保住几何，但固定分辨率的空间 KV 缓存会随场景扩张而增长。

要点：

  • 矛盾：流式 3D 重建必须在**有限显存**下保持几何质量，而原有 STAC 的**固定分辨率空间 KV 缓存会随场景扩张而增长**
  • STAC++ 是**即插即用、免训练**的框架，用来压缩并复用长程重建中的空间记忆
  • 核心是 **Adaptive Spatial KV Cache**：把 KV 状态组织成**八叉树**，在不同区域与不同层上使用自适应分辨率；再配合响应感知的缓存压缩策略

为什么值得看：八叉树正是稀疏体素与空间索引里的标准结构，用它组织 KV 缓存等于把「图形学的空间层次」搬进 transformer 记忆。这比均匀降低分辨率聪明得多——对任何长序列、大场景的流式重建都适用。

中文摘要：流式三维重建必须在有限显存下维持几何质量，而此前的 STAC 采用固定分辨率的空间键值（KV）缓存，会随场景扩张而持续增长。STAC++ 因此提出一个即插即用、免训练的框架，用来压缩并复用长程重建中的空间记忆：其核心是自适应空间 KV 缓存（ASKC），把 KV 状态组织成一棵八叉树，在不同区域、不同网络层上采用自适应分辨率；再配合响应感知的缓存压缩策略来控制开销。本质上，这是把图形学里成熟的空间层次结构引入 transformer 的记忆组织，比均匀降采样更贴合「大场景、局部精细」的实际需求。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

STAC++: Plug-and-Play Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Aware Cache Compression for Streaming 3D Reconstruction

Abstract

Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve geometry under limited memory, yet STAC’s fixed-resolution spatial key–value (KV) cache grows as scenes expand. We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that compresses and reuses spatial memory for long-term reconstruction in unbounded scenes. Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes KV states into an octree with adaptive resolutions across regions and layers. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by measuring attention-output changes, balancing storage savings with geometric preservation. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) reuses cached intermediate features and recomputes only a short backbone suffix to refine historical predictions with later observations. Integrated into four pretrained streaming backbones, STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on long sequences and large scenes, with further quality gains from refinement at limited computational overhead. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

1 Introduction

3D reconstruction is a fundamental problem in computer vision and computer graphics, with a wide range of applications including robotic mapping [44], augmented reality [28], and novel-view synthesis [26, 16]. Traditional image-based 3D reconstruction combines Structure-from-Motion (SfM) [30] for camera estimation and sparse structure recovery with Multi-View Stereo (MVS) [31] for dense geometry. These pipelines rely on explicit correspondence matching and iterative geometric optimization. Recent feed-forward geometric models instead infer scene geometry directly from images using pretrained networks, reducing reliance on scene-specific iterative optimization and improving reconstruction efficiency.

Feed-forward reconstruction methods can be broadly categorized into offline methods that process a fixed image collection and online methods that process incoming images sequentially. Offline methods include DUSt3R [42], which predicts pairwise pointmaps followed by global alignment, and VGGT [38], which jointly predicts cameras and dense geometry from multiple views. However, their computational and memory costs limit scalability to long sequences. Online methods [17, 54, 49, 5] instead reuse historical representations to reconstruct incoming frames incrementally. StreamVGGT [54] adapts VGGT to streaming inference through causal attention and cached historical key–value (KV) states, but its cache grows with sequence length. InfiniteVGGT [49] controls this growth with a bounded rolling cache and diversity-aware token pruning, enabling long-sequence inference within a fixed memory budget. However, these methods do not explicitly exploit 3D spatial information in KV-cache management. STAC [41] introduces a spatial KV cache that merges historical tokens into voxel-aligned representatives, reducing spatial redundancy while preserving geometric evidence. However, its fixed-resolution grid allows the number of occupied voxels to grow with scene extent, so long streams exploring unbounded environments can still exhaust GPU memory. Uniform voxel coarsening saves memory but risks losing fine geometric detail in complex regions.

STAC uses spatial memory to reconstruct incoming frames, yet earlier predictions remain fixed even when later views reveal the same surfaces more clearly. These limitations motivate our central question: How can we adaptively compress and actively reuse spatial KV memory to support long-term reconstruction of unbounded scenes, while preserving geometric detail and refining earlier predictions under limited memory and computational budgets? Answering this question poses two challenges. (1) Handling unbounded scenes requires spatial representations that accommodate continually expanding scene coverage while controlling cache growth and preserving geometric detail. (2) Operating within a bounded memory budget requires retaining informative historical evidence and efficiently reusing it to refine earlier predictions with later observations, without replaying the entire backbone.

To address these challenges, we propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that controls spatial memory growth and efficiently reuses historical evidence for long-term streaming reconstruction in unbounded scenes (see Fig. 1). Firstly, Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes spatial KV states into an octree hierarchy with different resolutions across scene regions and transformer layers. This hierarchy supports merging fine-grained cells into coarser representations as the scene expands. Secondly, Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by evaluating how candidate merges change the backbone’s attention outputs (hereafter referred to as responses). It identifies spatial representations that can be consolidated with limited response changes, balancing memory savings against geometric information preservation. Finally, Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) revisits historical frames after a fixed delay, using later observations and accumulated spatial memory to refine earlier predictions. By reusing cached intermediate features and recomputing only a short backbone suffix, TCR creates additional opportunities to exploit spatial memory while limiting the computation required for refinement. We implement STAC++ as an inference-time plugin for STream3R [17], StreamVGGT [54], InfiniteVGGT [49], and LingBot-Map [5], preserving their pretrained weights without additional training. Experiments across these four backbones demonstrate that STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality, scales to long sequences and large scenes, and further improves reconstruction quality through delayed suffix refinement with limited computational overhead.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that unifies adaptive spatial memory compression and historical evidence reuse for long-term streaming reconstruction in unbounded scenes without modifying pretrained backbone weights.

  • •

    We develop ASKC, RACC, and TCR for hierarchical spatial KV caching, response-guided merging, and suffix refinement of historical predictions, controlling memory and computation while preserving geometry.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Offline Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction

    DUSt3R [42] predicts pairwise pointmaps with global alignment; MASt3R [18] adds learned matching features. VGGT, Fast3R, and MUSt3R [38, 48, 3] extend prediction to multiple views, while FLARE [51] jointly recovers geometry, appearance, and cameras. π³[43] removes reference-view dependence through permutation equivariance, and VGGT-Ω[39] scales geometric learning with efficient register attention. Dense cross-view interaction nevertheless remains costly as the image collection grows.

    For scalability, MERG3R [8] partitions and aligns image subsets, while LiteVGGT [34] merges geometrically redundant tokens and reuses merge decisions across layers. VGG-T3, ZipMap, and Scal3R [11, 14, 47] compress context into test-time-trained states, using fast weights or synchronized adaptive memory to retain information across image chunks; Test3R [50] adapts reconstruction models at test time. These approaches address offline scalability or adaptation rather than adaptive causal KV storage. Octree-GS [29] provides hierarchical spatial detail for Gaussian rendering; our hierarchy instead compresses transformer KV memory for subsequent streaming inference.

    2.2 Online Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction

    Spann3R [37] queries external spatial memory to predict globally aligned pointmaps, CUT3R [40] maintains a recurrent scene state, and Point3R [45] introduces explicit spatial pointer memory. TTT3R [6] uses confidence-guided updates, while FILT3R [15] applies uncertainty-adaptive Kalman-style state updates without retraining. SLAM3R [22] learns local reconstruction and registration; MASt3R-SLAM and multi-agent MAGiSt3R [27, 12] additionally use geometric optimization. LASER [10] enables training-free streaming through layer-wise depth-scale alignment across windows. STream3R and StreamVGGT [17, 54] use causal KV caching; LongStream [7] adds cache-aware training and refresh, while LingBot-Map [5] separates anchor, local, and trajectory context for stable long-sequence reconstruction.

    Growing caches motivate selective retention. In language models, H2O [53], StreamingLLM [46], and SnapKV [19] retain attention-heavy tokens, attention sinks, or head-specific evidence. For geometry, InfiniteVGGT [49] uses diversity-aware pruning; OVGGT [23] protects anchors during residual-guided selection; RegVGGT [24] regulates incoming tokens. GHOST [4] performs geometry-guided eviction, whereas RetrieveVGGT [55] retrieves context through query–key similarity and poses. Selection reduces cache growth but can discard useful geometric evidence; spatial aggregation offers a complementary way to retain information from repeated observations. Slot3R [52] avoids prematurely fusing complementary views by preserving multiple states per spatial address, and SURE-Map [21] uses cross-view uncertainty for local correction and periodic keyframe-window inference for consistent geometry.

    Most closely related to our work, STAC [41] combines temporal token retention with spatial KV fusion on a fixed-resolution voxel grid, enabling historical reuse without retraining the backbone. We extend this design with adaptive spatial resolution and response-guided KV merging to control memory growth, and selective suffix refinement to improve earlier predictions using retained evidence.

    3 Preliminaries

    3.1 Causal Attention

    Causal attention enables streaming reconstruction by restricting each frame to information from the current and preceding frames, as adopted in STream3R [17] and StreamVGGT [54]. Let Fₜ denote the encoded features of frame t and Gₜ its geometric predictions. For a sequence of T frames, this process can be summarized as

    {Gₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ=Decoder (TemporalSelfAttn ({Fₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ)),

    		(1)

    where TemporalSelfAttn applies a causal mask so that frame t attends only to frames 1,…,t, and Decoder maps the attended features to per-frame geometric predictions. During streaming inference, historical keys and values are cached and reused without reprocessing preceding frames. Retaining the full KV history, however, makes cache storage grow linearly with sequence length.

    3.2 Spatio-Temporal KV Caching

    STAC [41] maintains complementary temporal and spatial KV caches. The temporal cache Mₜᵗᵉᵐᵖ retains first-frame references, recent frames and anchors. The spatial cache organizes temporally evicted patch tokens into voxels of side length δ according to their predicted 3D positions. Retrieval from this cache provides the spatial context Mₜˢᵖᵃᵗ.

    Spatial cache. Each voxel u stores up to P KV representatives Gᵤ and B buffered tokens 𝔼ᵤ, consolidating tokens through aggregation when capacity is reached. Representatives maintain fusion weights Wᵢ, importance scores Sᵢ, and represented-token counts Cᵢ, while buffered tokens retain importance scores and contribute only through aggregation. At frame t, retrieval searches the occupied voxels ℕₜ within neighborhoods extending two voxel steps (2δ) in both directions along each axis around voxels containing the preceding frame’s predicted 3D points. The spatial context is formed by selecting at most R representatives per attention head with the largest fusion weights:

    Mₜˢᵖᵃᵗ=Top_R^W (\bigcup_u∈ℕₜGᵤ).

    		(2)

    The retrieved spatial states, temporal cache, and current-frame KV Mₜᶜᵘʳ form the attention context ℂₜ=Mₜᵗᵉᵐᵖ∪Mₜˢᵖᵃᵗ∪Mₜᶜᵘʳ. This work focuses on the spatial cache.

    4 Method

    We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework for controlling spatial KV memory growth and reusing historical evidence in streaming 3D reconstruction. STAC++ combines three modules (Fig. 2). Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes historical states at multiple spatial resolutions. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) determines which states can be merged by measuring their effect on attention outputs. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) revisits historical frames after a delay, reusing cached intermediate features and recomputing a short backbone suffix to incorporate later observations. All three modules operate during inference and preserve the pretrained backbone weights.

    4.1 Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC)

    In unbounded scenes, fixed-resolution spatial caches grow with scene coverage and retain redundancy across neighboring voxels. Uniform coarsening saves storage but may discard locally distinct geometric evidence. ASKC instead organizes spatial KV states in an expanding octree, selectively merging neighboring fine-grained cells into coarser parents independently across layers while retaining finer representations where detailed evidence remains necessary.

    Layer-wise modeling. For a backbone with L global-attention layers, layer ℓ maintains octree Tₜ^(ℓ) at time t, with finest cell side length δ (Sec. 3.2). Layers share the same subdivision rule but merge independently, allowing each layer to use a different spatial resolution for the same scene region. All H heads in a layer share cells but store separate KV states. We denote the layer’s token inputs by Xₜ^(ℓ). Temporally evicted patch tokens enter cells containing their predicted 3D positions, including parents formed by earlier merges. We repeatedly double the shared root’s side length toward an out-of-bounds point until it is enclosed, retaining the old root as a child at each expansion step.

    Within-cell storage. Each cell u in layer ℓ and head h stores up to P representatives G_u,ℓ,h and B buffered tokens 𝔼_u,ℓ,h. Following STAC’s online aggregation [41], we omit cell, layer, and head indices and write each representative as mᵢ=(kᵢ,vᵢ), with key and value vectors kᵢ and vᵢ. When a new representative needs a slot but all P slots are occupied, we fuse i with smallest Wᵢ into the remaining representative j with highest key cosine similarity:

    mⱼ←Wⱼmⱼ+ωᵢⱼmᵢ/Wⱼ+ωᵢⱼ,

    		(3)

    where ωᵢⱼ=Wᵢ\exp(\cos(kᵢ,kⱼ)-1). We update Wⱼ←Wⱼ+ωᵢⱼ, Cⱼ←Cⱼ+Cᵢ, and Sⱼ←Sⱼ+Sᵢ. An incoming token sufficiently similar to a representative uses the same update with ωᵢⱼ=\exp(\cos(kᵢ,kⱼ)) and Cᵢ=1. Sufficiently dissimilar tokens passing the importance threshold enter the buffer. When full, its highest-scoring token seeds aggregation of all entries into a new representative using exponential cosine-similarity weights.

    Spatial retrieval. Let Ωₜ be the lookup neighborhoods of the preceding frame’s predicted 3D points, expanded by 2δ (Sec. 3.2), and ℕₜ^(ℓ) all active cells whose extents intersect Ωₜ, including merged parents. For head h, Eq. 2 with ℕₜ^(ℓ) and G_u,ℓ,h replacing ℕₜ and Gᵤ, respectively, yields M_t,ℓ,hˢᵖᵃᵗ under the same per-head budget R.

    Hierarchical coarsening. For each layer, an inactive parent is structurally eligible for merging if it has one to eight active direct children and no KV in its grandchildren or deeper descendants. Their consolidation into the parent is a parent proposal requiring RACC acceptance (Sec. 4.2).

    4.2 Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC)

    Merging spatially adjacent states saves memory but can alter the geometric evidence available to the backbone. A straightforward approach is to explicitly compute the attention responses before and after a candidate merge p and take their difference:

    Δo_p,ℓ,h=Att(q̂_ℓ,h,ℂ_p,ℓ,h)-Att(q̂_ℓ,h,ℂ_ℓ,h),

    		(4)

    where Att(·) denotes attention, q̂_ℓ,h is the shared query, and ℂ_ℓ,h and ℂ_p,ℓ,h are the contexts before and after the merge. The corresponding responses are denoted by o_ℓ,h and o_p,ℓ,h, respectively. However, directly evaluating this change for every candidate merge requires repeating query–key scoring, softmax normalization, and value aggregation over the full context, making evaluation costly. We therefore sample a small set of queries and compute response changes incrementally, reusing the reference response and normalizer while updating only the contributions of KV entries affected by each merge. RACC balances response preservation against storage savings.

    Merge scheduling. For merge keyframes spaced M frames apart, we retain Ω_t-M and full inputs X_t-M^(ℓ) to each global-attention layer. After keyframe t completes inference, we sample queries from these inputs at all special-token positions and a uniform 4×4 patch grid to evaluate eligible parents in Ω_t-M. This delay allows intervening frames to use the finer spatial representation before coarsening. Pending keyframes use the available context at sequence end.

    Parent proposal construction. At each layer ℓ, consider an eligible parent U in Ω_t-M with child positions uᵢ (i=1,…,8; empty branches give empty sets), omitting t-M below. Head h retains up to B buffered entries with highest importance from \bigcupᵢ₌₁⁸𝔼_uᵢ,ℓ,h in 𝔼_U,ℓ,h. Child representatives form G_U,ℓ,h unchanged when ∑ᵢ₌₁⁸|G_uᵢ,ℓ,h|≤P; otherwise, we repeatedly apply the representative re-merging rule in Sec. 4.1 using Eq. 3 until P remain. The pairs p_U,ℓ,h=(G_U,ℓ,h,𝔼_U,ℓ,h) form proposal p, saving

    ΔN_p,ℓ,h=∑ᵢ₌₁⁸(|G_uᵢ,ℓ,h|+|𝔼_uᵢ,ℓ,h|)(5)
    -|G_U,ℓ,h|-|𝔼_U,ℓ,h|.

    Summing over heads gives ΔN_p,ℓ=∑ₕ₌₁^HΔN_p,ℓ,h.

    Response change evaluation. For sampled q̂_ℓ,h, compute o_ℓ,h=Att(q̂_ℓ,h,ℂ_ℓ,h) over ℂ_ℓ,h=M_ℓ,hᵗᵉᵐᵖ∪M_ℓ,hˢᵖᵃᵗ∪M_ℓ,hᶜᵘʳ (time omitted). We retain Λ_ℓ,h=\log∑_i∈ℂ_ℓ,h\exp(zᵢ), where zᵢ=q̂_ℓ,h^⊤kᵢ/√d+\logCᵢ, suppressing layer/head indices on tokens; d is the key dimension and Cᵢ=1 for unmerged tokens. Proposal p replaces retrieved child representatives ℝₚ with distinct parent representatives Aₚ⊆G_U,ℓ,h containing their contributions, giving ℂ_p,ℓ,h=(ℂ_ℓ,h∖ℝₚ)∪Aₚ. The remaining context and retrieval ranking stay fixed. For i∈ℝₚ∪Aₚ, set αᵢ=\exp(zᵢ-Λ_ℓ,h) using the reference normalizer. Equation 4 becomes

    Δo_p,ℓ,h=(∑_i∈Aₚαᵢ(vᵢ-o_ℓ,h)-∑_i∈ℝₚαᵢ(vᵢ-o_ℓ,h))/(1+∑_i∈Aₚαᵢ-∑_i∈ℝₚαᵢ).

    		(6)

    Equation 6 is exact for the fixed query and specified substitution [25, 9]; only ℝₚ and Aₚ require new scores and value accumulations. Unchanged contributions are reused through o_ℓ,h and Λ_ℓ,h. Stacking reference responses and changes over sampled queries yields O_ℓ,h and ΔO_p,ℓ,h.

    Merge acceptance. We average normalized response changes across heads:

    E_p,ℓ=1/H∑ₕ₌₁^H(\lVertΔO_p,ℓ,h\rVert_F)/(\max(\lVertO_ℓ,h\rVert_F,εₘ)),

    		(7)

    with εₘ=10⁻⁸ for stability. We accept p when

    E_p,ℓ≤τₘ+λ(ΔN_p,ℓ)/(H(P+B)).

    		(8)

    Here τₘ sets the baseline tolerance and λ weights storage savings. Each layer makes an independent decision shared across all heads; acceptance replaces child storage cells with their parent.

    4.3 Temporal Context Refinement (TCR)

    During causal streaming inference, each frame is reconstructed using only the observations available when it arrives. Later frames may provide complementary viewpoints and additional geometric evidence for previously observed regions, enriching the spatial cache. However, this updated memory benefits subsequent inference without automatically revising earlier predictions, which remain tied to their original, more limited context. The most direct approach is to reprocess historical frames through the entire backbone using the updated context. However, this repeats substantial feature computation. We therefore introduce TCR to refine historical predictions after a fixed delay using the updated temporal and spatial context. TCR retains intermediate features during initial inference and recomputes only a short backbone suffix, allowing earlier frames to reuse later observations while limiting the additional computation.

    Refinement scheduling. During initial inference, we retain each frame’s decoder features from layers 5 and 12, the intermediate input needed for suffix recomputation, and its spatial lookup region. After a delay of D frames, we revisit the historical frame once using the updated context. The refinement delay is independent of the merge interval, and merge keyframes share their retained inputs with RACC.

    Refinement process. At time t, we refine frame t-D by resuming from its retained intermediate features. At each recomputed attention layer, queries from this revisited frame attend to the current temporal cache, spatial states retrieved within its saved lookup region, and keys and values recomputed from the same frame’s features at that layer. Let X denote the retained intermediate input and ℂ the updated context. Recomputing layers 18–24 gives

    (F̃⁽¹⁸⁾,F̃⁽²⁴⁾)=Suffix_18:24(X,ℂ),

    		(9)

    where Suffix_18:24 denotes recomputation of backbone layers 18–24 from the retained input X using the updated context ℂ, returning the features at layers 18 and 24. Here F^(ℓ) denotes the feature at layer ℓ, tildes mark refinement, and the frame index is omitted. The decoder combines the cached features from layers 5 and 12 with the updated features from layers 18 and 24:

    G̃=Decoder (F⁽⁵⁾,F⁽¹²⁾,F̃⁽¹⁸⁾,F̃⁽²⁴⁾),

    		(10)

    where G̃ denotes the refined geometric predictions produced by the native dense and camera heads.

一句话：流式 3D 重建要在有限显存下保住几何，但固定分辨率的空间 KV 缓存会随场景扩张而增长。

要点：

  • 矛盾：流式 3D 重建必须在**有限显存**下保持几何质量，而原有 STAC 的**固定分辨率空间 KV 缓存会随场景扩张而增长**
  • STAC++ 是**即插即用、免训练**的框架，用来压缩并复用长程重建中的空间记忆
  • 核心是 **Adaptive Spatial KV Cache**：把 KV 状态组织成**八叉树**，在不同区域与不同层上使用自适应分辨率；再配合响应感知的缓存压缩策略

为什么值得看：八叉树正是稀疏体素与空间索引里的标准结构，用它组织 KV 缓存等于把「图形学的空间层次」搬进 transformer 记忆。这比均匀降低分辨率聪明得多——对任何长序列、大场景的流式重建都适用。

中文摘要：流式三维重建必须在有限显存下维持几何质量，而此前的 STAC 采用固定分辨率的空间键值（KV）缓存，会随场景扩张而持续增长。STAC++ 因此提出一个即插即用、免训练的框架，用来压缩并复用长程重建中的空间记忆：其核心是自适应空间 KV 缓存（ASKC），把 KV 状态组织成一棵八叉树，在不同区域、不同网络层上采用自适应分辨率；再配合响应感知的缓存压缩策略来控制开销。本质上，这是把图形学里成熟的空间层次结构引入 transformer 的记忆组织，比均匀降采样更贴合「大场景、局部精细」的实际需求。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-25

本期推送：2026-11-26

STAC++: Plug-and-Play Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Aware Cache Compression for Streaming 3D Reconstruction

Abstract

Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve geometry under limited memory, yet STAC’s fixed-resolution spatial key–value (KV) cache grows as scenes expand. We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that compresses and reuses spatial memory for long-term reconstruction in unbounded scenes. Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes KV states into an octree with adaptive resolutions across regions and layers. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by measuring attention-output changes, balancing storage savings with geometric preservation. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) reuses cached intermediate features and recomputes only a short backbone suffix to refine historical predictions with later observations. Integrated into four pretrained streaming backbones, STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on long sequences and large scenes, with further quality gains from refinement at limited computational overhead. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

1 Introduction

3D reconstruction is a fundamental problem in computer vision and computer graphics, with a wide range of applications including robotic mapping [44], augmented reality [28], and novel-view synthesis [26, 16]. Traditional image-based 3D reconstruction combines Structure-from-Motion (SfM) [30] for camera estimation and sparse structure recovery with Multi-View Stereo (MVS) [31] for dense geometry. These pipelines rely on explicit correspondence matching and iterative geometric optimization. Recent feed-forward geometric models instead infer scene geometry directly from images using pretrained networks, reducing reliance on scene-specific iterative optimization and improving reconstruction efficiency.

Feed-forward reconstruction methods can be broadly categorized into offline methods that process a fixed image collection and online methods that process incoming images sequentially. Offline methods include DUSt3R [42], which predicts pairwise pointmaps followed by global alignment, and VGGT [38], which jointly predicts cameras and dense geometry from multiple views. However, their computational and memory costs limit scalability to long sequences. Online methods [17, 54, 49, 5] instead reuse historical representations to reconstruct incoming frames incrementally. StreamVGGT [54] adapts VGGT to streaming inference through causal attention and cached historical key–value (KV) states, but its cache grows with sequence length. InfiniteVGGT [49] controls this growth with a bounded rolling cache and diversity-aware token pruning, enabling long-sequence inference within a fixed memory budget. However, these methods do not explicitly exploit 3D spatial information in KV-cache management. STAC [41] introduces a spatial KV cache that merges historical tokens into voxel-aligned representatives, reducing spatial redundancy while preserving geometric evidence. However, its fixed-resolution grid allows the number of occupied voxels to grow with scene extent, so long streams exploring unbounded environments can still exhaust GPU memory. Uniform voxel coarsening saves memory but risks losing fine geometric detail in complex regions.

STAC uses spatial memory to reconstruct incoming frames, yet earlier predictions remain fixed even when later views reveal the same surfaces more clearly. These limitations motivate our central question: How can we adaptively compress and actively reuse spatial KV memory to support long-term reconstruction of unbounded scenes, while preserving geometric detail and refining earlier predictions under limited memory and computational budgets? Answering this question poses two challenges. (1) Handling unbounded scenes requires spatial representations that accommodate continually expanding scene coverage while controlling cache growth and preserving geometric detail. (2) Operating within a bounded memory budget requires retaining informative historical evidence and efficiently reusing it to refine earlier predictions with later observations, without replaying the entire backbone.

To address these challenges, we propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that controls spatial memory growth and efficiently reuses historical evidence for long-term streaming reconstruction in unbounded scenes (see Fig. 1). Firstly, Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes spatial KV states into an octree hierarchy with different resolutions across scene regions and transformer layers. This hierarchy supports merging fine-grained cells into coarser representations as the scene expands. Secondly, Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by evaluating how candidate merges change the backbone’s attention outputs (hereafter referred to as responses). It identifies spatial representations that can be consolidated with limited response changes, balancing memory savings against geometric information preservation. Finally, Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) revisits historical frames after a fixed delay, using later observations and accumulated spatial memory to refine earlier predictions. By reusing cached intermediate features and recomputing only a short backbone suffix, TCR creates additional opportunities to exploit spatial memory while limiting the computation required for refinement. We implement STAC++ as an inference-time plugin for STream3R [17], StreamVGGT [54], InfiniteVGGT [49], and LingBot-Map [5], preserving their pretrained weights without additional training. Experiments across these four backbones demonstrate that STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality, scales to long sequences and large scenes, and further improves reconstruction quality through delayed suffix refinement with limited computational overhead.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that unifies adaptive spatial memory compression and historical evidence reuse for long-term streaming reconstruction in unbounded scenes without modifying pretrained backbone weights.

  • •

    We develop ASKC, RACC, and TCR for hierarchical spatial KV caching, response-guided merging, and suffix refinement of historical predictions, controlling memory and computation while preserving geometry.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Offline Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction

    DUSt3R [42] predicts pairwise pointmaps with global alignment; MASt3R [18] adds learned matching features. VGGT, Fast3R, and MUSt3R [38, 48, 3] extend prediction to multiple views, while FLARE [51] jointly recovers geometry, appearance, and cameras. π³[43] removes reference-view dependence through permutation equivariance, and VGGT-Ω[39] scales geometric learning with efficient register attention. Dense cross-view interaction nevertheless remains costly as the image collection grows.

    For scalability, MERG3R [8] partitions and aligns image subsets, while LiteVGGT [34] merges geometrically redundant tokens and reuses merge decisions across layers. VGG-T3, ZipMap, and Scal3R [11, 14, 47] compress context into test-time-trained states, using fast weights or synchronized adaptive memory to retain information across image chunks; Test3R [50] adapts reconstruction models at test time. These approaches address offline scalability or adaptation rather than adaptive causal KV storage. Octree-GS [29] provides hierarchical spatial detail for Gaussian rendering; our hierarchy instead compresses transformer KV memory for subsequent streaming inference.

    2.2 Online Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction

    Spann3R [37] queries external spatial memory to predict globally aligned pointmaps, CUT3R [40] maintains a recurrent scene state, and Point3R [45] introduces explicit spatial pointer memory. TTT3R [6] uses confidence-guided updates, while FILT3R [15] applies uncertainty-adaptive Kalman-style state updates without retraining. SLAM3R [22] learns local reconstruction and registration; MASt3R-SLAM and multi-agent MAGiSt3R [27, 12] additionally use geometric optimization. LASER [10] enables training-free streaming through layer-wise depth-scale alignment across windows. STream3R and StreamVGGT [17, 54] use causal KV caching; LongStream [7] adds cache-aware training and refresh, while LingBot-Map [5] separates anchor, local, and trajectory context for stable long-sequence reconstruction.

    Growing caches motivate selective retention. In language models, H2O [53], StreamingLLM [46], and SnapKV [19] retain attention-heavy tokens, attention sinks, or head-specific evidence. For geometry, InfiniteVGGT [49] uses diversity-aware pruning; OVGGT [23] protects anchors during residual-guided selection; RegVGGT [24] regulates incoming tokens. GHOST [4] performs geometry-guided eviction, whereas RetrieveVGGT [55] retrieves context through query–key similarity and poses. Selection reduces cache growth but can discard useful geometric evidence; spatial aggregation offers a complementary way to retain information from repeated observations. Slot3R [52] avoids prematurely fusing complementary views by preserving multiple states per spatial address, and SURE-Map [21] uses cross-view uncertainty for local correction and periodic keyframe-window inference for consistent geometry.

    Most closely related to our work, STAC [41] combines temporal token retention with spatial KV fusion on a fixed-resolution voxel grid, enabling historical reuse without retraining the backbone. We extend this design with adaptive spatial resolution and response-guided KV merging to control memory growth, and selective suffix refinement to improve earlier predictions using retained evidence.

    3 Preliminaries

    3.1 Causal Attention

    Causal attention enables streaming reconstruction by restricting each frame to information from the current and preceding frames, as adopted in STream3R [17] and StreamVGGT [54]. Let Fₜ denote the encoded features of frame t and Gₜ its geometric predictions. For a sequence of T frames, this process can be summarized as

    {Gₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ=Decoder (TemporalSelfAttn ({Fₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ)),

    		(1)

    where TemporalSelfAttn applies a causal mask so that frame t attends only to frames 1,…,t, and Decoder maps the attended features to per-frame geometric predictions. During streaming inference, historical keys and values are cached and reused without reprocessing preceding frames. Retaining the full KV history, however, makes cache storage grow linearly with sequence length.

    3.2 Spatio-Temporal KV Caching

    STAC [41] maintains complementary temporal and spatial KV caches. The temporal cache Mₜᵗᵉᵐᵖ retains first-frame references, recent frames and anchors. The spatial cache organizes temporally evicted patch tokens into voxels of side length δ according to their predicted 3D positions. Retrieval from this cache provides the spatial context Mₜˢᵖᵃᵗ.

    Spatial cache. Each voxel u stores up to P KV representatives Gᵤ and B buffered tokens 𝔼ᵤ, consolidating tokens through aggregation when capacity is reached. Representatives maintain fusion weights Wᵢ, importance scores Sᵢ, and represented-token counts Cᵢ, while buffered tokens retain importance scores and contribute only through aggregation. At frame t, retrieval searches the occupied voxels ℕₜ within neighborhoods extending two voxel steps (2δ) in both directions along each axis around voxels containing the preceding frame’s predicted 3D points. The spatial context is formed by selecting at most R representatives per attention head with the largest fusion weights:

    Mₜˢᵖᵃᵗ=Top_R^W (\bigcup_u∈ℕₜGᵤ).

    		(2)

    The retrieved spatial states, temporal cache, and current-frame KV Mₜᶜᵘʳ form the attention context ℂₜ=Mₜᵗᵉᵐᵖ∪Mₜˢᵖᵃᵗ∪Mₜᶜᵘʳ. This work focuses on the spatial cache.

    4 Method

    We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework for controlling spatial KV memory growth and reusing historical evidence in streaming 3D reconstruction. STAC++ combines three modules (Fig. 2). Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes historical states at multiple spatial resolutions. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) determines which states can be merged by measuring their effect on attention outputs. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) revisits historical frames after a delay, reusing cached intermediate features and recomputing a short backbone suffix to incorporate later observations. All three modules operate during inference and preserve the pretrained backbone weights.

    4.1 Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC)

    In unbounded scenes, fixed-resolution spatial caches grow with scene coverage and retain redundancy across neighboring voxels. Uniform coarsening saves storage but may discard locally distinct geometric evidence. ASKC instead organizes spatial KV states in an expanding octree, selectively merging neighboring fine-grained cells into coarser parents independently across layers while retaining finer representations where detailed evidence remains necessary.

    Layer-wise modeling. For a backbone with L global-attention layers, layer ℓ maintains octree Tₜ^(ℓ) at time t, with finest cell side length δ (Sec. 3.2). Layers share the same subdivision rule but merge independently, allowing each layer to use a different spatial resolution for the same scene region. All H heads in a layer share cells but store separate KV states. We denote the layer’s token inputs by Xₜ^(ℓ). Temporally evicted patch tokens enter cells containing their predicted 3D positions, including parents formed by earlier merges. We repeatedly double the shared root’s side length toward an out-of-bounds point until it is enclosed, retaining the old root as a child at each expansion step.

    Within-cell storage. Each cell u in layer ℓ and head h stores up to P representatives G_u,ℓ,h and B buffered tokens 𝔼_u,ℓ,h.     mⱼ←Wⱼmⱼ+ωᵢⱼmᵢ/Wⱼ+ωᵢⱼ,

    		(3)

    where ωᵢⱼ=Wᵢ\exp(\cos(kᵢ,kⱼ)-1). We update Wⱼ←Wⱼ+ωᵢⱼ, Cⱼ←Cⱼ+Cᵢ, and Sⱼ←Sⱼ+Sᵢ. An incoming token sufficiently similar to a representative uses the same update with ωᵢⱼ=\exp(\cos(kᵢ,kⱼ)) and Cᵢ=1. Sufficiently dissimilar tokens passing the importance threshold enter the buffer. When full, its highest-scoring token seeds aggregation of all entries into a new representative using exponential cosine-similarity weights.

    Spatial retrieval. Let Ωₜ be the lookup neighborhoods of the preceding frame’s predicted 3D points, expanded by 2δ (Sec. 3.2), and ℕₜ^(ℓ) all active cells whose extents intersect Ωₜ, including merged parents. For head h, Eq. 2 with ℕₜ^(ℓ) and G_u,ℓ,h replacing ℕₜ and Gᵤ, respectively, yields M_t,ℓ,hˢᵖᵃᵗ under the same per-head budget R.

    Hierarchical coarsening. For each layer, an inactive parent is structurally eligible for merging if it has one to eight active direct children and no KV in its grandchildren or deeper descendants. Their consolidation into the parent is a parent proposal requiring RACC acceptance (Sec. 4.2).

    4.2 Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC)

    Merging spatially adjacent states saves memory but can alter the geometric evidence available to the backbone. A straightforward approach is to explicitly compute the attention responses before and after a candidate merge p and take their difference:

    Δo_p,ℓ,h=Att(q̂_ℓ,h,ℂ_p,ℓ,h)-Att(q̂_ℓ,h,ℂ_ℓ,h),

    		(4)

    where Att(·) denotes attention, q̂_ℓ,h is the shared query, and ℂ_ℓ,h and ℂ_p,ℓ,h are the contexts before and after the merge. The corresponding responses are denoted by o_ℓ,h and o_p,ℓ,h, respectively. However, directly evaluating this change for every candidate merge requires repeating query–key scoring, softmax normalization, and value aggregation over the full context, making evaluation costly. We therefore sample a small set of queries and compute response changes incrementally, reusing the reference response and normalizer while updating only the contributions of KV entries affected by each merge. RACC balances response preservation against storage savings.

    Merge scheduling. For merge keyframes spaced M frames apart, we retain Ω_t-M and full inputs X_t-M^(ℓ) to each global-attention layer. After keyframe t completes inference, we sample queries from these inputs at all special-token positions and a uniform 4×4 patch grid to evaluate eligible parents in Ω_t-M. This delay allows intervening frames to use the finer spatial representation before coarsening. Pending keyframes use the available context at sequence end.

    Parent proposal construction. At each layer ℓ, consider an eligible parent U in Ω_t-M with child positions uᵢ (i=1,…,8; empty branches give empty sets), omitting t-M below. Head h retains up to B buffered entries with highest importance from \bigcupᵢ₌₁⁸𝔼_uᵢ,ℓ,h in 𝔼_U,ℓ,h. Child representatives form G_U,ℓ,h unchanged when ∑ᵢ₌₁⁸|G_uᵢ,ℓ,h|≤P; otherwise, we repeatedly apply the representative re-merging rule in Sec. 4.1 using Eq. 3 until P remain.     ΔN_p,ℓ,h=∑ᵢ₌₁⁸(|G_uᵢ,ℓ,h|+|𝔼_uᵢ,ℓ,h|)(5)
    -|G_U,ℓ,h|-|𝔼_U,ℓ,h|.

    Summing over heads gives ΔN_p,ℓ=∑ₕ₌₁^HΔN_p,ℓ,h.

    Response change evaluation. For sampled q̂_ℓ,h, compute o_ℓ,h=Att(q̂_ℓ,h,ℂ_ℓ,h) over ℂ_ℓ,h=M_ℓ,hᵗᵉᵐᵖ∪M_ℓ,hˢᵖᵃᵗ∪M_ℓ,hᶜᵘʳ (time omitted).     Δo_p,ℓ,h=(∑_i∈Aₚαᵢ(vᵢ-o_ℓ,h)-∑_i∈ℝₚαᵢ(vᵢ-o_ℓ,h))/(1+∑_i∈Aₚαᵢ-∑_i∈ℝₚαᵢ).

    		(6)

    Equation 6 is exact for the fixed query and specified substitution [25, 9]; only ℝₚ and Aₚ require new scores and value accumulations. Unchanged contributions are reused through o_ℓ,h and Λ_ℓ,h. Stacking reference responses and changes over sampled queries yields O_ℓ,h and ΔO_p,ℓ,h.

    Merge acceptance. We average normalized response changes across heads:

    E_p,ℓ=1/H∑ₕ₌₁^H(\lVertΔO_p,ℓ,h\rVert_F)/(\max(\lVertO_ℓ,h\rVert_F,εₘ)),

    		(7)

    with εₘ=10⁻⁸ for stability. We accept p when

    E_p,ℓ≤τₘ+λ(ΔN_p,ℓ)/(H(P+B)).

    		(8)

    Here τₘ sets the baseline tolerance and λ weights storage savings. Each layer makes an independent decision shared across all heads; acceptance replaces child storage cells with their parent.

    4.3 Temporal Context Refinement (TCR)

    During causal streaming inference, each frame is reconstructed using only the observations available when it arrives. Later frames may provide complementary viewpoints and additional geometric evidence for previously observed regions, enriching the spatial cache. However, this updated memory benefits subsequent inference without automatically revising earlier predictions, which remain tied to their original, more limited context. The most direct approach is to reprocess historical frames through the entire backbone using the updated context. However, this repeats substantial feature computation. We therefore introduce TCR to refine historical predictions after a fixed delay using the updated temporal and spatial context. TCR retains intermediate features during initial inference and recomputes only a short backbone suffix, allowing earlier frames to reuse later observations while limiting the additional computation.

    Refinement scheduling. During initial inference, we retain each frame’s decoder features from layers 5 and 12, the intermediate input needed for suffix recomputation, and its spatial lookup region. After a delay of D frames, we revisit the historical frame once using the updated context. The refinement delay is independent of the merge interval, and merge keyframes share their retained inputs with RACC.

    Refinement process. At time t, we refine frame t-D by resuming from its retained intermediate features. At each recomputed attention layer, queries from this revisited frame attend to the current temporal cache, spatial states retrieved within its saved lookup region, and keys and values recomputed from the same frame’s features at that layer. Let X denote the retained intermediate input and ℂ the updated context. Recomputing layers 18–24 gives

    (F̃⁽¹⁸⁾,F̃⁽²⁴⁾)=Suffix_18:24(X,ℂ),

    		(9)

    where Suffix_18:24 denotes recomputation of backbone layers 18–24 from the retained input X using the updated context ℂ, returning the features at layers 18 and 24. Here F^(ℓ) denotes the feature at layer ℓ, tildes mark refinement, and the frame index is omitted. The decoder combines the cached features from layers 5 and 12 with the updated features from layers 18 and 24:

    G̃=Decoder (F⁽⁵⁾,F⁽¹²⁾,F̃⁽¹⁸⁾,F̃⁽²⁴⁾),

    		(10)

    where G̃ denotes the refined geometric predictions produced by the native dense and camera heads.
